items.q: A task you have done by hand appears for the third time this month. What actually happens?
items.layman: When a repeat chore shows up again and again, do you keep doing it manually, or does a system now handle it? “Agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Loop” = a setup where the work runs, gets checked, and improves on its own.

opts.t: I do it by hand again.
I have a saved template or prompt that speeds it up.
An agent does it; I review each run.
A loop runs it, verifies its own output, and only escalates exceptions.

items.q: If you disappeared for two weeks, how much of your output would continue?
items.layman: If you went completely off-grid, would any of your work still get produced and delivered without you touching a keyboard?

opts.t: None. Everything routes through me, live.
Scheduled posts and canned automations only.
Agents continue routine production; queues wait for my review.
Production, verification, and memory updates continue. I return to a briefing, not a backlog.

items.q: What decides what you work on each morning?
items.layman: Is your day driven by whoever emails loudest, or does a system prepare a ranked agenda for you before you start?

opts.t: Whatever is loudest — inbox, messages, the latest fire.
A to-do list I maintain by hand.
A prioritized queue assembled from my own systems.
A generated briefing: exceptions, verdicts due, and opportunities, ranked before I sit down.

items.q: A new opportunity arrives — a client, a project, a collaboration. How is it evaluated?
items.layman: Do you decide new offers by gut feel in the moment, or do you have written rules — even automated checks — for what you say yes to?

opts.t: Gut feel, in the moment.
I sleep on it and decide by instinct.
Against written criteria: thesis fit, rate floor, time cost.
Scored by my system against captured doctrine before it even reaches me.

items.q: You realize mid-afternoon that you have written nearly the same email three times this week. What do you do with that observation?
items.layman: When you notice repetition in your own work, does anything change — a saved draft, a template — or do you keep typing it fresh each time?

opts.t: Nothing. I keep writing each one fresh.
I copy an old sent email and edit it, when I remember to.
I save it as a template or snippet and reuse it deliberately.
I keep a library of templates and prompts; noticing repetition triggers adding one.

items.q: It is the last day of the month and three invoices need to go out. How do they get made?
items.layman: When routine paperwork comes due, do you rebuild it every time, or has the repeatable part been saved somewhere — a template you fill in rather than a page you start from zero?

opts.t: I open a blank document and build each one from scratch.
I duplicate last month’s invoice and change the numbers by hand.
I fill in a saved invoice template; only the details change.
Templates exist for every recurring document I send — invoices were just the first.

items.q: You want to stay current on developments in your field. What does “staying current” actually look like this week?
items.layman: Do you go hunting for news in your field from memory, or have you set up saved searches, newsletters, or feeds so the information arrives on its own?

opts.t: I browse around when I remember, wherever the feed takes me.
I keep a mental list of sites and check them when I think of it.
Saved searches, subscriptions, or feeds bring the sources to me.
Every topic I track has its saved search or feed; a new interest gets one the day it appears.

items.q: Someone asks for thirty minutes of your time next week. How does the meeting get booked?
items.layman: A “booking link” is a page (Calendly and similar) where people pick directly from your open slots. When someone wants a meeting, do you negotiate times by email or hand them the link?

opts.t: A back-and-forth of emails until a slot survives.
I glance at my calendar and paste a few free slots into a reply.
I send a booking link; they pick a slot that already respects my rules.
The booking link is the default everywhere my time is requested — signature, profile, replies.

items.q: You sit down to write a post for the platform you publish on. Where do you start?
items.layman: A “prompt” here is a saved instruction you reuse with an AI. When you write for social media, do you begin from nothing, or from something you deliberately saved to begin from?

opts.t: A blank box, every time.
I scroll my old posts for one to imitate.
I start from a saved format or prompt that captures my structure and voice.
A small library of formats and prompts — one for each kind of post I make.

items.q: A new client signs. The first week involves the same dozen small steps it always does. How do you keep track of them?
items.layman: When a repeating occasion arrives — a new client, a launch — do you work from memory, or from a saved checklist you made the last time it happened?

opts.t: In my head. I usually remember most of them.
I scroll the last client’s emails to reconstruct what I did.
A saved onboarding checklist I copy for each new client.
Checklists exist for every recurring occasion; finishing something without one is my cue to write it.

items.q: A collaborator you are onboarding asks what setup you give the AI before it writes for you. What can you actually hand over?
items.layman: A “prompt” = the instructions you give an AI before it works — tone, format, context. If someone needed your exact AI setup, does it exist as a thing you can send, or only as a habit in your fingers?

opts.t: Nothing. The setup lives in my head; I improvise it each session.
I dig through old chats and copy out what I typed last time.
I send the saved prompt or snippet I use myself.
I share the relevant piece of my prompt library — organized, current, and written to be handed over.

items.q: It is time to look at last month’s money. What does the ritual involve?
items.layman: For your monthly look at income and spending, do you improvise with whatever is at hand, or does a reusable structure — a spreadsheet, a tool — already exist and simply get updated?

opts.t: Logging into accounts one by one and eyeballing the numbers.
I dig up whatever spreadsheet I used last time and adapt it.
A standing spreadsheet or tool I built once; each month I fill in the new column.
The structure is fixed and reused everywhere — finances were just one of the rituals I templated.

items.q: You are about to push an update to something live — a site, a product, a system. Where do the steps live?
items.layman: A “runbook” is a written list of the exact steps for a technical routine. A “snippet” = a small saved piece of text or command. When you ship changes to something live, are the steps written down or recalled?

opts.t: In my head. I have done it enough times.
In an old chat or note I search for whenever it is time.
In a written runbook or saved command snippets I follow deliberately.
Every risky routine has its runbook; performing one from memory is treated as an error.

items.q: A piece you wrote did well, and you want a version for a different channel. How does the second version get made?
items.layman: “Repurposing” means turning one piece of content into another format — a post into a thread, an article into an email. A “prompt” = a saved AI instruction. Do you improvise that conversion each time, or has the recipe been saved?

opts.t: I rewrite it from scratch for the new channel.
I paste the original into an AI and improvise instructions on the spot.
I run it through a saved prompt built for exactly this conversion.
Saved conversion prompts exist for every channel pair I actually use.

items.q: Your newsletter goes out every week. How does an issue actually come into being?
items.layman: Is producing your newsletter a repeatable procedure with known steps, or a fresh improvisation assisted by whatever tools are lying around? “Versioned” = the procedure itself is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Differently every week. I open the editor and see what happens.
I have templates and prompts I reach for, in whatever order feels right.
A defined sequence — collect, draft, edit, schedule — with the same inputs and outputs every week.
The sequence is written down and versioned, and an issue ships only after passing its checklist.

items.q: A client’s monthly report is due — the same report you delivered last month and the month before. How does this month’s get produced?
items.layman: For work you deliver on a schedule, is there a written recipe you follow every time — defined inputs, steps, and result — or do you re-derive the path each month? “Versioned” = saved with a history of changes. “Acceptance checklist” = the written test the finished work must pass.

opts.t: I reconstruct the process from memory and last month’s file.
Pieces are templated — the shell, some prompts — but I improvise the path between them.
One documented procedure, start to finish: what goes in, what comes out, in what order.
The procedure is versioned, and the report passes a written acceptance checklist before the client sees it.

items.q: An email arrives from a stranger who might become a client. What determines what happens next?
items.layman: “Intake” = the process of sorting and handling new inquiries. When a potential client appears, does a standard procedure kick in, or does each one get improvised treatment? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: My mood and my inbox. Each inquiry gets handled its own way.
I have reply templates, but when and how I use them varies.
A defined intake path: every inquiry gets the same qualifying questions, the same next steps.
The path is documented and versioned, with written criteria for who advances and who gets a polite no.

items.q: Between “the work is done” and “the money is requested” there is a chain of small steps. Could you say them out loud, in order?
items.layman: Finishing work and getting paid are connected by small steps — logging time, drafting the invoice, sending, recording. Is that chain a defined routine or a monthly improvisation? “Versioned” = the routine is saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: Not really. Billing happens when I remember, however it happens.
I use the same invoice template, but the surrounding steps shift each time.
A fixed billing routine: same trigger, same steps, same records updated, every cycle.
The routine is written and versioned, with a checklist that catches missed line items before anything sends.

items.q: You have gathered a week of interesting links and notes. How do they become something useful instead of a pile?
items.layman: When you collect research — links, notes, articles — is there a standard procedure that turns the pile into a usable summary, or does the pile simply grow? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: Mostly they stay a pile. I revisit them when guilt strikes.
I summarize with AI now and then, differently each time.
A repeatable digest process: same sources in, same summary format out, on a schedule.
The process is documented and versioned, and a digest ships only if it meets its own written standard.

items.q: A trusted peer offers to cover one of your recurring tasks for a month. What can you actually hand them?
items.layman: This tests whether your process exists outside your head: if someone competent had to run one of your routines, is there a document that would let them? “Acceptance checklist” = the written test for whether the result is good enough. “Versioned” = saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: A long conversation and my phone number for questions.
Some example outputs and the templates I use.
A written procedure — inputs, steps, outputs — they could follow without calling me.
The procedure plus its acceptance checklist, versioned, so they know both what to do and how to tell they did it right.

items.q: Releasing an update involves a dozen steps, and skipping one has burned you before. What stands between you and skipping one again?
items.layman: For technical routines where a missed step causes damage — shipping updates, going live — is there a written procedure you actually follow, or does safety depend on your focus that day? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: Attention and adrenaline.
Notes from last time, if I can find them.
A written release procedure I follow step by step, every time.
The procedure is versioned, has a pre-flight checklist, and I record each run against it.

items.q: One long piece is supposed to become a thread, an email, and two short clips. How reliably does that fan-out happen?
items.layman: When you turn one piece of content into many — a thread, an email, clips — is there a written, repeatable procedure with the same steps every time, or a hope? “Versioned” = the procedure is documented with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Rarely. Repurposing happens if I find the energy.
I have prompts for some conversions and improvise the rest.
A defined, repeatable procedure I run each time: the long piece goes in, the derivative set comes out.
The procedure is documented and versioned, with a checklist defining what a publishable derivative looks like.

items.q: Halfway through a routine task you discover a genuinely better way to do it. What happens to that discovery?
items.layman: When you improve how you do something, does the improvement get written into a documented procedure — so it persists — or does it live and die in your memory? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of changes, so old and new ways are both on record.

opts.t: I enjoy it today and forget it by next time.
It survives in my head; the task goes faster when I remember.
The written procedure gets updated the same day.
The procedure is versioned, so the change lands with a date and a reason — the old way retrievable, the new way default.

items.q: Friday afternoon is when the small recurring chores get done — filing, follow-ups, bookkeeping entries. What shape does that block have?
items.layman: For the recurring administrative sweep — the little tasks that keep the operation running — is there a defined, repeatable routine, or a vague session that ends when you are tired? “Versioned” = the routine is written down with a history of its changes.

opts.t: No shape. I do whatever chores I remember until the energy runs out.
A rough mental loop, sped up by a few templates.
A named routine with a fixed list: same chores, same order, same done-state, every week.
The routine is written and versioned, and ends with a checklist confirming nothing was skipped.

items.q: It is newsletter day. Before you have touched anything, what already exists?
items.layman: An “agent” is an AI that carries out multi-step work on its own. “Escalated” = passed up to you because it fell outside the rules. On the day a recurring publication is due, has a system already produced the draft — or does production start when you do?

opts.t: Nothing. The issue exists only after I perform every step.
My templates and prompts are ready; the steps still wait for my hands.
A complete draft, assembled end-to-end by an agent, waiting for my review.
The draft sits in my review queue with sources cited; anything odd was already escalated by rule.

items.q: A promising inquiry lands in your inbox at midnight. What has happened to it by the time you wake up?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Qualified” = checked against your criteria for a good client. “Escalated” = flagged for you because it fell outside the rules. Overnight, does inbound interest get worked, or just get older?

opts.t: Nothing. It waits, unread, for me.
An auto-responder acknowledged it. The real handling waits for me.
An agent has qualified it, drafted a tailored reply, and queued both for my approval.
Routine inquiries were answered outright by rule; only the unusual one waits — flagged with why it was escalated.

items.q: How does news in your field reach you — and how much of the reading do you personally do?
items.layman: The question is who does the reading. Do you scan raw sources yourself, or does an AI agent — software that works through multi-step tasks alone — read them end-to-end and hand you a short distilled brief of what matters? “Escalate” = urgent items jump the schedule to reach you at once.

opts.t: I go looking when I have time, and read everything myself.
Feeds and alerts collect sources for me; I still read and sort the pile.
An agent reads the pile and delivers a distilled brief; I review the brief, not the sources.
Briefs arrive on schedule, urgent items escalate immediately, and each brief links its sources for spot-checking.

items.q: Billing day arrives. What is your role in getting invoices out the door?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Approval-by-exception” = routine cases proceed automatically and only unusual ones stop for you. On billing day, are you the machine, or the machine’s reviewer?

opts.t: I am the whole process — gather, draft, send, record.
Templates and a checklist make it fast, but every step is mine.
An agent assembles the invoices from my records; I approve each batch before it sends.
Standard invoices go out on approval-by-exception; only anomalies — odd amounts, new clients — wait for my eyes.

items.q: Your publishing cadence says something goes out today. Who moves it from idea to posted?
items.layman: “Cadence” = your regular publishing rhythm. “Queue” = the lineup of scheduled posts. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Escalate” = flag for your attention by rule. Does keeping the rhythm require your hands every day, or your judgment at review time?

opts.t: I do — write, format, schedule, post, each time.
I batch-write with saved prompts; posting still runs through my hands.
An agent drafts and schedules the queue; I review before anything goes live.
The queue self-fills on schedule; posts outside my usual topics or tone escalate, the rest I clear in one weekly sitting.

items.q: You finish a substantial piece of work. Who makes the derivative versions — the thread, the email, the clips?
items.layman: “Derivatives” = smaller pieces cut from one large piece of content. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. When the big piece is done, does the fan-out happen without your labor — with you checking results rather than producing them?

opts.t: Me, on the rare occasion they get made at all.
Me, faster, running each saved prompt by hand.
An agent produces the full derivative set unprompted; I review before release.
The set arrives scored against my style rules; weak derivatives are flagged for rewrite, strong ones queue for one-click release.

items.q: A routine release is due — the kind you have shipped fifty times. How much of it runs without your keystrokes?
items.layman: A “pipeline” = an automated chain of technical steps. “Green checks” = automated tests passing. “Pages me” = sends me an urgent alert. For releases you have done many times, are you the executor or the authority the system reports to?

opts.t: None of it. I perform every step, even the ones I could recite asleep.
Scripts handle fragments; I run and babysit each one in order.
The pipeline runs end-to-end; I review the result and give the final go.
Releases proceed on green checks; the pipeline halts and pages me only when a check fails.

items.q: A month of transactions needs sorting before you can see how the business is doing. Who sorts them?
items.layman: “Categorizing” = labeling each transaction (software, travel, income) so reports mean something. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. Does that labor belong to you, or to an agent whose work you check?

opts.t: I do, line by line, when I finally sit down to it.
Rules in my banking or accounting app catch some; I hand-sort the rest.
An agent categorizes the month and drafts the summary; I review and correct.
The books stay current continuously; a scheduled review queue holds only the transactions the agent was unsure about.

items.q: For the third week running, you fix the same stiff phrasing in your newsletter agent’s draft. What does the third fix change?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Written back” = saved into the durable memory the system actually reads on its next run. “Verdict” = your ruling on an output plus the reason. When you correct AI work, does the correction outlive the moment?

opts.t: The draft. Next week I will fix it a fourth time.
I keep meaning to note it somewhere; the note exists, loosely.
The correction goes into the instructions the agent reads before every draft — week four arrives clean.
My edit is logged as a verdict — rewrite, with reason — written back to memory, and I would be alerted if the write failed.

items.q: Your triage agent scored a lead as low-priority; it turned out to be your best client this year. Where does that lesson end up?
items.layman: A “triage agent” = the AI that sorts and scores incoming inquiries. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling plus the reason. When it misjudges and you catch it, does your correction become part of the system’s memory — the rules it reads next time — or just part of yours?

opts.t: In the war story I tell. The agent scores the next one the same way.
I watch that category more closely myself from then on.
The scoring criteria are updated in the agent’s memory; the miss becomes a rule.
The reversal is recorded as a verdict with reasoning, the write is verified, and similar borderline leads now escalate instead of sinking.

items.q: Compare your review workload today with six months ago, for the same delegated tasks. What has happened to it?
items.layman: “Acceptance rate” = how often you approve an agent’s work unchanged. An “agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. If review is getting lighter, the honest question is why: because the system is learning, or because you are surrendering?

opts.t: There is no review workload — nothing is delegated, or nothing is reviewed.
It shrank because I got tired and stopped looking closely.
It shrank because corrections accumulate — the agents genuinely make fewer of the old mistakes.
Acceptance rates are tracked per task; autonomy expands by measured rule, not by my fatigue.

items.q: One of your overnight loops died quietly three days ago. In your current setup, how do you find out?
items.layman: A “loop” = an automated job that runs on its own schedule. “Verified writes” = the system checks that its results actually landed in permanent storage. Silence from a machine can mean working — or dead. Can you tell which?

opts.t: When a client asks where the thing is.
When I eventually notice its output is missing.
An alert fired the first morning; the failure never got a second day.
The loop verifies its own writes; a missing or malformed result is itself a detected event, alerted with context.

items.q: You have a firm private preference — say, how dates are written in everything you send. How do your agents come to honor it?
items.layman: “Agents” = AIs doing multi-step work for you. “Durable instructions” = a saved rule-set the system reads every run, not a one-off chat message. “Provenance” = the record of where a rule came from and why. Do your standards live in you, or in the system?

opts.t: They don’t. I repair the formatting in every output, forever.
I mention it in prompts when I remember to.
It is written once into the durable instructions every agent reads; new agents inherit it on day one.
It lives in memory with provenance — when and why it was set — and a check flags any output that violates it.

items.q: An agent’s output quality erodes slowly — a little blander each week, never failing outright. What catches the slide?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. “Verdict logs” = the recorded history of your accept/reject/rewrite rulings on its work. “Acceptance rate” = how often you approve unchanged. Gradual decay is invisible from inside a single day; only memory across runs can see a slope.

opts.t: Nothing, until the day it embarrasses me publicly.
My mood. Some weeks I read closely and wince.
Scheduled reviews with notes I fold back into its instructions; the slide gets corrected in batches.
Verdict logs make the trend visible — my acceptance rate for that agent is charted, and a drop alerts me before I would have felt it.

items.q: You hand an agent a chore it has never done. What is the path between its first attempt and you barely checking anymore?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. The question is how it earns autonomy. “Acceptance-rate threshold” = a preset bar (say, 95% of outputs approved unchanged) that must be cleared before review loosens.

opts.t: There is no path. Either I keep doing the chore myself or I stop watching and hope.
I re-explain the task each run until the explanations get shorter.
Each review adds corrections to its instructions; trust grows because its memory does.
Graduation is defined — a written acceptance-rate threshold moves it from full review to spot-checks, enforced by the system, not my whim.

items.q: Last month your bookkeeping agent filed a client refund as revenue and you caught it. Another refund has just arrived. What happens?
items.layman: A “bookkeeping agent” = an AI that maintains your financial records. “Miscategorization” = a transaction labeled wrongly in the books. The test of a correction is the next occurrence: does the system remember what you taught it, or only you?

opts.t: The same miscategorization. I catch it again, or I don’t.
I remember refunds are a weak spot and check them by hand.
It is filed correctly — last month’s correction became a rule the agent reads.
Filed correctly, and the rule’s application is itself checked: if a refund ever skips it, I get an alert, not a surprise at tax time.

items.q: The platform hosting your agents announces it is shutting down in thirty days. What do those thirty days look like?
items.layman: “Agents” = AIs doing multi-step work for you. “Stack” = the set of tools and services your system runs on. “Tool-independent” = described so any equivalent tool could implement it. “Config” = a settings change rather than a rebuild. If your automation vendor vanished, would your operation vanish with it?

opts.t: Grief, then rebuilding my working life from scratch.
Frantic exporting of whatever the platform deigns to give me, then months of reconstruction.
Busy but calm: workflows are documented tool-independently and memory is already exported — rebuilding is execution, not archaeology.
Mostly a formality. I have rehearsed this on a second stack; the shutdown changes a config, not an operation.

items.q: Where do your system’s standing instructions — every agent’s rules, prompts, and criteria — actually live?
items.layman: “Doctrine” = your accumulated written rules for how work is done. “Version control” = software that tracks every change with history. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Provenance” = each rule records where it came from. Do your rules belong to you, or to your vendors’ databases?

opts.t: Inside each tool’s settings screens, wherever I typed them.
Scattered: some in tools, some pasted into a notes app, versions disagreeing.
In plain-text files I own, under version control; the tools are fed from there.
One canonical doctrine source in an open format, with provenance per rule — every agent on any stack reads from it.

items.q: A model twice as good at half the price ships tomorrow. What does moving your loops onto it involve?
items.layman: A “model” = the underlying AI engine. A “loop” = an automated job that runs, gets checked, and improves on its own. An “eval suite” = your saved battery of test tasks that scores any model on your actual work. Is the intelligence in your system a swappable part, or a load-bearing wall?

opts.t: Nothing moves. My automations only exist inside one provider’s product.
Rebuilding each automation by hand around the new model’s quirks.
Changing a configuration value — the loops treat models as interchangeable parts.
Running my eval suite against both models and switching on the evidence, the same afternoon.

items.q: A fresh agent on an entirely different stack needs to inherit everything your current agents have learned — every correction, preference, and rule. Can it?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. “Stack” = the set of tools it runs on. “Proprietary store” = data kept in a format only one vendor’s tools can read. “Portable substrate” = plain, open files any tool can read. Is your system’s accumulated learning transferable, or hostage?

opts.t: There is nothing to inherit; the learning lives in old chats and in me.
The memory exists but in one vendor’s proprietary store; extraction would be lossy.
Memory is exported regularly to open formats a new stack could ingest.
Memory lives natively in a portable substrate — the new agent queries the same files the old ones did, and starts smart.

items.q: Who noticed the last pattern in your own judgments — the rule you kept applying without ever having written it down?
items.layman: “Verdict logs” = the saved record of your accept/reject/rewrite rulings and their reasons. “Doctrine” = your written rulebook. “Ratified” = you approved the machine’s proposal. A mature system does not just follow the rulebook — it helps write it.

opts.t: No one. My judgments leave no record to find patterns in.
I did, eventually, after the pattern had cost me something.
I did, during a scheduled review of my verdict logs — and wrote the rule down that day.
The system did: it mined my verdicts, proposed the rule with citations to the judgments behind it, and I ratified it.

items.q: When did you last actually test restoring your operation from your own exports — not export the data, restore from it?
items.layman: An untested backup is a hope, not a plan. A “restore drill” = deliberately rebuilding your system from saved data to prove the saves are sufficient. “Second stack” = a different set of tools than your usual. “Loop” = a scheduled automated job. Have your exports ever been asked to do their job?

opts.t: Never. There are no exports to test.
Never. Exports accumulate, untested, like fire extinguishers no one has squeezed.
Once, deliberately: I rebuilt a core workflow from exports alone and fixed what the drill exposed.
On a schedule. The rebuild is rehearsed on a second stack, and the drill itself is one of the loops.

items.q: A genuinely impressive new automation platform launches. By what process does it enter — or fail to enter — your stack?
items.layman: “Stack” = the set of tools your system runs on. The trap with each new tool is deepening dependence. “Swappable part” = a component you could replace without rebuilding. “Exit path” = a proven way to leave with your data and workflows intact. Does adoption strengthen your system, or your captivity?

opts.t: Enthusiasm. I start moving work in and adapt to its way of doing things.
I experiment alongside my setup and keep whatever happens to stick.
It is admitted only if it reads and writes my existing formats — my memory does not move into it.
It joins as a swappable part behind my own interfaces, and the exit path is tested before real work depends on it.

items.q: Count the external services your automated operation would not survive losing. Can you actually produce that list?
items.layman: A “dependency map” = a written inventory of every outside service your system needs, ranked by how critical it is. A “fallback” = the substitute you would switch to if one failed. Sovereignty starts with knowing exactly where you are exposed.

opts.t: No. I have never traced what depends on what.
Roughly, from memory — I would discover the real list during an outage.
Yes: a written dependency map, with each service marked by how badly its loss would hurt.
Yes, and every critical entry has a tested fallback — the map itself is reviewed on a schedule.

items.q: An agent makes a costly call, correctly following a rule in its memory — but the rule itself turns out to be wrong. How long until you know where that rule came from?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI acting on your saved rules. “Provenance” = the recorded origin of each rule or memory: what judgment created it, when, and why. A “verdict” = the recorded ruling that judgment produced. When automation acts on remembered rules, you need to be able to audit the rules themselves.

opts.t: Forever. There is no record that rules exist, let alone their origins.
Hours of spelunking through old chats, with no guarantee.
Minutes: rules live in my files with dates and context attached.
Seconds: every entry carries provenance — the source verdict, the date, the reasoning — so a bad rule is traceable and correctable at the root.

items.q: Suppose you stopped improving your system today — no new rules, no new loops, only whatever maintenance it demands. How long does it keep producing value?
items.layman: A “loop” = a scheduled automated job. “Self-verify” = each job checks that its own results landed correctly. “Doctrine still extends” = the rulebook keeps growing from your recorded verdicts — your saved rulings and reasons. The final test of agency: is the system a tool you push, or an institution that runs?

opts.t: It stops when I stop; there is no system apart from my effort.
A few weeks, until the first unhandled breakage quietly ends it.
Months. Loops self-verify, failures alert me, and degradation is graceful rather than sudden.
Indefinitely, and it would keep improving: verdicts still accrue to memory, doctrine still extends, and decay is detected by the system before it is felt by me.

items.q: The same “how do I get access?” question appears in your paid community for the fifth time this month. What happens on the fifth time?
items.layman: When members keep asking the same thing, do you retype the answer each time, or does a saved reply — a pinned post, a stock answer you paste — do the repeating for you?

opts.t: I type the answer out again, from scratch, slightly differently each time.
I hunt down the last time I answered it and copy that reply.
I paste my saved answer, or point to the pinned post that holds it.
Recurring questions get a pinned answer or saved reply as a matter of course — the pins are the community’s front door.

items.q: Tomorrow you run your paid workshop again — same links to send, same slides to stage, same room settings. How do you set it up tonight?
items.layman: For a live session you have run before, do you rebuild the setup from memory each time, or work through a saved list of the exact steps?

opts.t: From memory. I usually catch what I missed once participants are in the room.
I scroll back through last session’s messages and files to reconstruct the setup.
I work through a saved setup checklist — links, slides, settings, reminder — ticking as I go.
Every session type has its checklist, and running one without the list would itself feel like a skipped step.

items.q: Three orders for your hardware kit came in overnight. How does each box get packed and labeled?
items.layman: For a physical product you ship repeatedly, is there a saved packing list and a reusable label setup, or do you reassemble the routine in your head at the workbench?

opts.t: I gather the parts from memory; occasionally a box ships with something missing.
I keep a photo of a correctly packed box and glance at it as I pack.
A printed packing list sits at the bench, and the shipping labels come from a saved template.
Packing list, label template, and customs text are all saved artifacts — every repeat task at the bench has one.

items.q: Another bug report arrives on your open-source project with no version number and no steps to reproduce. What do you send back?
items.layman: An “open-source project” = software you publish for anyone to use, where users file bug reports. An “issue template” = a saved form that asks reporters the standard questions before you ever see the report. Do you retype “what version are you on?” each time, or has that request been saved?

opts.t: A freshly typed request for the missing details, worded anew each time.
I copy my ask from an older bug thread, when I can find one.
A saved reply — or the issue template already asked the standard questions on my behalf.
The template gathers the details up front, and saved replies cover every recurring situation the template misses.

items.q: You are handing this month’s design work to your subcontractor — the same kind of hand-off as every month. How does the brief get written?
items.layman: A “brief” = the written instructions you give someone doing work for you: scope, references, deadline. Do you compose it from a blank message each month, or fill in a saved structure?

opts.t: A blank message; I write the whole arrangement out again and hope I forget nothing.
I dig up last month’s brief and edit it in place, when I remember it exists.
I fill in a saved brief template — scope, references, deadline — so only the specifics change.
Every recurring hand-off has its template, and a hand-off that goes badly gets its template amended the same week.

items.q: It is grocery day again, and the household needs roughly what it needed last week. Where does the shopping list come from?
items.layman: For a chore that repeats weekly, do you rebuild the list in your head each time, or maintain a saved master list you adjust?

opts.t: My head, in the store aisles. Something is forgotten most weeks.
I scribble a fresh list from memory before leaving.
A saved master list I duplicate and adjust — staples preloaded, only the week’s extras change.
The master list is one of many — the household’s recurring chores each have their saved starting point.

items.q: Writing tonight, you need that perfect quote you read last month — you can picture the page. How does it get back into your hands?
items.layman: When your reading keeps escaping you, the fix is a capture habit: saving quotes and their sources into one findable place at the moment you read them. Do you have one, or do you re-search the internet for things you already found?

opts.t: I search the web again for something I have already read once.
I dig through browser history and open tabs, with mixed success.
It is in my notes — captured with its source when I first read it, findable by search.
Everything I read with intent gets captured the same way; re-finding something twice is my cue that the habit slipped.

items.q: A school form asks — again — for the details every form asks: policy numbers, dates, emergency contacts. How do those details get onto the page?
items.layman: For paperwork that keeps requesting the same family facts, do you go hunting through drawers and old emails each time, or keep one saved reference note you copy from?

opts.t: A hunt through drawers, old emails, and photographed cards, every time.
I remember which old form has them and copy from a photo of it.
One saved note holds every recurring detail; forms are filled by copying from it.
The reference note covers the whole family’s recurring paperwork, and a new recurring question joins it the first time it appears.

items.q: Your studio’s clients keep missing appointments, so you text each one a reminder the night before. How does each text get written?
items.layman: For a message you send over and over with only the name and time changing, do you thumb it out fresh per client, or reuse a saved message?

opts.t: Typed fresh per client, in whatever words come to me that evening.
I copy the last reminder I sent and swap the details.
A saved reminder message — the name and time are the only blanks I fill.
Saved messages exist for every routine client touch — reminders, confirmations, aftercare — reminders were merely the first.

items.q: The month ends, and each of your retainer clients expects their usual results summary. How does each summary take shape?
items.layman: A “retainer client” = one who pays you monthly for ongoing work. When the same report is owed to several clients on a schedule, does each start from a saved shell — a document with the structure prebuilt — or from an empty page?

opts.t: An empty page per client, arranged however that evening goes.
I duplicate whichever client’s last report looks best and overwrite it.
A saved report shell — sections prebuilt, I drop in each client’s numbers and notes.
Every recurring client deliverable has its shell, and improving one improves it for all of them.

items.q: A new member just paid to join your community. Could you say out loud, in order, what happens to them in their first week?
items.layman: When someone new joins, is there a defined welcome path — same steps, same order, for every member — or does each arrival get whatever greeting you improvise? “Versioned” = the written path is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: They get whatever I improvise when I notice they joined.
I have a welcome message saved; what happens after it varies.
A defined welcome path: same greeting, same orientation steps, same first-week check-in, every member.
The path is written and versioned, with a checklist confirming each new member actually completed it.

items.q: Your workshop runs again next month, as it did last month and the month before. Where does “how we run this” actually live?
items.layman: A “run-of-show” = the written sequence for an event: what happens before, during, and after, in order. For a session you deliver repeatedly, does one exist, or does each delivery lean on your memory of the last? “Versioned” = saved with a history of changes.

opts.t: In my memory of previous runs, reconstructed each time.
In scattered pieces — a slide deck here, an old email there — gathered afresh each time.
In a written run-of-show: preparation, delivery, and follow-up steps in fixed order.
The run-of-show is versioned, and a delivery counts as done only when its closing checklist is clear.

items.q: An order for your physical product arrives while you are deep in client work. What exactly happens between “order received” and “parcel handed over”?
items.layman: The steps between an order and a shipped parcel — pull stock, pack, label, record, notify — either follow a written procedure in the same order every time, or get improvised per parcel. “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Improvisation per parcel, fitted around whatever else the day holds.
The labels and packaging are standardized; the steps around them float.
A written fulfillment procedure: same steps, same sequence, same records updated, every order.
The procedure is versioned and ends with a checklist — stock counted, tracking sent — before the parcel leaves my hands.

items.q: A contributor submits a change to your open-source project. What does your review consist of — this time, and every time?
items.layman: “Open-source” = software you publish where outsiders can contribute changes. A “review” = your checking of a contributed change before accepting it; to “merge” = to accept it into the project. Is that check a defined sequence you repeat, or a feeling that varies by contributor and mood? “Versioned” = the written sequence keeps a history of its changes.

opts.t: I read the change and go by feel; no two reviews look alike.
I usually check the same few things, from memory, in no particular order.
A written review sequence — the same checks in the same order for every contribution.
The sequence is versioned and doubles as an acceptance checklist a change must clear before it merges.

items.q: Your subcontractor delivers the month’s batch of work. What determines whether it gets accepted?
items.layman: When work arrives from someone you hired, is there a defined checking procedure — the same inspections, in the same order, against written standards — or does acceptance ride on a skim and a feeling? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: A skim and a feeling, sized to how busy I am that day.
I compare it loosely against the brief and against past deliveries.
A defined checking procedure: the same inspections against written standards, every delivery.
The procedure is versioned, and we both hold the acceptance checklist — they know the bar before they deliver.

items.q: A medical bill arrives for a family member. What happens to it between the envelope and “resolved”?
items.layman: Handling a medical bill has real steps — match it against the insurer’s statement, question errors, pay, file. Is that a written routine you repeat each time, or a fresh scramble per envelope? “Versioned” = the routine is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: A scramble: it sits in a pile until urgency forces a session of untangling.
I remember roughly what worked last time and rebuild the steps.
A written routine — verify against the statement, dispute what fails, pay what clears, file the record — in the same order for every bill.
The routine is versioned with a closing checklist, so no bill is “done” until every step is confirmed.

items.q: You accept an invitation to give a talk — your fourth this year. How does the talk get built between the yes and the stage?
items.layman: Preparing a talk has repeatable stages: outline, slides, rehearsal, tech check. After several talks, do those stages exist as a written procedure you run, or do you rediscover them against each deadline? “Versioned” = the procedure is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Panic-shaped: whatever the deadline forces, in whatever order.
I reuse old slides and remember most of the stages, unevenly.
A written prep procedure — outline, draft, slides, rehearsal, tech check — run the same way each talk.
The procedure is versioned, and “ready” is defined by a checklist, not by how the rehearsal felt.

items.q: A client project reaches its end. What happens between “the work is approved” and “the relationship is properly closed”?
items.layman: Closing a project has small, forgettable steps — final invoice, file hand-over, access cleanup, archive, the referral ask. Is that a defined closeout routine, or whatever you remember before the next project swallows you? “Versioned” = the routine is written down with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Whatever I remember. Some clients still have access to folders from two years ago.
A rough mental list; most steps happen for most projects.
A written closeout routine — invoice, hand-over, access removed, archive, referral ask — run for every project.
The routine is versioned with a completion checklist, and a project stays open in my records until the checklist clears.

items.q: You have a new product ready for the marketplace where you sell. How does its listing come into existence?
items.layman: A “listing” = the product page buyers see: photos, description, keywords, price. Is creating one a documented sequence with known steps and standards, or a session of improvising until the page looks right? “Versioned” = the sequence is saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: I improvise in the listing editor until the page looks right.
I open a past listing that sold well and imitate it side by side.
A documented listing sequence — photo set, description structure, keyword steps, pricing rules — the same for every product.
The sequence is versioned, and a listing goes live only after passing its written checklist.

items.q: It is closing time at your studio. What stands between “last customer out” and “lights off”?
items.layman: Closing a physical space has consequences when a step is skipped — an unlocked door, an unbalanced till, an unsaved record. Is the closing sequence written and followed, or carried in your head and subject to your tiredness? “Versioned” = the written sequence keeps a history of its changes.

opts.t: My head, and my tiredness. Some nights, steps get skipped.
A dry-erase list from months ago that half matches what I actually do.
A written closing sequence — till, records, equipment, locks — followed in order every night.
The sequence is versioned, each night’s run is ticked off against it, and a skipped step is visible the next morning.

items.q: You open your community after a day away. Twelve member questions came in. What state are they in when you arrive?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Escalated” = flagged for you by rule because it was unusual. While you were absent, did the questions simply age — or were draft answers already prepared for your review?

opts.t: Twelve unanswered questions, aging. I start typing.
My saved replies make the typing faster; working through them is still mine.
An agent has drafted an answer to each from my past replies and the community’s docs; I review and post.
Routine answers sit queued for one-click posting; the two questions touching refunds and conduct were escalated, each with a note on why.

items.q: Twenty students submitted this week’s course assignment. Who produces the individual feedback each one receives?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. A “rubric” = your written grading standards. “Escalate” = flag a case to you by rule. Does feedback exist because you wrote it, or because you reviewed what was written?

opts.t: I do — twenty submissions read and responded to, one by one.
I grade with a rubric and paste from a comment bank, but every word passes through my hands.
An agent drafts feedback on each submission against my rubric; I review each before it goes out.
Clear passes and clear reworks arrive drafted and queued; the submissions the agent scores as borderline escalate to me first.

items.q: Orders for your hardware kit arrived through the night. What has already happened to them by the time you reach the workbench?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. An “exception” = a case outside the rules, flagged for you. Between a customer’s click and your packing bench there is paperwork — labels, stock counts, notifications. Whose hands does it pass through?

opts.t: Nothing has happened. Each order waits for me to process it end to end.
Payment confirmations went out on their own; labels, stock, and messages wait for me.
An agent prepared the labels, updated the stock counts, and drafted the customer notifications; I review the batch and pack.
The routine paperwork completed itself and the stock counts are current; one address that failed verification waits for me, flagged as the exception.

items.q: Your open-source project’s dependencies drift out of date every month. Who keeps them current?
items.layman: “Dependencies” = outside code your project builds on, which needs regular updating. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. A “test suite” = your saved battery of automatic checks; to “merge” = to accept a change into the project. Is updating a chore you perform, or work you approve?

opts.t: I do, when I notice — a manual afternoon of updating and fixing.
A tool notifies me when dependencies go stale; the updating is still my hands.
An agent prepares each update, runs the test suite, and queues the passing ones; I review and merge.
Clean updates merge by rule once tests pass; anything failing, or touching a critical dependency, escalates to me with context.

items.q: The first of the month means assembling work packages for your two subcontractors — specs, assets, deadlines. Who assembles them?
items.layman: A “work package” = everything a hired person needs to start: instructions, files, dates. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Escalate” = flag to you by rule. Does the assembly consume your morning, or await your approval?

opts.t: I do, from scratch — a morning of gathering and writing, twice over.
My brief templates speed the writing; the gathering and assembling stay mine.
An agent assembles both packages from my project records and templates; I review before they send.
Packages assemble on schedule and send after my one-pass review; anything with missing inputs escalates instead of sending incomplete.

items.q: School emails, activity sign-ups, appointment notices — the family’s logistics arrive as a drizzle of messages. How do they become calendar entries?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Escalate” = flag to you by rule. Between “the email arrived” and “the family knows about it” — is that conversion your recurring chore, or your quick review?

opts.t: I read each message and type each event into the calendar myself.
I forward them to one folder and batch-enter them when I remember.
An agent extracts the dates and details and drafts the calendar entries and reminders; I confirm them in one sitting.
Routine entries land on the calendar by rule; conflicts, money, and consent forms escalate to me.

items.q: You finish three long reads for your current research project. How do they enter your notes?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. When a source is finished, someone must extract the quotes, arguments, and citations into your note system. Is that someone you — or a system whose output you check?

opts.t: Mostly they don’t. Highlights stay in the source, half-remembered.
I extract the notes myself, by hand, when I can spare the hour.
An agent processes each finished source into structured notes — quotes, claims, citation — in my system; I review and correct them.
Processing happens on completion, notes arrive linked to related entries, and anything the agent could not verify against the source is flagged rather than guessed.

items.q: Friday is client-status day: each retainer client gets a summary of the week’s progress. Where do those summaries come from?
items.layman: A “retainer client” = one paying monthly for ongoing work. An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. Do the weekly summaries exist because you assembled them — or because you approved them?

opts.t: From me: I reconstruct each client’s week from memory and messages, then write.
From my report shell and my notes, filled in by hand, client by client.
An agent drafts each summary from the project trackers and the week’s activity; I review and send.
Drafts arrive with anomalies flagged — slipped deadlines, unusual hours — and the routine ones go out after my single pass.

items.q: Competitors on your marketplace shift prices daily, and your stock moves with every sale. Who keeps your listings in step?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Escalate” = flag to you by rule. Keeping listings current — prices against the market, stock counts against reality — is either your recurring chore or your review queue.

opts.t: Me, on the days I remember to check — the listings drift in between.
Alerts tell me when something is off; the adjusting is still mine.
An agent monitors the market and my stock and proposes each adjustment; I approve them in a daily batch.
Adjustments inside my written bounds apply on their own; anything outside them — a price war, a listing about to sell out — escalates to me at once.

items.q: Tomorrow your studio has nine client appointments. What has already happened about them by the time you lock up tonight?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. The night before a full day, someone must send confirmations, absorb the reschedules, and prepare the day’s schedule sheet. You — or a system you check?

opts.t: Nothing yet. Tonight I text the confirmations and rework the schedule myself.
Reminder texts went out on their own; the replies and the reshuffling wait for me.
An agent sent the confirmations, processed the reschedules against my rules, and drafted tomorrow’s day sheet; I give it a final look.
The day sheet is final except one flagged conflict; everything routine resolved itself, and the exception carries its reason.

items.q: Your community agent keeps citing the old refund window in its drafted answers, and you keep fixing it before posting. What does your fix actually touch?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that drafts multi-step work for you. “Written back” = saved into the reference the agent actually reads before drafting. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling plus its reason. Does your correction change one draft, or every future draft?

opts.t: The draft in front of me. The next draft will carry the same old number.
I keep meaning to update the agent’s background docs; meanwhile I catch it live.
The policy file the agent drafts from — the correction lands where it reads, so future answers start out right.
The fix is logged as a rewrite-verdict with its reason, the policy write is verified, and an answer citing a stale policy would trip an alert.

items.q: Reviewing your course agent’s drafted feedback, you notice it keeps crediting effort where your rubric demands working results. You reword a third draft. Then what?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI drafting work you review. A “rubric” = your written grading standards, which the agent reads. “Written back” = your correction saved into that rubric, not just into one draft. “Acceptance rate” = how often you approve the agent’s work unchanged. Does the third reword become a rule, or a habit of yours?

opts.t: Nothing. Rewording lenient feedback is simply part of my reviewing now.
I make a mental note to watch that rubric point closely.
The rubric itself gets the clarification, with an example — the next batch is graded against the corrected standard.
The change lands as a verdict with reasoning, the rubric write is verified, and drift on that point would surface in my acceptance rate before I felt it.

items.q: A customer orders your two-kit bundle, and your stock agent decrements one kit instead of two — you catch it during review. The next bundle order arrives Friday. What happens to it?
items.layman: A “stock agent” = an AI keeping your inventory records. “Decrements” = subtracts from the count. “Written back” = your fix saved into the rules the agent reads, not just into that day’s numbers. The test of a correction is the next occurrence.

opts.t: The same undercount. Bundles are just a thing I check by hand now.
I fixed Friday’s count in advance, from memory of the flaw.
It decrements correctly — the bundle rule was written into the agent’s instructions when I caught the miss.
Correct, and audited: the correction is a logged verdict, and a bundle order that skips the rule raises an alert rather than a phantom kit.

items.q: Your issue-triage agent keeps labeling crash reports from one platform as “feature requests,” and you keep relabeling them. Where does the relabeling accumulate?
items.layman: A “triage agent” = an AI that sorts and labels incoming bug reports. “Written back” = saved into the criteria the agent reads next run. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling and its reason. Do your relabelings train the system, or only tire your wrist?

opts.t: Nowhere. I relabel the same mistake indefinitely.
In my habits — I now scan that platform’s reports myself first.
In the labeling criteria the agent reads: that platform’s crash pattern became a written rule after the second miss.
Each relabel is a verdict with a reason, the criteria update is verified, and reports matching a corrected pattern escalate for one confirming look before automatic labeling resumes.

items.q: Your checking agent passes your subcontractor’s deliveries, yet twice this quarter you have caught a licensing problem it missed. After the second catch, what changes?
items.layman: A “checking agent” = an AI that inspects delivered work against your standards before you accept it. “Written back” = your catch saved into the checks it actually runs. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling plus reason. Do your catches become new checks, or remain your private vigilance?

opts.t: Nothing changes. Licensing is apparently mine to catch, forever.
I add a personal habit: after the agent passes something, I do my own licensing pass.
The licensing check is written into the agent’s inspection list — my catch became a check it runs on every delivery.
The new check carries its origin verdict, the write is verified, and the agent’s misses are tracked — a second catch in any category triggers a review of that category’s checks by rule.

items.q: Your household agent drafts the weekly grocery order, and for the second week you delete the peanut granola — your daughter’s new allergy. What does the second deletion change?
items.layman: A “household agent” = an AI handling domestic routines like grocery orders. “Written back” = saved into the standing preferences the agent reads before every draft. Does the allergy live in the system’s memory, or only in your reviewing eye?

opts.t: One order. The granola will be back next week, and the week after.
My vigilance sharpens — the grocery review now has a mental danger item.
The allergy is written into the household preferences the agent reads — every future draft starts from a world without peanuts.
It lands as a dated rule with its reason, the write is verified, and a drafted item matching the allergen would be blocked and alerted, not merely omitted.

items.q: Your research agent’s summaries keep dropping the caveats — sample sizes, disclaimers, “preliminary.” You have now restored them by hand in three summaries. What did the third restoration produce?
items.layman: A “research agent” = an AI that turns your sources into notes and summaries. “Written back” = your correction saved into the instructions it reads before every run. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling plus its reason. Does the system learn your standard of care, or do you re-teach it per document?

opts.t: A better summary, and nothing else. The fourth will drop the caveats too.
A sticky note to myself: check summaries for missing caveats.
An instruction update the agent reads every run — caveats are now part of its definition of a complete summary.
A logged rewrite-verdict with reasoning, a verified instruction write, and a sampling check that would catch caveat-stripping if it ever crept back.

items.q: On a call, a retainer client bans a phrase from all their copy — a competitor’s tagline they nearly got sued over. Where does that prohibition go when the call ends?
items.layman: A “retainer client” = one paying monthly for ongoing work your agents help produce. A “client profile” = the durable per-client rules your agents read before working on that account. “Provenance” = the record of where a rule came from and why. Does the ban outlive your memory of the call?

opts.t: Into my memory of the call, and nowhere else.
Into my meeting notes, which nothing else ever reads.
Into the client’s profile — the rules every agent reads before touching that account, starting with tonight’s drafts.
Into the profile with provenance — date, call, reason — plus a check that flags the phrase in any draft before it ever reaches the client.

items.q: During a sale event, your repricing agent priced one product below your cost, and you caught it in the daily batch. What does your catch become?
items.layman: A “repricing agent” = an AI adjusting your marketplace prices within your rules. “Landed cost” = what a product truly costs you, shipping included. “Written back” = saved into the rules it reads before every adjustment. A “verdict” = your recorded ruling plus its reason. Is the near-loss a story, or now a rule?

opts.t: A story I tell about why I check every price by hand now.
A closer eye on sale events; the rules the agent follows are unchanged.
A cost-floor rule written into the pricing rules the agent reads — no future price can be proposed below landed cost.
A verdict with reasoning, a verified rule write, and an alert whenever a proposed price so much as reaches the floor — the rule’s own application is watched.

items.q: You keep moving the appointments your booking agent places in your protected evening hours — third week running. What does the third move accomplish?
items.layman: A “booking agent” = an AI that schedules client appointments by your rules. “Written back” = your correction saved into the scheduling rules it reads before every booking. Does the boundary you keep enforcing by hand finally enter the system?

opts.t: One clear evening. Next week’s bookings will trespass again.
A resigned routine: reviewing new bookings for evening trespass is part of my week now.
The protected hours become a written scheduling rule the agent reads — evenings stop appearing as options at all.
The rule lands with a dated reason, its write is verified, and an attempted evening booking is itself an alert — evidence the rule was reached, not an appointment to move.

items.q: You are weighing a move of your community to a different platform — better calls, better threads. Setting feelings aside, what would actually transfer?
items.layman: A community’s operational layer = member records, roles, rules, welcome flows, accumulated docs. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Export” = pulling your data out in usable form. Is your community an asset you host somewhere, or a feature of someone else’s product?

opts.t: Almost nothing. Members, roles, history, and my welcome flows exist only as that platform’s features.
A partial export — the member list as a spreadsheet, perhaps — with the flows and accumulated knowledge left behind.
The operational layer — member records, rules, flows, docs — lives in open files I own; the platform is fed from them.
I have already run a trial migration to a second venue from those files; moving is a decision, not a project.

items.q: A corporate client wants your course delivered inside their own training system. How large is the gap between your course and “your course, elsewhere”?
items.layman: A course lives somewhere — videos, lessons, exercises, quizzes, sequencing. “Canonical source” = one authoritative copy in open formats you own, from which any venue is populated. Is your course a portable asset, or a set of pages on one platform?

opts.t: Enormous. The course exists only as configured screens inside my course platform.
I could export the videos; the structure, quizzes, and sequencing would need rebuilding by hand.
The canonical course lives in my own files — content, structure, assessments — and any venue, mine or theirs, is populated from it.
It has already run from those files in a second venue; delivering into their system is configuration, not reconstruction.

items.q: The marketplace where you sell has three years of your buyers — their orders, their reviews, their trust. If you opened your own channel tomorrow, could those customers come with you?
items.layman: Marketplaces show you your customers but usually own the relationship — the order history, the reviews, the ability to contact buyers. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. Does your relationship with the people who buy from you exist anywhere the marketplace does not control?

opts.t: No. The marketplace owns the customers; I would start from zero.
I can see order history in their dashboard, but nothing leaves it.
Customer records flow into a store I own, in open formats — orders, contacts, history under my custody.
Proven: I have already re-engaged those customers from my own records, through a channel the marketplace never touched.

items.q: You bring on a co-maintainer for your open-source project — including the automation you run around it. What must you hand over beyond repository access?
items.layman: A “co-maintainer” = a trusted person sharing responsibility for a public code project. Automation that “dies with your accounts” = jobs, rules, and memory living only under your personal logins, unusable by anyone else. Can a second human operate what you built, or is the system inseparable from you?

opts.t: Everything, awkwardly: the automation runs under my personal accounts and its rules live in my chat histories — none of it survives my leaving.
A long screen-share tour, some passwords, and my continued availability for questions.
Little: the jobs, instructions, and memory live in the project’s own space, in open files — access is membership, not inheritance from me.
Nothing but access: onboarding is documented and rehearsed, and the system has already been operated end-to-end by someone who is not me.

items.q: A new subcontractor’s firm forbids the collaboration platform your workflow runs through. How much of your process survives the veto?
items.layman: A process can live in a tool, or merely pass through it. “Tool-independent” = written so any equivalent venue can host it: briefs, hand-offs, checks, in files you own. When a tool is vetoed, do you lose a venue, or an operation?

opts.t: Very little. The briefs, checkpoints, and history are that platform’s objects; without it we would be improvising by email.
I could reconstruct most of the process from memory into whatever tool they allow, over a few weeks.
All of it: the process is defined tool-independently in my own files — we pick any venue they allow and feed it from the same source.
This has already happened and cost an afternoon: the process ran unchanged in a different venue, because venues are interchangeable by design.

items.q: Your partner asks, reasonably: “If you were in a hospital bed for a month, could I run the household systems you set up?” What is the honest answer?
items.layman: Household systems = the bill payments, grocery routines, and family logistics you have arranged, possibly with AI help. “Locked to your accounts” = running under logins and settings only you hold. A “shared vault” = a password-manager space both of you can open. The systems may run without your effort — but do they run without your identity?

opts.t: No. Everything runs under my personal logins, by rules only I know; my absence strands it.
Partially — some things would keep running, but nothing could be inspected, fixed, or changed by anyone else.
Yes: the systems are documented in shared files, credentials live in a shared vault, and everything runs from spaces we both hold.
Yes, provenly — they have run it for a week as a drill, from the documentation, without calling me once.

items.q: A new local AI tool promises brilliant answers over a personal research corpus. Yours is years deep. Could the new tool actually read it?
items.layman: A “research corpus” = your accumulated notes, sources, and citations. A “local AI tool” = one running on your own machine. “Open format” = plain files any software can read; a “proprietary store” = a format only one vendor’s product understands. Is your corpus yours, or your note app’s?

opts.t: No. The corpus lives inside one note app’s cloud, readable only through that app’s own features.
In theory — the app has an export, untested, which reportedly mangles links and attachments.
Yes: the corpus is plain files in open formats on storage I control; the note app is just my current window onto it.
Yes, and this is routine — three different tools already read the same corpus today, and each new one is pointed at the files, not fed a copy.

items.q: A retainer client’s new contract adds a clause: on exit, you hand over the system you run for them, in working order. Could you sign it?
items.layman: The system you run for a client = their workflows, agent rules, and accumulated memory under your management. “Separable” = the client’s parts can be extracted whole from your setup. A “retainer client” = one paying monthly for ongoing work. Is what you run for them an asset of theirs, or a tangle of yours?

opts.t: No. Their workflows are threaded through my personal accounts and mixed with other clients’ — separation would be surgery.
Reluctantly — extraction is imaginable, but their rules and memory sit in my vendors’ stores, under my name.
Yes: each client’s workflows, rules, and memory live in a separable space in open formats — handover is packaging, not surgery.
Yes, and I have rehearsed it: a dry-run handover produced a working system on their side, and the clause is now my selling point.

items.q: Your research agent learns something your client-facing agents need — a retraction of a study you have been citing. How does that knowledge travel between agents?
items.layman: “Agents” = AIs doing multi-step work for you, possibly on different vendors’ products. A “memory silo” = knowledge trapped inside one tool, invisible to the others. A “shared substrate” = one owned store of files all agents read and write. “Provenance” = the record of where a piece of knowledge came from. Is what your system knows one body of knowledge, or several strangers?

opts.t: It doesn’t. Each tool holds its own memory; the retraction lives in one silo while the others keep citing the study.
Through me: I notice the lesson in one tool and paste it into the others, when I remember.
Through the shared substrate: every agent reads and writes one owned memory store, so a lesson landed anywhere is read everywhere.
The write carries provenance, its propagation is verified, and a client-facing draft citing the retracted study would be caught — the substrate is one body of knowledge, and it is mine.

items.q: Your accountant asks for direct, ongoing access to your studio’s records — bookings, sales, customer counts. What are your options?
items.layman: An all-in-one business platform holds bookings, payments, and customer records — convenient, until something outside it needs the data. “Egress” = data’s path out of a system. An “owned data layer” = your own store, in open formats, that outside tools and people connect to. Does your business data have an exit?

opts.t: Screenshots and hand-typed summaries. The records exist only inside the platform, and only I can look.
Monthly manual downloads of whatever the platform’s export button produces, in whatever shape it chooses.
A standing sync: the records flow on schedule into open files I own, and the accountant — like any tool — connects to those.
The owned data layer is already the source of record: the platform writes into it, several tools read from it, and adding the accountant took minutes.

items.q: Can you state, in one sentence, the specific constraint your work removes — and for whom?
items.layman: Could you instantly finish this sentence: “I remove ___ for ___”? A “thesis” here means your written, one-line reason for what you build and who it serves.

opts.t: Not cleanly.
I can improvise a decent version on the spot.
It is written down and stable.
It is written, published, and tested against paying reality.

items.q: When you hand work to an AI, how do you define success before it starts?
items.layman: Before the AI begins, do you tell it exactly how the result will be judged — like a checklist it must pass? “Acceptance criteria” = that checklist. “Evals” = automated tests that grade AI output.

opts.t: I describe the task and hope.
I give examples of what good output looks like.
I give explicit acceptance criteria.
Criteria live as versioned specs or evals the output is tested against automatically.

items.q: Could a stranger reconstruct what you are building from your written artifacts alone?
items.layman: If someone — or an AI agent — read only your documents, with no conversation, could they understand your project and continue it correctly?

opts.t: No. It lives in my head.
Scattered notes exist; a stranger would struggle.
Current documentation covers the core; a capable person could continue.
Docs, specs, and doctrine are complete enough that an agent onboards from them alone.

items.q: How do you decide what NOT to build?
items.layman: Do you have written rules for what is out of scope — things you deliberately refuse to build — or do projects just keep growing?

opts.t: I build whatever excites me at the time.
I drop things when I get overwhelmed.
Each project has explicit, written non-goals.
A written doctrine of exclusions exists, and my system flags scope drift against it.

items.q: At dinner, a friend asks, “So what do you actually do these days?” What comes out?
items.layman: When someone asks what you do, is the answer something you once wrote down and settled on, or do you invent it fresh — and differently — every time?

opts.t: A different rambling answer every time someone asks.
A rough answer I have repeated enough that pieces of it are stable.
A line I wrote down once and actually use — the same sentence, on purpose.
The written line exists, and writing one is a reflex — every new effort gets its sentence before it gets my time.

items.q: You sign up for a new platform and hit the empty bio box. What happens next?
items.layman: When a website asks you to describe yourself in a few lines, do you paste in a description you keep somewhere, or compose a new one on the spot?

opts.t: I stare at it, type something plausible, and never think about it again.
I hunt down an old profile and adapt whatever I said there.
I paste the description I keep saved for exactly this moment.
One saved description, reused everywhere — and rereading it at each signup is how I notice when it has gone stale.

items.q: A new side project is about to get its first hour of work. What exists before the code or the canvas?
items.layman: Before you start building something new, do you write down — even one sentence — what it is for and who it serves, or do you just start?

opts.t: Nothing. I open the editor and follow the excitement.
A name, maybe a folder. The purpose is obvious to me, so it goes unwritten.
A sentence or two, saved with the project: what it is, who it is for.
Writing that sentence is the ritual that starts every project — no line, no first hour.

items.q: A prospective client emails, “What exactly do you offer?” How is the reply produced?
items.layman: When someone asks what your services are, is the answer written somewhere you can reuse, or do you compose it from scratch each time — with the risk that every version differs?

opts.t: I write it fresh, and each prospect probably reads a slightly different offer.
I dig out the last email like this and rework it.
I keep a written description of what I offer and send it, tailored lightly.
The description is written, current, and public — the email mostly points at it.

items.q: You reopen a project you abandoned six weeks ago. How do you rediscover what it was supposed to be?
items.layman: When you come back to old work, is there a written note telling you what you were building and why — or do you reconstruct the intent from the files themselves?

opts.t: I read my own files like a detective and guess at the intent.
Fragments help — a to-do here, a comment there — but the why is gone.
A note at the top says what this is and why it exists. I read it and resume.
Every project opens with that note; abandoning one means the note says why that, too.

items.q: You are about to ask an AI for help with a piece of work. What does it get first?
items.layman: Before typing a request to an AI, do you first write out what you actually want — the goal, the audience — or start typing and clarify as you argue with the output?

opts.t: Whatever I type first. We negotiate the goal as we go.
A quick request; I clarify when the answer comes back wrong.
A sentence stating what I want and who it is for, written before the request.
Stating the goal in writing first is automatic — for AIs, and for myself before any real task.

items.q: Someone asks who your work is actually for. Can you point at an answer, or only produce one?
