items.layman: Is there a written description anywhere of the specific person or kind of customer you build for — or does the answer exist only when you improvise it aloud?

opts.t: For whoever shows up. I have never really pinned it down.
I can describe them on the spot, differently each telling.
It is written down — a short description of who I serve — and I keep using it.
Written before I built anything, and rewritten when the real audience taught me otherwise.

items.q: Two small gigs arrive in the same week and you can only take one. What do you consult to choose?
items.layman: When choosing between offers, do you have any written statement of the direction you are trying to go — even a note — to check against, or is the choice made entirely by feel?

opts.t: My mood on the day of the decision.
A gut check, maybe a chat with a friend — nothing of mine in writing.
A note I keep about what I am building toward; the gig that serves it wins.
The direction note exists, and every yes or no gets a one-line reason written next to it.

items.q: You sit down to write the headline for your own site. Where do the words come from?
items.layman: Is the sentence naming what you do already written somewhere and merely retrieved, or is it invented at the keyboard whenever a headline is needed?

opts.t: The keyboard. I invent it there and then, and second-guess it for days.
Cobbled together from old taglines and things people have said about me.
Retrieved — the one-liner already exists in my notes; the headline is a copy.
Retrieved from a line written before the site existed — the site conforms to the sentence, not the reverse.

items.q: An idea for something worth building arrives at midnight. Where is it by morning?
items.layman: When inspiration strikes, do you capture it in writing — what it is and why it matters — or trust your memory to keep it?

opts.t: In my memory, if it survived the night.
A two-word note on my phone that will puzzle me next week.
A saved note: what it is, who it is for, why it matters.
Captured where all my intents live, in the same shape every time — findable months later.

items.q: A new client project starts Monday. What document exists by the Friday before, and what does it contain?
items.layman: Before work begins, do you write a kickoff document — what will be delivered, what will not, what the client provides — or does the project start from an email thread and goodwill? “Versioned” = saved with a history of its changes.

opts.t: No document. The proposal email is the project’s founding text.
Notes from the sales calls, scattered across apps.
One kickoff doc: deliverables, exclusions, what the client provides, what done means.
That doc, versioned — and the client has signed off on the checklist the work must pass.

items.q: You are handing a design task to a freelancer you trust. What do they receive?
items.layman: When you hand a task to a person, is the request a single structured brief — goal, constraints, what the result must include — or a conversation they must assemble into one? “Brief” = a short written document stating what is wanted and why.

opts.t: A voice note and a promise to answer questions as they come.
A long chat message with most of what matters, somewhere in it.
A brief: the goal, the constraints, examples, and what the deliverable must include.
The brief follows my standard template and ends with the checklist we will both judge the work against.

items.q: A stranger stars your side project and opens the README. What do they learn?
items.layman: Does your project’s front-page document state what the project is, who it serves, and what it deliberately does not do — or is it an install command and a shrug? “Scope” = the defined edges of what the project covers.

opts.t: The project’s name, and how to install it.
A description I wrote in a hurry that undersells it and misleads slightly.
What it is, who it is for, what it covers, and what it deliberately leaves out.
All of that, kept current with each release — the README changes when the scope does.

items.q: Mid-project, the client asks, “Wait — is the mobile version included?” Where does the answer live?
items.layman: When scope questions come up, is there a written document that already settles them, or does the answer depend on memory and negotiation? “Scope” = the agreed edges of the work. “Versioned” = every change kept with its history.

opts.t: In whatever we each remember agreeing to. Negotiation follows.
Somewhere in the email thread, if either of us can find it.
In the project doc — scope was written down before work began. I quote it.
In the current version of the scope doc, which records every change since kickoff — the answer comes with its history.

items.q: Launch day approaches and the announcement needs writing. What is it written from?
items.layman: When you announce something you built, does the announcement draw on an existing written description of what it is and who it is for — or do you work out the message while writing the post? “Positioning” = your written statement of what this is, for whom, and why it is different.

opts.t: A blank page and adrenaline. The message emerges as I type.
Screenshots and feature notes; the framing is improvised around them.
The project’s positioning doc — the announcement is a restatement, not a discovery.
The positioning doc, plus a launch checklist the announcement must satisfy before it ships.

items.q: Your services page lists three packages. What sits behind each name and price?
items.layman: For each thing you sell, is there a written definition — what is included, what is excluded, what the buyer must bring — or does each sale rediscover the boundaries? “Deliverables” = the concrete things the buyer receives.

opts.t: A name and a price. What is inside gets worked out per client.
A rough mental list of inclusions; clients occasionally discover the edges the hard way.
A written definition per package: deliverables, exclusions, what the buyer provides.
Written definitions the sales conversation quotes verbatim — and revising a package means revising its document first.

items.q: You need an AI to draft a proposal overnight. What do you write before you write the prompt?
items.layman: When you hand real work to an AI, do you first produce a structured brief — audience, goal, required sections, tone — or type a request and steer through retries? “Brief” = a short document stating what is wanted, for whom, and what the result must contain.

opts.t: Nothing. The prompt is the plan, composed in the box.
A few bullet points pasted above the request.
A brief: audience, goal, required sections, tone, and what the draft must contain to count.
The brief comes from my standard format and is saved with the project — the prompt just delivers it.

items.q: A user of your side project requests a feature that feels adjacent-but-maybe. How do you find the answer?
items.layman: When someone asks your project to do more, is there a written statement of what the project covers that decides the question — or does the decision get made fresh, by enthusiasm? “Scope” = the defined edges of what the project is meant to do.

opts.t: Enthusiasm decides. If it sounds fun, it is in.
I have an instinct for what fits, but nothing written to check it against.
The project doc defines what this covers; the request is measured against it.
The doc defines coverage and exclusions, and my reply quotes the line — accepted requests amend the doc first.

items.q: You give yourself two weeks for a solo sprint on your own product. What is written before day one?
items.layman: Before a stretch of self-directed work, do you write a plan — what will exist at the end, what counts as finished — or start building and let the fortnight define itself? “Acceptance checklist” = the written test the finished work must pass.

opts.t: Nothing. Day one begins wherever my energy points.
A loose list of things I would like to get to.
A written plan: what will exist by day fourteen, and what finished means for each piece.
The plan plus an acceptance checklist — day fourteen is judged against the paper, not the memory of my hopes.

items.q: You are adding last quarter’s work to your portfolio. What does each case study get written from?
items.layman: When you present past projects, is each account built from the project’s original written brief — the problem, the intent, the boundaries — or reverse-engineered from screenshots and recollection? “Brief” = the short document stating what was wanted and why.

opts.t: Recollection. I look at the finished thing and infer what I must have meant.
Old emails and fragments; the story gets assembled per telling.
The original brief for each project — the case study restates intent that was written at the time.
Briefs, plus the recorded outcome against them — the portfolio shows what was promised and what happened.

items.q: A collaborator starts on your project Monday. What does their first week actually look like?
items.layman: When someone joins your project, can they onboard from your written material — reading, then doing — or is week one a series of calls where you narrate the project into their head?

opts.t: Meetings. I explain the project live, repeatedly, because nowhere else contains it.
Docs exist to skim, but the real transfer happens in my calendar.
They read the project’s docs and ship something real by Friday; I answer edge cases, not basics.
An onboarding path exists — ordered docs, plus written rules for what they may decide alone and what comes to me.

items.q: Mid-task, your agent stops and asks a clarifying question. What does that question reveal?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. “Brief” = the written instructions it works from. When it has to ask, is the answer genuinely missing from what you wrote — or was it there all along and the writing failed?

opts.t: Nothing unusual — the agent always has to ask, because the brief is mostly vibes.
That I explained it in the chat once but never in the brief; I answer live, again.
A real gap — briefs usually suffice, and the answer gets written into the brief, not just the chat.
Rarely happens: the brief states what to assume, what to decide alone, and what must come back to me.

items.q: You go trekking for a week, unreachable, while a subcontractor continues the build. What did you have to do before leaving?
items.layman: If someone must work from your project’s written material while you cannot be asked anything, do the documents carry enough — decisions, constraints, priorities — or did you spend the final days recording voice memos to compensate?

opts.t: Cancel the trek, effectively — the work cannot proceed without me answering things.
A frantic final week producing ad-hoc notes and walkthrough videos.
Point at the existing docs. They already contain what the week needs.
Almost nothing — the docs even say which decisions can be made without me and which must wait.

items.q: Walking to lunch, you dictate a two-sentence task to your agent — and the result comes back right. What made two sentences enough?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you. “Specs” = written statements of what is being built. Terse instructions only work when written context already exists — project descriptions, definitions, standards the agent can consult. Otherwise every task needs a lecture.

opts.t: Two sentences are never enough; every task begins with a long re-explanation.
Luck, and the agent’s guesses — sometimes right, often plausible and wrong.
Standing written context: the specs carry the project, so the task only carries the difference.
Specs plus my written glossary and standards — the agent quotes them back in its plan before starting.

items.q: You open a fresh AI chat to work on your main project. What happens in the first minute?
items.layman: A new AI session starts knowing nothing. Do you re-narrate your project every time, or does written project context exist — a document the session ingests — that stands in for the conversation?

opts.t: The ritual re-explanation: what the project is, who it is for, told again from memory.
I paste fragments from old chats and hope they still describe the truth.
The session reads the project’s standing context doc and is oriented before I ask anything.
Every session boots from the same maintained context files — and clarifications go into the files, not the chat.

items.q: A prospect books a call after reading your site and proposal. How much of the call is spent explaining what you do?
items.layman: Do your public written materials carry your offer — what you do, for whom, what is excluded — well enough that strangers arrive already aligned? Or does every call begin at zero?

opts.t: Most of it. The materials say little; the call is the explanation.
Half — they arrive with a fuzzy, partly wrong picture I must correct.
Almost none. They arrive knowing what I do and do not do; we discuss their case.
None — prospects self-select or self-reject from the materials alone; unqualified calls rarely happen.

items.q: You are flattened by flu when the client emails, “Just confirming — does phase two include the migration?” Who can answer?
items.layman: When you are out, could anyone — a partner, an assistant, an agent — answer a scope question from the project’s written artifacts alone? “Scope” = the agreed edges of the work.

opts.t: No one. The answer exists in my head, and the client waits for my recovery.
Someone could dig through threads and guess, nervously.
Anyone with access — the scope doc answers it plainly, no interpretation needed.
It was answered before I saw it — the artifacts are complete enough that others reply confidently in my absence.

items.q: A newsletter wants to feature your project this week — no time for an interview. What do you send?
items.layman: Can written material alone give a stranger an accurate account of your project — what it is, who it is for, what it is not — or does accuracy require your live narration?

opts.t: A plea to reschedule; without talking to me they would get it wrong.
Links to scattered posts that each tell a slightly different story.
A one-pager that gets it right: what it is, for whom, what it deliberately is not.
A link to public docs so complete their draft needs no correction — including what the project refuses to be.

items.q: A good customer asks for a feature you are not going to build. What does your “no” stand on?
items.layman: When you refuse a request, can you point to written non-goals — a list of things your product deliberately will not do — or is each refusal invented, and thus negotiable? “Non-goals” = the explicitly recorded things you have decided not to build. “Versioned” = kept with a history of changes.

opts.t: Not much — I usually say yes to good customers and cope later.
Instinct. The no is real but improvised, and it wobbles under pressure.
Written non-goals. The refusal quotes the document, with the reasoning.
Non-goals are versioned and public; requests are checked against them before they ever reach me.

items.q: Three weeks into a build, the project has quietly grown a second purpose. What noticed?
items.layman: When work drifts away from its stated intent, what catches it — a scheduled comparison against the written spec, an automatic check, or a bad feeling that arrives too late? “Spec” = the written statement of what is being built and what done means. “Drift” = the slow, unannounced widening of that intent. “Versioned” = every change kept with its history.

opts.t: Nothing. I discover the drift when the deadline does.
A nagging feeling, eventually — the correction is a scramble, and nothing records it.
A standing habit: work is compared against the written spec at set points, and drift gets named early.
The system flags it — outputs are checked against the versioned spec, and divergence raises its hand before I feel it.

items.q: The market shifts and your one-line thesis quietly stops being true. What happens to the sentence?
items.layman: “Thesis” = your written one-line statement of what you build and for whom. When reality contradicts it, does the sentence get deliberately revised — with the change and the reason recorded — or does it just rot?

opts.t: There is no sentence to stop being true.
I rewrite it when the embarrassment peaks, and the old version simply vanishes.
It is revised deliberately: the new line, the old line, and the reason are all kept.
Evidence against the thesis is collected by my system and surfaced — revision is triggered, not remembered.

items.q: You took a project “just this once” that your own rules said to refuse. A month later, where does that exception live?
items.layman: When you break one of your own written rules about what work you take, is the exception recorded — which rule, and why — or does it silently loosen the rule? “Doctrine” = your accumulated written rules for what you build and refuse.

opts.t: Nowhere. There were no written rules to break.
In my conscience. The rule survives on paper and erodes in practice.
Logged against the doctrine: the rule, the exception, the reason it was worth it.
Logged — and the system counts exceptions, flagging when “just this once” has become my actual policy.

items.q: An agent drafts your marketing copy overnight. What is the draft judged against in the morning?
items.layman: When AI writes in your name, is there a written positioning document — your claims, your voice, what you never promise — that the output is explicitly checked against, or do you judge it by feel? “Positioning” = the written statement of what you offer, for whom, and what you refuse to claim. “Machine-readable” = structured so software can check against it.

opts.t: My mood. If it reads well, it ships.
Memory of what I usually say — inconsistencies slip through.
The positioning doc: claims, voice, forbidden promises — the draft is checked against it line by line.
The doc is machine-readable and the check is automatic — off-positioning copy never reaches my desk.

items.q: Your side project is three months old. Is it working — and how do you know?
items.layman: Did you write down, before launching, what success would look like by now — specific outcomes you could check — or is “working” a feeling you consult? “Success criteria” = the written, checkable definition of what this project must achieve. “Versioned” = kept with a history of changes.

opts.t: It feels alive, which I take as a yes.
I look at the numbers when curious, with no line marking enough.
Success criteria were written at the start; I review reality against them on schedule.
The criteria are versioned and my dashboard tests reality against them — misses get flagged, not rationalized.

items.q: A new kind of customer keeps showing up — adjacent to your stated audience, not in it. What decides whether you widen?
items.layman: Your “audience definition” = the written description of exactly who you build for. When reality offers you a different customer, is the definition consulted and deliberately amended or defended — or does the audience just become whoever pays?

opts.t: Revenue decides. Whoever pays is the audience now.
I notice the drift and feel ambivalent about it, in private.
The written audience definition is consulted — widened on purpose, or held on purpose, and the decision recorded.
Incoming work is screened against the definition automatically; mismatches surface as a decision, not a surprise.

items.q: Mid-build, the client changes their mind about a core requirement. What happens to the spec?
items.layman: “Spec” = the written statement of what is being built. “Versioned” = every change kept with its history. “Acceptance checks” = the tests a deliverable must pass. When requirements change, does the document change with them — or does the truth move into chat while the spec fossilizes?

opts.t: There is no spec to change; the chat thread is the requirement.
We agree on the call and I mean to update the doc, mostly.
The spec is amended and versioned the same day; work tracks the current version, not the conversation.
Amended, versioned — and the acceptance checks are regenerated from it, so the old requirement cannot silently pass.

items.q: The tool holding your specs and project docs announces it is closing in sixty days. What, exactly, is at risk?
items.layman: “Specs” = written statements of what you are building. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Canonical” = the single authoritative version. “Stack” = the set of tools you run on. If your documentation tool vanished, would your articulated intent vanish with it?

opts.t: Everything. My thinking lives in that tool’s pages and nowhere else.
The words survive a messy export; the structure and links mostly do not.
Nothing essential. The canonical files are open formats I own — the tool was only a window onto them.
Nothing — and I know, because the corpus already renders on a second stack; the shutdown is a bookmark change.

items.q: You hand your venture to a successor and close your accounts behind you — every login, every workspace, gone. What do they run it from?
items.layman: “Thesis” = your one-line statement of what you build and for whom. “Specs” = written statements of what is being built. “Non-goals” = the recorded things you refuse to build. “Doctrine” = your accumulated rules and their reasoning. If the artifacts defining your venture live inside your tools and accounts, a handover dies with the logins. “Open formats” = plain files any tool can read; a “stack” = the set of tools a venture runs on. Are the artifacts portable enough to change hands — and stacks?

opts.t: Nothing. The venture’s definition lived in those workspaces, and it left with them.
Documents exist, but they live in my tool stack and assume my accounts — a successor inherits the logins or nothing.
Portable artifacts: thesis, specs, non-goals, and doctrine in open formats their own tools can read — no account of mine required.
That has been proven — a successor on a different stack has already run a real stretch from the artifacts alone, and their questions became doctrine.

items.q: You switch AI vendors on a Tuesday. What happens to everything your agents knew about your intent?
items.layman: “Agents” = AIs doing multi-step work for you. “Doctrine” = your written rules for what you build and refuse. “Tool-independent” = written so any equivalent tool can use it. If the briefs, rules, and context that tell an AI what you are building live inside one vendor’s product, a switch erases them.

opts.t: It evaporates. Months of accumulated context belonged to the old vendor.
I paste what I can salvage into the new one and rebuild the rest from memory.
Nothing — intent lives in my own tool-independent files, and the new vendor’s agents are pointed at them.
Nothing, provably — I have run both vendors from the same doctrine files, and the swap is a Tuesday, not an event.

items.q: If your website vanished tonight, where would tomorrow’s copy come from?
items.layman: “Positioning” = your written statement of what you offer, for whom, and what makes it different. “Canonical” = the single authoritative version. Is the website the only home those words have, or do they live in a source you own — one anyone could rebuild the site from?

opts.t: From memory of what the site used to say.
From a scrape, a cached copy, whatever the archive kept.
From the canonical positioning files I own; the words never lived only on the site.
From those files, by hands other than mine — an agent has already regenerated the whole site from the source, on different infrastructure.

items.q: A painful project teaches you a new rule about what you refuse to build. Where does that rule go?
items.layman: “Doctrine” = your accumulated written rules for what you build and refuse. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Provenance” = a record of where each rule came from. When you learn a new rule, does it enter one authoritative, portable source that all your tools read — or get scattered into whichever app is open?

opts.t: Into the story I tell about that project. Nowhere structural.
Into whichever tool is open — a note here, a prompt tweak there, versions diverging.
Into the one doctrine source, in an open format — every tool and agent that needs it reads from there.
Into the doctrine with its provenance attached — and often the system drafts the rule from the incident before I do.

items.q: Your laptop is stolen and every SaaS login is temporarily locked. From your exported files alone, could the venture’s intent be reconstructed?
items.layman: “Thesis” = your one-line statement of what you build and for whom. “Specs” = written statements of what is being built. “Non-goals” = the recorded things you refuse to build. Strip away accounts and platforms: do the files you actually possess contain what you are building, for whom, and what you refuse — or does that knowledge live only inside services?

opts.t: No. The files are fragments; the meaning was in the apps, and in me.
Partially — enough to reconstruct the what, with the why mostly lost.
Yes. The owned files carry thesis, specs, and non-goals in formats anything can open.
Yes, and it has been tested — a clean machine, the files, and a working reconstruction, rehearsed.

items.q: You start a second venture. How much of the first venture’s clarity apparatus comes with you?
items.layman: “Clarity apparatus” = your formats for stating intent — how you write a thesis (the one-line statement of what you build and for whom), specs, and non-goals — the machinery, not the content. Is that machinery reusable and tool-independent, or was it welded to venture number one?

opts.t: None. I start the new one the way I started the old one: from zero.
Habits transfer; the artifacts themselves are too entangled with the first venture to reuse.
The formats travel as portable templates — the new venture’s thesis and specs are written into them on day one.
The second venture has already been bootstrapped this way — the apparatus proved itself by producing another operation.

items.q: A new collaborator refuses, on principle, to use any of your apps. Can they still work from your specs?
items.layman: “Specs” = written statements of what is being built. “Open format” = plain files (text, standard documents) readable without a specific product or account. “Canonical” = the single authoritative version; “canon” = that authoritative body itself. Do your specs and doctrine require your tool stack to be legible, or can anyone, on anything, read them?

opts.t: No — reading my specs means getting accounts on my stack.
I export copies for them, which drift from the originals within a week.
Yes — the canonical files are open formats; their tools read the same source mine do.
Yes, provenly — collaborators on alien stacks have shipped from those files, and their edits merged back into the canon.

items.q: Your doctrine says “never build white-label.” A new partner asks why. What can you show them?
items.layman: “Doctrine” = your written rules for what you build and refuse. “White-label” = work sold under someone else’s brand. “Provenance” = each rule carrying its origin — the date, the incident, the evidence that created it. Can your rules explain themselves, or do they depend on your memory to be credible?

opts.t: A shrug and a war story I half-remember.
The rule, written — but its reason lives only in my memory of a bad year.
The rule with its provenance: when it was made, what happened, in files I own.
The rule cites its evidence, and the system cites the rule when it fires — the partner reads the whole chain without me.

items.q: Your richest thinking lives in one tool’s databases, boards, and embeds. Run the export — what comes out the other side?
items.layman: Many tools hold your meaning in proprietary structures — linked databases, canvas boards, embedded blocks — that turn to rubble when exported. “Canon” = your single authoritative body of specs and rules. Does your articulated intent survive leaving the tool, or was the tool the intent’s only true home?

opts.t: Rubble. The meaning was the structure, and the structure does not export.
Readable wreckage — the words arrive, the relationships and reasoning mostly die.
Nothing is lost, because the canon was never in the proprietary structures — meaning lives in plain formats; the fancy views are disposable.
A tested round-trip: export, reimport elsewhere, and verify nothing of the intent was lost — done, on a schedule.

items.q: You are opening a small online community for the people who follow your work. The invite link is ready to send. What tells a newcomer what this place is for?
items.layman: Before people arrive in a community space you run, is its purpose written anywhere — what the space is for, what it is not — or will members work that out from whatever gets posted?

opts.t: Nothing. The channels are named; the purpose will emerge from whoever shows up.
I explain it in the invite message, a little differently each time I send one.
A short written statement, pinned where newcomers land: what this space is for, and what it is not.
The statement was written before the first invite — and no space of mine opens without one.

items.q: A registrant emails about your upcoming workshop: “Honestly — is this for someone at my level?” What produces the reply?
items.layman: When someone asks whether your course fits them, is there a written statement of who it is for and what they should already know — or do you weigh each asker case by case, from scratch?

opts.t: A case-by-case judgment call. I have never pinned down who the workshop is for.
I improvise from a sense of the typical attendee; the answer shifts with my mood.
A written line about who this serves and what they should already know — I quote it and let them decide.
That line was written before the workshop was priced — nothing of mine goes on sale without its who-this-is-for sentence.

items.q: The parts order for your hardware side project is one click from checkout. What, if anything, does the cart answer to?
items.layman: When you buy components for a physical build, is there a written statement of what you are making — even a sentence — that decides what belongs in the order, or does the pile of parts gradually define the product?

opts.t: Nothing. The cart is the plan — the product will be whatever the parts become.
A sketch on a whiteboard somewhere, roughly current.
A written line kept with the project — what this object is for — and parts that serve no line stay unbought.
The line predates the first order, and rereading it before checkout is the habit that keeps the bench from filling with maybes.

items.q: A well-made pull request arrives that would take your open-source project somewhere you never intended. What does your decision rest on?
items.layman: A “pull request” is a proposed change someone offers to your public code project. When a change does not fit your intentions, is there anything written about what the project is meant to be — or does the merge decision run on that day’s feeling?

opts.t: Mood and momentum. If the code is good, it probably goes in.
A settled instinct about what fits — real, but written nowhere the contributor could see.
A written note on what this project is meant to be; I check the request against it and answer from it.
The note has existed since the project’s first day, and my reply links to it — the contributor sees the reason, not just the verdict.

items.q: A forty-minute call with your subcontractor ends with a clear agreement about what happens next. Where is that agreement an hour later?
items.layman: A “subcontractor” is someone you hire to do part of your work. After you settle something on a call, does the decision get written down anywhere — or does it live in two memories that will quietly diverge?

opts.t: In two heads, already drifting apart.
In my rough call notes, findable if I ever need to argue about it.
Written and shared the same day — what was decided, who does what.
Written before we hang up, in the same place every decision goes — the call is not over until the sentence exists.

items.q: After some back-and-forth, you and your partner settle how the household will handle a recurring expense. A month later the question resurfaces. What settles it this time?
items.layman: When a household decision gets made, is it written down anywhere the two of you can point to — or does the same discussion happen again from memory?

opts.t: The same discussion, again, from scratch.
Whoever remembers the outcome more confidently wins.
A shared note where the decision was written — we point at it instead of re-arguing it.
The note, kept with every other settled household decision — writing the outcome down is how our discussions end.

items.q: Halfway through a long draft, you stop and ask yourself what this piece is actually arguing. Where do you look?
items.layman: Before you started writing, did you state the piece’s argument in a sentence you can return to — or does the argument only exist in whatever the draft has become?

opts.t: At the draft. The argument is whatever these paragraphs turn out to mean.
At my memory of the excitement that started it, which has faded.
At the sentence I wrote before drafting — the piece’s stated argument, kept at the top.
At that sentence, which every piece of mine gets before its first paragraph — no stated argument, no draft.

items.q: Three months into a retainer, the client asks what the engagement is meant to achieve this quarter. What do you consult before replying?
items.layman: A “retainer” is an ongoing paid arrangement with a client. Is the engagement’s current goal written down somewhere — one settled sentence — or do you reconstruct it from recent conversations each time it comes up?

opts.t: Nothing — I compose a plausible goal from the last few calls.
The proposal from three months ago, which no longer quite describes the work.
The goal we wrote down for this quarter — I restate it and check we still agree.
The written goal, which gets restated and re-agreed at each quarter’s start — the question has a standing answer before it is asked.

items.q: A buyer messages your shop asking whether your product will work for a use you never imagined. What do you check before answering?
items.layman: For each thing you sell, is its intended use written down — what it is for, what it is not built to do — or do you decide the product’s limits on the spot, per question?

opts.t: Nothing — I decide the product’s limits right there in the reply.
Old messages, to see what I told the last buyer who asked something similar.
The written intended-use note I keep per product — what it is for and what it is not built to do.
The note, which existed before the first listing — buyers mostly find its words in the listing and never need to ask.

items.q: A regular at the counter asks, without hostility, why your prices went up this year. What does your answer come from?
items.layman: When you change your prices, do you write down the reasoning — what the new price covers and why — or does each justification get invented in the moment it is demanded?

opts.t: Improvisation. The reasoning gets invented at the counter, differently per customer.
A half-remembered calculation from the week I changed the sign.
The note I wrote when I set the price — what it covers and why — retold in a sentence.
That note, which exists for every price in the shop — pricing changes start as writing, not as a new number on the sign.

items.q: You hand moderation of your community to its first volunteer. What do they receive besides the extra permissions?
items.layman: A “moderator” is someone who keeps a community space in order. When you hand that role over, does it come with one written document — what the space allows, what gets removed, how the gray areas lean — or with scattered advice? “Versioned” = kept with a history of its changes.

opts.t: The permissions and a “use your judgment” — the rules live in how I have behaved.
A scroll through old incidents and some advice in a direct message.
One written guide: what this space is for, what gets removed, and how the gray areas lean.
The guide, versioned — plus a checklist of worked examples we both judged, so we know our lines match.

items.q: Seats for your six-week course go on sale Friday. What exists, in writing, describing what those six weeks will actually deliver?
items.layman: Before selling a course, is there a syllabus — a structured document stating what each part covers, what students leave able to do, and what the course does not teach — or a sales page written from enthusiasm? “Cohort” = one group taking the course together. “Versioned” = kept with a history of changes.

opts.t: A sales page written from enthusiasm the night before.
Topic notes scattered across the slides I have started.
A syllabus: what each week covers, what students leave able to do, what this course does not teach.
The syllabus, versioned across cohorts — with a written checklist of what a student must be able to do for the course to count as delivered.

items.q: The first batch comes back from the fabricator wrong — in a way you realize you never actually specified. What did the order rest on?
items.layman: A “fabricator” is a shop that manufactures parts to order. When you sent the job, was there a specification — a document stating dimensions, materials, and what an acceptable part is — or a conversation with pictures? “Versioned” = each change kept with its history.

opts.t: A chat thread and some photos. The gaps were filled by their assumptions.
Annotated sketches, mostly right, scattered across messages.
A spec sheet: dimensions, materials, finish, and what an acceptable unit looks like.
The versioned spec, plus a written checklist of measurements every batch is judged against — this defect adds a line to it.

items.q: A stranger wants to contribute to your open-source project and asks what kinds of changes you would welcome. What can you point them to?
items.layman: For a public code project, is there a written contribution guide — what kinds of changes are wanted, what will be declined, how submissions are judged — or does each would-be contributor have to ask you? “Versioned” = kept with a history of its changes.

opts.t: Nothing — I answer each person individually, when I get to it.
A few scattered issue comments where I have explained my preferences before.
A contribution guide: what the project wants, what it will decline, and how submissions are judged.
The guide, versioned with the project — including the checklist a change must pass before I will look at it.

items.q: The same subcontractor has taken work from you most months this year. Where is it written how the two of you actually work — deadlines, revisions, what “finished” means?
items.layman: A “subcontractor” is someone you hire for part of your work. For an ongoing working relationship, is there one written agreement covering the standing rules — turnaround, revision limits, what counts as done — or do the rules live in precedent and goodwill? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: Nowhere. The rules are whatever we have drifted into.
Spread across a year of messages — each rule findable, none collected.
One working agreement: turnaround, revisions, rates, and what finished means for each kind of job.
The agreement, versioned as we learn — and each handoff cites the checklist its deliverable must pass.

items.q: The yearly round of family health admin — renewals, checkups, claims — is starting again. What does this year’s round run from?
items.layman: For recurring household administration, is there one written rundown — what has to happen, by when, what counts as handled — or does the season run on memory and whatever letters arrive? “Versioned” = updated each year with its history kept.

opts.t: Memory, and whatever envelopes arrive to remind us.
Last year’s scattered notes and a few calendar entries, partly stale.
One written rundown: every task, its deadline, and what handled means for each.
The rundown, versioned each year with what changed — and the round is not closed until every line is checked off.

items.q: Two weeks into a research project, every interesting source has pointed at three more. What keeps the inquiry from becoming infinite?
items.layman: Before open-ended research, do you write the question down — what you are trying to answer, what is deliberately out of bounds, what a sufficient answer looks like — or does the reading decide where the reading goes? “Scope” = the declared edges of the inquiry.

opts.t: Nothing. The reading decides where the reading goes.
A working title and a folder of saved links.
A written question with declared edges — what this inquiry covers, what it deliberately ignores, what a sufficient answer contains.
That page, revised in writing when the question legitimately shifts — plus the checklist an answer must meet before the reading stops.

items.q: On the kickoff call, two people at your client describe the campaign’s goal in two different ways. What ends the ambiguity?
items.layman: When client stakeholders disagree about what the work is for, is there a single written brief — objective, audience, message, exclusions — that everyone approves, or does the loudest recollection govern? “Brief” = a short document stating what is wanted and why. “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: Nothing yet — I keep both versions in mind and steer between them.
My meeting notes, which record the disagreement without resolving it.
A single brief — objective, audience, message, exclusions — circulated until both of them approve one text.
The brief, versioned and signed off against a checklist — later disagreements get settled by amending it, not by relitigating the call.

items.q: Your product sells on two marketplaces, and you notice the two listings now describe it differently. Which one is true?
items.layman: When the same product is described in several places, is there one master document — the product’s authoritative description, features, and limits — that every listing is written from, or is each listing its own little truth? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: Neither, exactly — each listing grew on its own, and the product sits somewhere between them.
The newer one, probably. I would have to read both to be sure.
The master product doc both listings were written from — the listings are copies, and the stray one gets corrected.
The versioned master doc — every listing change starts there, and a release checklist walks each marketplace copy back into line.

items.q: A custom order comes in at the counter — specific size, specific date, specific finish. What captures it?
items.layman: When you take custom work face to face, does each order get a structured written form — the specifics, the price, the pickup date, what is not included — or does the agreement live in the conversation?

opts.t: The conversation. We both nod, and the details ride home in two memories.
A line in my notebook with the size and a phone number.
An order form: the specifics, the price, the date, and what is not included — one copy for each of us.
The form, numbered and kept — changes get written onto it and initialed, and pickup is checked against it line by line.

items.q: A member asks in your community whether promoting their own product is allowed. A moderator answers within minutes, correctly, by quoting. Quoting what?
items.layman: A “moderator” is a volunteer keeping a community space in order. Can questions about what the space allows be answered by anyone from the written rules — or are you the only reliable source, because the real rules live with you?

opts.t: Nothing — questions like that sit until I appear, because only I know the answer.
Their memory of my past rulings, which is usually close but sometimes inverts one.
The written guidelines — the answer was on the page, and quoting it settled the matter.
The guidelines, which also told them this case was theirs to settle — the written boundary between what mods decide and what comes to me.

items.q: Another instructor will run your workshop in a city you will never visit. What do they teach from?
items.layman: If someone else delivers your course, do the materials alone carry it — the intent of each exercise, what to emphasize, what to skip when time runs short — or does a faithful delivery require hours of your live walkthrough?

opts.t: My walkthrough, delivered over several calls — the materials are slides that only I can narrate.
The slides plus my old session recordings; they reverse-engineer the intent.
A facilitator guide: each exercise’s purpose, the talking points, what to cut when time runs short.
The guide, plus written boundaries — what they may adapt to their room, and what must stay fixed for it to remain this workshop.

items.q: A friend with a good workshop offers to assemble the next ten units of your device. How much of you do they need?
items.layman: Could someone competent build your hardware from the written build documentation alone — parts, steps, tolerances, the checks along the way — or does a correct build require you at their shoulder? “Tolerances” = the allowed margins of error in a part’s dimensions.

opts.t: All of me — the build lives in my hands, so I would be standing at their bench for days.
A parts list and my photos; they would call me at every ambiguous step.
The build doc: parts, steps, tolerances, and the checks along the way — their questions are rare and real.
The doc plus its written stop-points — the places where they must pause and ask rather than improvise — so their ten units match mine.

items.q: A first-time contributor ships a substantial change to your open-source project with almost no back-and-forth. What did the aligning?
items.layman: When strangers contribute to your public code project, do the written materials — purpose, contribution guide, roadmap — align them before they start, or does every contribution get shaped through rounds of correction in review?

opts.t: Nothing usually does — contributions arrive misaimed and get reshaped through rounds of review.
The code itself; they inferred the intent from patterns, and half-guessed right.
The written materials — purpose, contribution guide, roadmap — the change arrived already aimed where the project is going.
Those, plus the written line between what can simply be submitted and what needs a discussion first — so even the disagreements arrive well-formed.

items.q: Your subcontractor chose speed over polish on yesterday’s deliverable without asking you. Whose call was that, really?
items.layman: A “subcontractor” is someone you hire for part of your work. When they face a trade-off — fast versus fine, cheap versus thorough — do your written project materials already state which way to lean, or does every judgment call become a gamble on reading your mind?

opts.t: A gamble on my mind — nothing written states the priorities, so every trade-off is a bet on my reaction.
Half mine — precedent from past corrections guided them, unevenly.
Mine, in advance — the project doc states the priorities, and they leaned the way the writing leans.
Mine, in advance and by tier — the doc ranks the priorities and marks which trade-offs are theirs and which must come back to me.

items.q: Three siblings share your father’s care admin. The pharmacy calls with a question while you are in a meeting. What happens?
items.layman: For shared family responsibilities, is the essential information — medications, history, decisions already made, preferences — written where any of you can act from it, or are you the sibling who holds it all?

opts.t: It waits for me. I am where the information lives, so everything routes through my phone.
A sibling answers from fragments in the group chat, then double-checks with me after.
Whichever sibling is free answers from the shared care file — it holds what the question needs.
The file answers it, and its notes say which decisions any sibling may make alone and which need all three — the call never needed me specifically.

items.q: A peer asks to build on your unpublished research and you send the working notes. What happens next?
items.layman: Could another researcher continue from your notes alone — the question, the method, what you found, what remains open — or do the notes only make sense with you talking over them?

opts.t: A long call, because the notes are private shorthand that only works with me narrating.
They proceed, misread two things, and we spend a week untangling what I actually meant.
They proceed correctly — the notes carry the question, the method, and the findings in full sentences.
They proceed, and the notes even mark what is settled versus still open — so they extend the work instead of re-arguing it.

items.q: Mid-engagement, your client hires a new marketing director, who reads the project file before your first call. How does that call open?
items.layman: When a new stakeholder inherits your engagement, can the written record brief them — what is being done, why, what was decided and ruled out — or does the relationship restart from your mouth?

opts.t: From zero — the file tells them little, so I re-pitch the whole engagement live.
With corrections — they arrive with a partial, slightly wrong picture assembled from fragments.
In the present tense — they arrive current on the work and the goals, and we spend the call on what is next.
In the present tense, with history — the record carries the reasoning behind past choices, so nothing already settled gets relitigated.

items.q: Five requests for custom work sit in your marketplace inbox this morning. How many ask for things you would never make?
items.layman: Does your shop state publicly, in writing, what you will customize and what you refuse — so strangers can rule themselves in or out before writing to you — or does every request require your personal no?

opts.t: Most of them — nothing public says what I refuse, so the inbox is where strangers find out.
Some — regulars have learned my lines, but each new buyer needs the no delivered personally.
Few — the shop states in writing what I customize and what I refuse, and requests mostly arrive inside the lines.
Almost none — the stated lines carry their reasons, and the rare edge case quotes my own words back to me while asking.

items.q: You take two real weeks of holiday and the shop stays open under your one employee. How often does your phone ring?
items.layman: Could your business run for a fortnight on its written material — prices, policies, how situations get handled — or is the knowledge in you, making every unusual customer a phone call?

opts.t: Daily — the shop’s knowledge is me, so every unusual customer becomes a call.
Every few days — my hasty pre-trip notes cover the till but not the judgment calls.
Rarely — the written policies answer the fortnight’s questions, and the employee acts on them without flinching.
Once, socially — the policies even say which decisions are theirs and which wait for my return, so nothing needed to ring.

items.q: A member appeals a moderator’s removal of their post in your community. What is the appeal judged against?
items.layman: A “moderator” removes posts that break a community’s rules. When a removal is contested, is there a written rule the decision cites and the appeal is tested against — with hard cases amending the rules — or does the appeal come down to whoever feels more strongly? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: Feelings — mine, theirs, and the mood of the room that day.
Memory of how similar cases went, argued from both sides.
The written rule the removal cited — and when a case fits no rule, the rules get amended, in writing.
The cited rule, in versioned guidelines — appeals are tallied per rule, and a rule that keeps generating appeals gets flagged for rewriting.

items.q: Your course page promises that students leave able to do three specific things. Cohort three just finished. Does anyone check?
items.layman: When you sell an outcome, do you treat the promise as criteria — checking each group’s actual results against it on a schedule, and revising the page or the course when they diverge — or does the promise just sit in the copy? “Cohort” = one group taking the course together.

opts.t: No. The promise is copy, not a measurement.
Informally — glowing messages feel like confirmation, silence feels like doubt.
Yes, on schedule — after each cohort, results are reviewed against the three promises, and the page or the course is revised in writing.
Structurally — each cohort’s exit work is scored against the promises, and a widening gap flags itself before I would have felt it.

items.q: The prototype on your bench keeps getting better and keeps not shipping. What, in writing, defines finished?
items.layman: For a physical product, did you write criteria for what the first shippable unit must be — and does anything check the build against them at set points — or does “done” recede as your standards rise? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: Nothing — finished is a feeling, and the feeling keeps moving.
A features list from months ago that no longer matches what I am polishing.
Written ship criteria for version one — and each build review checks the bench against the list, not against my mood.
Versioned criteria with a status against every line — the gap to shippable is visible at a glance, and raising the bar means editing the document, not just feeling dissatisfied.

items.q: Your library’s README promises “zero dependencies, under ten kilobytes.” A well-meant contribution would quietly break both. What catches it?
items.layman: A “README” is a code project’s front-page document; a “dependency” is other people’s code your project relies on; “the build” = the automatic process that assembles and checks the project when its code changes. When your project makes public promises about what it will remain, are they living criteria something actually checks each change against — or prose that drifts from the truth?

opts.t: Nothing — the promise is prose, and nobody rereads prose while merging.
Possibly me, during review, if I happen to remember what the README claims.
The release ritual — the stated promises are a checklist every release is walked through before it ships.
The build itself — the promises are encoded as automated checks, and a change that breaks the README’s word fails before it lands.

items.q: A subcontractor’s deliverable misses the mark. Before anything else — what gets checked against what?
items.layman: A “subcontractor” is someone you hire for part of your work; a “brief” is the written statement of what you wanted. When work disappoints, do you test the miss against the brief — was this actually written down? — and amend the brief’s template when it was not, or does the miss just become an opinion about the person?

opts.t: Nothing against nothing — I form an opinion about the person and vent.
The work against my intentions as I remember them, which is not quite a document.
The work against the brief, first — if the brief was silent, the brief’s template gains a line before the redo.
Same check, kept as a running record — misses are tallied by cause, and the template evolves on that evidence, so the same silence cannot bite twice.

items.q: In January you and your partner wrote a page about what money is for this year. It is August. What has that page been doing?
items.layman: When a household writes down its financial intent, does anything check reality against the page on a schedule — with deliberate amendments when life changes — or does the page become a relic of January’s optimism?

opts.t: Aging. Nobody has opened it since February.
Serving as ammunition, consulted mid-disagreement and then reshelved.
Governing, monthly — we review the month’s spending against the page and amend it in writing when life changes.
Governing continuously — spending is categorized against the page as it happens, and drift surfaces as a number before it becomes a discussion.

items.q: You list twelve candidate topics for next quarter’s issues of your publication. What do the twelve pass through before any get written?
items.layman: A “premise” here is your publication’s written statement of what it covers, for whom, and what it leaves alone. At planning time, are candidate ideas actually tested against that premise — rejections recorded — or does the calendar fill by enthusiasm? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: My enthusiasm, ranked. The premise, if one exists, is not consulted.
A vague felt sense of what my readers expect — applied unevenly.
The written premise — each candidate is tested against it at planning, and the rejects get recorded as rejects, with reasons.
The versioned premise — and the archive is audited against it each quarter, so the doc and the published record keep each other honest.

items.q: Every month, someone at your client proposes a tactic that quietly contradicts the strategy you both signed. What does each proposal run into?
items.layman: When agreed strategy exists in writing, is each new request openly measured against it — with deviations requiring a written amendment — or does the strategy erode one enthusiastic suggestion at a time? “Versioned” = changes kept with their history.

opts.t: My diplomacy. I absorb or deflect each one ad hoc, and the strategy quietly bends.
My memory of the strategy, asserted with confidence but with nothing on the table.
The signed strategy doc — each proposal is measured against it in the open, and going off-strategy requires amending it in writing.
The versioned doc plus a running request log — we can both see which parts of the strategy attract pressure, and those parts get reviewed on schedule.

items.q: A marketplace buyer asks for a bulk discount on a large order. What produces the number you quote?
items.layman: Do written pricing rules exist that produce your quotes — with off-rule exceptions logged and reviewed — or is each price a fresh negotiation with yourself?

opts.t: A fresh negotiation with myself, settled by mood and how the month is going.
Whatever I quoted the last similar buyer, if I can find the message.
The written pricing rules — the number falls out of them, and a deviation gets logged with its reason.
The rules, encoded where quoting happens — an off-rule price requires an explicit override, and the overrides are reviewed against the rules on schedule.

items.q: A customer arrives for a service your website still advertises — one you quietly stopped offering in spring. What should have made that impossible?
items.layman: Your public statements — website, printed menu, signage — describe what your business offers. Is there one authoritative service list that every surface is generated from and checked against on a schedule — or does each surface drift from reality at its own speed? “Canonical” = the single authoritative version; “render” = to generate a copy from that source.

opts.t: Nothing exists to prevent it — each surface gets updated when someone happens to notice.
My intention to update everything eventually, which spring evidently outran.
The standing review — on a schedule, every public statement is checked against what we actually offer, and changes propagate the same week.
An automated reconciliation runs on a schedule — every public surface is checked against the offering list, and any that has drifted is flagged before a customer hits it.

items.q: You decide, calmly and on your own schedule, to move your community to a different platform. What actually transfers?
items.layman: A community’s articulated identity — its stated purpose, rules, norms, accumulated decisions — can live in files you own, or it can be welded into one platform’s pinned posts, channel layout, and settings. “Charter” = the written statement of what the space is for and how it runs. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Canonical” = the single authoritative version. Which is yours?

opts.t: Members, at best. The space’s purpose, rules, and norms were the platform’s structure, and structure does not emigrate.
The words, roughly — I copy pins and rules out by hand, and the connective tissue stays behind.
Everything that matters — charter, rules, and decisions are canonical open files I own; the platform only displayed them.
Everything, provenly — the community has made a move like this before, governed by the same files, and members mostly noticed new furniture.

items.q: Your online course lives on a course platform. A corporate client asks you to deliver it as a two-day live training. How much must be rebuilt from scratch?
items.layman: A course’s substance — intended outcomes, the intent of each lesson, exercises, sequencing — can exist as a curriculum you own in plain files, with any platform build being one rendering of it. Or the platform’s lesson builder can be the course. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read. “Rendering” = one generated form of the same source. Which describes yours?

opts.t: Nearly all of it — the course exists as that platform’s lessons and quizzes; there is no course outside the builder.
Most of it — I can pull the videos and text out, but the design lives in the platform’s structure and my memory.
Little — the curriculum is owned open files (outcomes, lesson intents, exercises); the platform build is one rendering, the live training is another.
None, provenly — the same curriculum files have already produced more than one delivery form, and edits flow from the files outward.

items.q: A second manufacturer asks for your product’s design package so they can quote a batch. What can you send that they can actually build from?
items.layman: A hardware product’s design intent — drawings, dimensions, materials, tolerances, the reasoning behind choices — can live as a package in open formats any competent shop can use, or it can be entangled with one vendor’s proprietary tools and one factory’s tribal knowledge. “Tolerances” = the allowed margins of error in dimensions. “Open format” = file types any standard software can read.

opts.t: Not much — the design lives in one tool’s cloud project and one factory’s accumulated know-how; a quote would require untangling both.
Geometry only — exported shapes travel, but the tolerances, materials, and reasoning live in old threads with the first factory.
The package itself — drawings, specs, materials, tolerances, and the choices’ reasoning, in open formats, buildable by any competent shop.
The package, provenly — a second shop has already produced a conforming batch from it, and their questions were folded back into the documents.

items.q: A contributor mirrors your open-source repository to another code-hosting site, as your license allows. How much of the project’s mind makes the trip?
items.layman: “Mirroring” = copying a code repository to another hosting service; a “forge” = such a hosting service, with its issues, wiki, and discussion features. A project’s mind — purpose, roadmap, decisions, non-goals (what it refuses to become) — can live in files inside the repository itself, or in the forge’s features, which do not travel with the code. “Canon” = the single authoritative body of those files.

opts.t: Almost none — the purpose, plans, and decisions live in the forge’s issues, wiki, and discussion threads; the mirror is code without a mind.
A sliver — the README travels, but the roadmap and the reasoning stay behind in forge features.
All of it — purpose, roadmap, decision records, and non-goals are files in the tree; wherever the repository goes, the mind goes.
All of it, provenly — the project already operates from more than one forge, and the in-tree files are the canon both defer to.

items.q: For six months, the project with your subcontractor has lived in their workspace — their boards, their docs. The engagement is ending on good terms. What do you actually hold?
items.layman: A “subcontractor” is someone you hire for part of your work. When collaboration happens inside someone else’s tools, the project’s articulated intent — decisions, specs, reasoning — can quietly accumulate in their custody instead of yours. “Canonical” = the single authoritative version; “canon” = that authoritative body itself. “Open format” = plain files any tool can read.

opts.t: An invoice trail and my memory — the engagement’s record was their workspace, and it was never mine to keep.
A farewell export — the words arrive in a heap, the structure and decision history mostly do not.
The canon — decisions, specs, and reasoning lived in my open files throughout; their workspace was a work surface, not the record.
The canon, provenly — the next subcontractor has already started from those files alone, mid-stream, without an archaeology phase.

items.q: Your household runs on one company’s ecosystem of shared notes, lists, and calendars. Your partner announces they are switching phone platforms. What breaks?
items.layman: A household’s working agreements — plans, lists, key information, decisions — can be plain files both of you own regardless of device, or they can be welded to one vendor’s apps and sharing features. “Open format” = plain files any platform reads. “Canon” = the single authoritative body of those files.

opts.t: The system itself — our shared agreements and plans exist as that ecosystem’s features, and half the household is about to leave the building.
The sharing — the content survives as awkward exports, and we limp along on screenshots for a while.
Nothing important — the household canon is plain files both platforms read; the apps were always just windows.
Nothing, provenly — the household already runs across two ecosystems from the same files, and the switch is a settings afternoon.

items.q: You open the research notes you wrote ten years ago, looking for a thread you remember starting. What do you find?
items.layman: Notes hold their value only if future tools can read them. A research practice can keep its canon — questions, sources, findings, reasoning — in plain formats chosen to outlive any app, or inside whichever clever tool each era offered. “Canon” = the single authoritative body of your notes. “Open format” = plain files readable without a specific product. Which did past-you choose?

opts.t: Files in a proprietary format nothing I now own can open — which is to say, the notes barely exist.
A scattering — some readable fragments across old tools and exports, the thread itself lost between formats.
The thread — the notes are plain, open files, organized the same way then as now, and they open like they were written yesterday.
The thread, still load-bearing — those decade-old files sit in the same living canon my current work reads and cites, proven through every tool migration between then and now.

items.q: The two-year engagement ends well, and the client asks for “everything” — the strategy, the reasoning, the rules you built for them. What do they receive?
items.layman: Agency work produces articulated intent for the client — positioning, strategy, doctrine (accumulated rules and their reasons). That body of thought can exist as a portable canon in open formats the client’s own team can operate from, or as decks and pages entangled with your tools. “Canon” = the single authoritative body of that thinking. “Open format” = plain files any tool reads. “Stack” = the set of tools a team runs on.

opts.t: Decks — renderings of thinking whose working form was my workspace, which they do not get to keep.
Exports — my tool’s pages in bulk, structured for how I work, which their team will mine for fragments.
A portable canon — strategy, positioning, rules with their reasoning, in open formats their own stack can hold and their team can operate from.
The canon, provenly — their in-house team already runs quarter to quarter from it, and did so before the engagement even formally closed.

items.q: Your shop has grown, and you decide to open a second sales channel beside the marketplace where you started. How does the second channel get its words?
items.layman: A shop’s articulated identity — product descriptions, policies, positioning, what you refuse to sell — can live as a canon in files you own, rendered into whichever channel needs it, or it can exist only inside the first marketplace’s listing boxes. “Canon” = the single authoritative body of those files. “Rendered” = generated as a copy from that source. “Open format” = plain files any tool reads.

opts.t: From blank fields — the shop’s identity was typed straight into the first marketplace’s boxes, and only lives there.
From copy-paste — I migrate listing by listing, and the two channels begin drifting apart immediately.
From the canon — descriptions, policies, and positioning are my own files; each channel is a rendering of the same source.
From the canon, provenly — the second channel was generated from the files, and a wording change edits one file and reaches every channel.

items.q: A friend in another town wants to open a shop like yours — with your blessing, from your papers, using their own suppliers and systems. What can you hand them?
items.layman: A business’s way of operating — what it offers and refuses, its standards, its methods, its reasoning — can exist as a written doctrine buildable by someone else with different tools, or as habits welded to your particular premises, devices, and routines. “Doctrine” = your accumulated written rules and their reasons. “Open format” = plain files any tool reads.

opts.t: Good wishes — the shop’s way exists as my routines and my configured systems, and neither can be handed across a table.
A folder of fragments — supplier lists, a recipe binder, till settings — each assuming my exact setup to mean anything.
The doctrine — offer, standards, methods, refusals, and their reasons, in open files, buildable with their suppliers and their tools.
The doctrine, provenly — their shop already runs from it a town away, and the questions they asked while opening were written back into it.

items.q: Your most important tool vanishes tomorrow. What happens to your core workflow?
items.layman: If your favorite app or AI shut down tonight, could you rebuild your way of working somewhere else — because you understand how it works underneath, not just which buttons to press?

opts.t: I would be stuck for a long while.
I would limp along and slowly relearn a replacement.
I could rebuild the workflow on another stack within days.
The design is documented and tool-independent; migration is mostly execution.

items.q: How do you operate in a domain where you lack expertise?
items.layman: When you do not know a field, do you avoid it, trust AI blindly, or use AI while checking it against reality — experts, primary sources, or small real-world tests?

opts.t: I avoid it or outsource it entirely.
I ask AI and generally trust the answer.
I use AI, then verify against primary sources or experts.
I build small tests or experiments so reality — not confidence — grades the answer.

items.q: Something in your system breaks. What is your debugging posture?
items.layman: When something stops working, do you poke at it until it works again, or can you find the real cause — and prevent a repeat?

opts.t: Panic, then trial and error until it works.
Search and ask AI until it works, without fully knowing why.
Isolate, reproduce, fix — and understand the cause before closing it.
Instrumentation surfaced the cause before I looked; the fix ships with a regression check.

items.q: How deep does your understanding of your AI tools actually go?
items.layman: Do you know roughly how your AI tools work underneath — their limits, costs, and failure modes — or are they magic boxes that usually cooperate? A “context window” is how much text a model can consider at once, “tokens” are the pieces text is billed and measured in, and a “tool call” is the model invoking an external action.

opts.t: I use the chat box.
I know prompting patterns that tend to work.
I understand context windows, tokens, and tool calls — and design around them.
I understand the substrate well enough to rebuild the harness: APIs, memory, evaluation.

items.q: A dialog box appears mid-task: an error message, three lines of text, an OK button. What do you actually do with those three lines?
items.layman: When a tool shows an error, do you read what it says and use it, or dismiss it and hope the problem goes away? An “error message” is the tool’s own description of what went wrong.

opts.t: Click OK and try the same thing again, harder.
Paste it into a search or an AI without really reading it, and follow whatever comes back.
Read it. Most errors say what went wrong — I use the message to work out my next move.
Read it, and if it is new to me, reproduce it on purpose once — so I know exactly what triggers it.

items.q: Your daily tool has a menu item you have never once clicked. It has been there for two years. What is your relationship with it?
items.layman: Do you deliberately explore the tools you rely on — reading what a feature does, trying it on something unimportant — or do you use the three buttons you know and treat the rest as scenery?

opts.t: Nonexistent. I use the buttons I know and treat the rest as decoration.
I will click it the day a problem forces me to.
I have skimmed what it does; when a feature looks useful I read the docs and try it deliberately.
I run small experiments with unused features — a few minutes on a throwaway file — because that is how I found half my current workflow.

items.q: You follow a tutorial step by step, and at step four your screen shows something the tutorial does not. What happens next?
items.layman: Tutorials go stale — apps change their menus faster than guides change their screenshots. When the instructions and reality disagree, do you stop, or can you work out what the step was trying to achieve?

opts.t: I stop. The tutorial is broken, so I am stuck.
I hunt for a newer tutorial that matches my screen exactly.
I work out what step four was trying to achieve and find the equivalent in my version.
Same — and I note the difference, because next time the gap between docs and reality will be somewhere else.

items.q: After an hour of trial and error, the export finally comes out right. You needed the same export two months ago and fumbled it then too. What happens in the next five minutes?
items.layman: When you finally get a fiddly thing to work, do you capture how — a note, a saved copy of the settings — or trust that future-you will remember what present-you barely reconstructed?

opts.t: Relief. I move on, and in two months I will fumble it again.
I try to memorize the trick, which works until it doesn’t.
I write down the steps and the setting that mattered, somewhere I will look first next time.
I write it down and test the note — could I redo it cold from what I wrote? If not, I fix the note.

items.q: A tool does something you did not expect — the file lands in a different folder, the AI answers a question you did not ask. Mildly surprising, easily ignored. Do you look into it?
items.layman: When a tool behaves surprisingly but harmlessly, do you shrug, or spend two minutes finding out why? A surprise is usually the tool telling you your mental picture of it is wrong somewhere.

opts.t: No. If it still basically works, surprises are background noise.
I make a mental note to be careful around that behavior.
I spend a couple of minutes finding out why — a surprise means my picture of the tool is wrong somewhere.
I reproduce it deliberately until I can predict it. Predicting a tool is the test of understanding it.

items.q: You install a new app you expect to use daily. What does your first hour with it look like?
items.layman: When you adopt a tool, do you click around and hope, or deliberately learn it — a pass through the getting-started guide, a test run on something unimportant, a look at what it does with your data?

opts.t: I click around until something works and settle into whatever I stumble on.
I watch a video overview, then mostly wing it.
A pass through the getting-started guide and a deliberate test run on something that doesn’t matter.
Guide, test run, and a short list of questions to answer before I trust it — what it does with my data, where its limits are.

items.q: The thing that worked yesterday fails today. You changed nothing — as far as you know. What is your first move?
items.layman: When a tool suddenly misbehaves, do you assume it hates you, or ask the obvious question: what changed? An update, a different file, a new setting — something is always different.

opts.t: Retry it several times, then give up or wait for it to fix itself.
Restart everything and hope.
Ask what changed — an update, a different input, a setting — and check the most likely one first.
Check what changed, and when I find it, note the culprit — my list of usual suspects is built from exactly these mornings.

items.q: You need a spreadsheet formula you do not know, so you copy one from the internet. It works. Do you know what it does?
items.layman: A “formula” here is spreadsheet logic — the =SOMETHING(…) that computes a cell. When you borrow one, do you learn what its parts mean, or paste and pray it keeps working when your data changes?

opts.t: No, and I would rather not touch it in case it breaks.
Roughly. I could not change it without breaking it.
I take a few minutes to learn what each part does, so I can adjust it when my data changes.
I learn it, then rebuild it from scratch once without looking — the fastest way I know to make it mine.

items.q: The tool offers two modes for the same job — “fast” and “accurate”, say — and you must pick one for a task that matters. How do you pick?
items.layman: When a tool offers options you don’t understand, do you guess, or run a small comparison on something unimportant so you can see the difference for yourself?

opts.t: Whichever is the default. Options are for other people.
I ask around or search for which one people prefer.
I read what each actually does, then try both on a small sample and compare.
I keep a scratch file for exactly these experiments — two minutes of testing beats a guess I would have to defend later.

items.q: An AI gives you six steps to fix a problem in your accounting tool. The steps work. What did you gain besides a fixed problem?
items.layman: When an AI walks you through a fix, do you follow blindly — cured but no wiser — or track what each step did, so the next problem of this kind is yours to fix?

opts.t: A fixed problem. I could not repeat the fix tomorrow without asking again.
A vague sense of which part of the tool the problem lives in.
I follow along asking what each step does, so next time this class of problem is mine to fix.
Afterward I test which step actually mattered — half of them usually don’t — and keep the one-line version.

items.q: It is invoicing day. The run touches your time records, your invoicing tool, and your email. Where does the knowledge of how to do it correctly live?
items.layman: For a recurring task that crosses several tools, is there a written procedure — the steps in order, what each step needs, what to check before sending — or does it live in your head and go slightly differently each month?

opts.t: In my head, loosely. Each month it goes slightly differently.
In my head, firmly — I have done it so often I rarely slip. Rarely.
