In a written procedure: the steps in order, the inputs each step needs, and what to check before anything is sent.
In a procedure I actually open each time, with a change history — when a step burned me, the document got the scar.

items.q: A peer asks, “When you publish a post, what actually happens between hitting save and it appearing on your site?” Can you answer?
items.layman: Can you name the moving parts of your own setup — this tool hands the file to that service, which does this to it — or is the middle of the process a fog that usually clears on its own?

opts.t: Honestly, no. I hit save and the site updates. The middle is fog.
I can name the tools involved but not what each one actually does.
I can walk them through it part by part: what each piece takes in, what it hands to the next.
I keep a simple diagram of it, and when reality surprises me, the diagram is what I correct.

items.q: Data moves from your form tool into your spreadsheet and the dates arrive scrambled. Is this a mystery or a diagnosis?
items.layman: When two tools disagree about a format — dates, names, currencies — do you know what each side expects at the handoff, or do you just retry the transfer and resent both tools?

opts.t: A mystery. I retype the dates by hand and resent the tools.
A familiar annoyance — I have a trick that usually unscrambles them, though I couldn’t say why it works.
A diagnosis. I know what format each side expects, so I can say where the scrambling happens and fix that.
Diagnosed once, written down: my notes list what each tool expects at every handoff, so the next mismatch is a lookup, not an investigation.

items.q: Your fix for the sync problem is “turn it off and turn it on again” — and it works. Do you know what the restart actually resets?
items.layman: Rituals that work are still rituals. Do you know which part of the tool the fix clears — a stuck connection, a stale saved copy (a “cache”) — or only that the incantation succeeds?

opts.t: No idea. It works, and I am not going to jinx it by asking questions.
I assume it clears something stuck, somewhere.
I know which part it resets — a stale cache — which also tells me the gentler fix for when a restart is inconvenient.
I traced what keeps going stale and why; my notes now say when to expect it and which of three fixes fits which symptom.

items.q: Your laptop dies on a Tuesday. Setting up its replacement, how much of your working environment do you reconstruct from memory?
items.layman: Is your setup — the tools, the settings that matter, the order to install things — written down anywhere, or does rebuilding it mean archaeology through your own habits?

opts.t: All of it. Weeks later I am still discovering missing pieces mid-task.
Most of it — I remember the big tools and rediscover the small settings the hard way.
Little of it. A setup document lists the tools, the settings that matter, and the order to install them.
The document exists, and the last rebuild followed it literally — every line that had drifted from reality got corrected on the spot.

items.q: Your file-storage tool emails you: you are near your plan’s limit. Is this news?
items.layman: Do you know your own usage numbers — how much you store, send, or process in a month — and the ceilings of the plans you are on? Or do the tools know, and you find out by email?

opts.t: Complete news. I don’t know my usage or what my plan allows.
Half news — I knew I was a heavy user, but the numbers are the tool’s business, not mine.
Not news. I know my usage roughly and the plan’s ceiling exactly, so I saw this coming.
I keep a one-page inventory of every tool’s limits against my actual numbers — reviewed when my usage shifts, not when emails arrive.

items.q: Your AI writing assistant produces a draft that ignores half your instructions. Do you know what the assistant could actually see when it wrote?
items.layman: AI tools work from what is in front of them — the instructions, documents, and chat history they were given, usually with a size limit. Do you have a working picture of what yours can and cannot see, or is its attention a mystery?

opts.t: See? It sees what I typed, presumably. The rest is mystery.
I have noticed patterns — long chats make it forgetful — but couldn’t say why.
Yes. I know what it was given, what it wasn’t, and where its size limit sits — “ignored instructions” usually means I buried them.
I keep notes per assistant: what it is shown, where the limit bites, and how I order instructions so the important ones survive.

items.q: The client deliverable is finished at midnight, and their system wants it in a specific file format. What do you know about that format’s hidden traps before you hit send?
items.layman: A “deliverable” is the concrete thing the client receives. File formats and export tools hide traps — an export that silently caps rows, text encoding the receiving system misreads, a long field that quietly truncates. Is that knowledge written next to your sending procedure, or discovered whenever a client discovers it?

opts.t: Traps? The file downloaded, so it is done. Whatever their system makes of it is their weather.
I know arrivals sometimes go wrong, so I eyeball the file before sending and hope tonight isn’t one of those nights.
The traps this format hides are written next to the procedure — the silent row cap, the encoding their system expects, the field that truncates — and I check exactly those before sending.
That, and when anything in the chain changes — my tool updates, their system migrates — I probe the handoff on a test file for new traps before real work rides it.

items.q: The same failure interrupts you most weeks — the upload stalls, the export truncates. When it happens, what do you reach for?
items.layman: For a failure you meet regularly, do you have written, ordered checks — look at this first, then this, and what each result means — or do you re-improvise the investigation each time from anecdotes?

opts.t: Nothing. Each time I flail through the same rediscovery.
Memory. There are three things that usually fix it, in an order I improvise.
A written page: the checks in order, what each one rules out, and the fix for each cause.
The page — which I actually open rather than trust my memory of it — and every new cause gets a line the day it appears.

items.q: A snippet someone gave you years ago still runs your weekly report. Your data format changed slightly. Can you touch the snippet?
items.layman: A “snippet” is a small piece of reusable code or formula. When one you rely on needs adjusting, can you name its parts and change the right one — or is it a sealed black box that must never be disturbed?

opts.t: Touch it? I arrange my data around the snippet. It must never be disturbed.
I can tweak the obvious numbers in it; anything structural means finding a different snippet.
Yes. I have read it and know what each part does, so the change is small and confident.
I rewrote it myself long ago — understanding it beat depending on it — and my version carries notes for the next change.

items.q: You hand a subcontractor a piece of build work you have never done yourself. Their invoice says done. What can you actually tell about the work?
items.layman: When you pay someone for work in a domain you only partly know, can you specify it precisely and spot a wrong or lazy result — or must you take “done” on faith? A “spec” is the written statement of what the work must do.

opts.t: That it cost what it cost. I take “done” on faith.
I can tell whether it looks finished — the surface, not the substance.
I specced it tightly enough to judge it: I know what right looks like and can spot a wrong or lazy result.
The spec included acceptance checks — small tests that pass only if the work is actually right — so reality judges it before I do.

items.q: A client asks you to quote a fixed price for work that is one-third familiar, two-thirds new to you. Where does your number come from?
items.layman: Estimating unfamiliar work is a test of understanding: can you break the job into parts, know which parts you truly understand, and treat the rest honestly — or does one confident-sounding number cover the fog?

opts.t: Gut, doubled. One confident number covers the fog.
I ask an AI or a peer what such work usually costs and quote that.
I decompose it: the parts I understand get real estimates, and I can name exactly which parts are fog and why.
The fog gets a timeboxed probe — a day of real attempt — so the final quote is priced by evidence, not bravado.

items.q: An AI wrote the configuration that will move your client’s data tonight. You didn’t write a line of it. What stands between it and running?
items.layman: “Configuration” here means written instructions a tool executes — code by another name. When an AI produces work you must ship, can you read it well enough to catch a wrong step, and check it against something sturdier than its confidence?

opts.t: Nothing. It looked plausible and the AI seemed sure.
I ran it once on nothing important and it didn’t complain.
I read it line by line — I know this domain well enough to catch a wrong step — and checked the risky parts against the official docs.
I ran it on a rehearsal copy of the real data and compared the result to what I predicted. Reality graded it before the client’s data met it.

items.q: Two competing tools could fill the same slot in your stack. Their websites both say they are the obvious choice. How do you decide?
items.layman: A “stack” is the set of tools your work runs on. When choosing between two similar tools, do you judge on popularity and marketing, or against requirements you understand — and can you design a fair comparison?

opts.t: The more popular one. A million users can’t be wrong.
I ask an AI for a comparison and take its recommendation.
I write down my actual requirements first, then read past the marketing — docs, limits, pricing edges — and judge each against my list.
Shortlist, then a head-to-head trial on a slice of my real workload, scored against criteria I fixed before I started.

items.q: The client dashboard that took two seconds now takes thirty. Nothing is broken — just slow. Can you say where the time is going?
items.layman: When a system slows down, understanding means naming the stages a request passes through, forming a guess about which stage is eating the time, and checking the guess — rather than restarting things at random.

opts.t: No. I restart things at random and escalate to hoping.
I can guess the usual suspect, and I pay for a bigger plan to make the guess irrelevant.
Yes. I can name the stages the request passes through, form a hypothesis about which one is eating the time, and check it.
I time each stage with a quick measurement first — the numbers pick the suspect, and my hypothesis starts where the evidence points.

items.q: A vendor demos a tool that will “solve your whole content problem.” The demo is genuinely impressive. What do you ask before believing it?
items.layman: Judging a pitch requires knowing your own requirements well enough to ask the questions the demo was designed to avoid — your data volumes, your edge cases, how you leave. Can you interrogate a claim, or only admire it?

opts.t: Nothing. If the demo works, I sign up and find the limits later.
I check reviews and what people on forums say about it.
The disqualifying questions my requirements imply — the ones the demo avoided: my data volumes, my edge cases, how I get my data out.
I define success criteria first, then run a pilot on my real work. The claim gets graded by my data, not their demo.

items.q: A peer wants to copy your stack wholesale. Which parts do you tell them not to copy?
items.layman: A “stack” is the set of tools your work runs on. Understanding a stack means knowing not just what each part does, but why it is there, what it trades away, and which choices only make sense for your particular situation.

opts.t: None — I couldn’t say which parts are load-bearing and which are habits.
I can list the tools and vouch that they work for me. Why, exactly, is thinner ice.
Several — I know why each part is there, what it trades away, and which choices only make sense for my situation, not theirs.
I ask about their constraints first and redesign the stack for them — the parts were always answers to questions, and their questions differ.

items.q: Your documented procedure covers the normal case. Today’s case is abnormal — the procedure’s step three simply does not apply. What happens?
items.layman: A procedure you understand can be adapted; a procedure you merely follow cannot. Off the standard path, can you reason about what each step was for, improvise a sound detour — and know that it is sound?

opts.t: The work stops until someone or something tells me what to do.
I improvise something plausible and hope the difference didn’t matter.
I know what step three was protecting against, so I can design a detour that protects the same thing — and say why it is sound.
I test the detour on a disposable copy first, and the abnormal case gets a written variant — the procedure grows.

items.q: A problem you diagnosed painfully in March returns in June, wearing a slightly different shirt. What greets it?
items.layman: When the same class of problem recurs, does your past effort compound — a written diagnosis you reread, a check that recognizes it — or do you pay the full diagnostic price again? A “regression check” is a small automatic test that fails if an old problem returns.

opts.t: The same panic as March. June-me starts from zero.
A nagging déjà vu. I re-derive most of the diagnosis before remembering I have done this before.
March’s write-up. The cause, the fix, and the shortcut are recorded where June-me looks first.
A regression check caught it before I did — March’s diagnosis became a test, so the problem announces itself.

items.q: At 6 p.m. you finally crack why the sync corrupts the occasional record — a timezone edge case. The fix works. What ships along with it?
items.layman: A fix can travel alone or with company: a small automatic check that fails if the problem ever returns (a “regression check”), and a note on the cause. Do your fixes accumulate protection, or just relief?

opts.t: Nothing ships — I nudge the corrupted records by hand and stay watchful.
The fix ships alone. The understanding retires with the adrenaline.
The fix, a regression check for that timezone case, and a line in my notes on the cause.
That, plus a sweep for siblings — an edge case rarely travels alone, so the check covers the class, not the instance.

items.q: You catch your research agent confidently citing a paper that does not exist. You fix the report. What happens to the catch itself?
items.layman: An “agent” is an AI doing multi-step work for you. When you catch it making a class of error, the catch can be spent once — one fixed report — or invested: the cause understood, and the catch turned into a permanent automatic test (an “eval”) that future runs must pass.

opts.t: Nothing. I fix the report and trust myself to catch the next one.
I add “do not invent citations” to the instructions and hope that holds.
I work out why it fabricated — where the task invited invention — and add a citation-existence check its output must pass.
The catch joins a growing eval suite every run is graded against; my corrections are the curriculum.

items.q: Under deadline, you duct-taped a workaround into the system. The deadline passed three weeks ago. Where is the duct tape?
items.layman: A “workaround” is a quick patch that dodges a problem without fixing its cause. The question is whether workarounds get revisited — cause understood, patch replaced or knowingly adopted — or silently become architecture.

opts.t: What duct tape? Whatever I did that week is invisible to me now.
Still there. It works, so it has quietly become part of the system.
Gone or legitimized: I went back, understood the actual cause, and either fixed it properly or kept the patch knowingly — documented as a decision.
It was logged in a workaround register the day I made it, with a review date — duct tape that cannot silently become architecture.

items.q: A silent limit burned you last quarter — the export truncates at 10,000 rows, and you shipped a report missing a month. Where does that lesson live now?
items.layman: Tools have limits that fail without an error — size caps, quiet truncation. Once a limit has cost you, is the knowledge recorded where you will meet it again — a “runbook” is your written procedure for the task — or better, enforced by a check that refuses to let the mistake repeat?

opts.t: In the apology email I sent the client. Otherwise, nowhere.
In me. I flinch near big exports now, which works until I am busy.
In the runbook, at the step where it bites: the limit, how it fails, and the check to run — written where future-me will actually reread it.
In a guard: the workflow now counts what went in against what came out, and refuses to proceed on a mismatch. The lesson enforces itself.

items.q: Your monthly AI bill arrives at triple the usual. Is the bill the first you are hearing of it?
items.layman: Systems have cost models — which tasks burn money and why. “API costs” are per-use charges for AI and other services. Do you understand your system’s cost drivers well enough to notice a spike before the invoice does?

opts.t: Yes — and honestly the usual amount is also a mystery to me.
Yes. I investigate after the bill, find a plausible culprit, and turn something off.
Mostly no. I understand which tasks drive cost and why, so the bill confirms a story I can already tell — and the fix ships with a note on the cause.
No. Cost per task is tracked and an alert fired in week one; the spike was diagnosed while it was still small.

items.q: You open a corner of your system you have not touched since winter. How well do the notes you find there match what is actually running?
items.layman: Understanding decays as systems change. The question is whether your recorded knowledge — notes, diagrams, runbooks (written procedures) — is updated as part of making changes, or drifts until it is fiction with a confident tone.

opts.t: There are no notes. Winter-me trusted winter-me’s memory.
Notes exist but describe an earlier system — fiction with a confident tone.
They match. Updating the notes is part of making a change, not a chore for later.
They match, and I would know if they didn’t — a periodic check compares what the notes claim against what is actually configured.

items.q: You are adopting a new tool next week. What do the scars from its predecessors contribute?
items.layman: Every tool that failed you taught you a failure mode — silent data loss, surprise limits, hostile exports. Do those lessons exist as a recorded list the new tool must be tested against, or do you learn each one again, personally?

opts.t: Nothing. Each tool gets to teach me the same lessons personally.
Instinct. I feel vague distrust in certain areas but test nothing in particular.
A written vetting list built from past failures — every way a tool has burned me is now a question I ask the next one before trusting it.
The list, plus rehearsal: I deliberately push the new tool to the old failure points on disposable data and record what it did.

items.q: Explain your system to a sharp peer — with one rule: no product names allowed. How far do you get?
items.layman: A system understood at the level of concepts can be described as data flowing between responsibilities, rules that must always hold (“invariants”), and known ways it fails — without naming a single vendor. A system understood at the level of buttons cannot.

opts.t: Not far. My explanation is a guided tour of specific screens; ban the names and the knowledge goes silent.
I can gesture at what the parts accomplish, but every precise statement reaches for a product name.
All the way. The design exists in my head and my docs as data flow, invariants, and failure modes — the products are just the current cast.
All the way, and it has been tested: that vendor-free description has already guided a working build on tools I don’t use.

items.q: Your automation platform doubles its prices overnight. Setting the migration labor aside — how much of your understanding of your own system would survive the move?
items.layman: An “automation platform” is the service your automated workflows run on. Understanding can live at two levels: the vendor’s idioms — their triggers, their modules — or the design underneath: what flows where, what must always hold. Only one of those levels survives a move.

opts.t: Little. What I know is how to work that platform, not what my system actually does.
Some. The big picture would survive; the thousand load-bearing details are written in the vendor’s idioms and would need re-deriving.
Nearly all. The design is documented in vendor-neutral terms; moving is translating a design I understand into a new dialect.
All — demonstrated, not hoped: a slice of the system already runs on an alternative, ported deliberately so this decision could never hold me hostage.

items.q: The rules that route your leads exist as forty conditions built in your no-code tool’s visual editor. If that editor is the only place they exist, what do you actually own?
items.layman: A “no-code tool” is software where you build logic by clicking rather than coding. Logic that exists only inside one vendor’s editor is understanding held in escrow — readable there and nowhere else. The question is whether it also exists as a plain written specification anyone could reimplement.

opts.t: The subscription. The logic exists only in those forty boxes; I reread my own thinking through their interface or lose it.
Exports and screenshots — the logic preserved in a form only that vendor can revive.
A plain written specification of the rules — what routes where, and why — that the visual editor merely implements. Anyone could rebuild it from the page.
The specification is the source of truth: changes are written there first, then mirrored into the tool — and it has been reimplemented elsewhere once, as proof.

items.q: The AI model your whole quality bar was tuned against is deprecated next month. What happens to your knowledge of what good output means?
items.layman: “Deprecated” means the vendor is retiring it. “Evals” are saved test cases with graded answers, used to measure output quality. Quality knowledge can live as model-specific incantations — phrasings that worked on one model — or as portable definitions and test cases that can grade any model.

opts.t: It expires with the model. My quality bar was a feel for that model’s moods.
It partially survives. My prompts are incantations tuned to its quirks; I would rediscover “good” by trial and error on the successor.
It survives intact. Quality is written down as model-independent criteria and eval cases — the successor gets graded against the same bar on day one.
The swap is routine. The evals already run against multiple models on a schedule, so I knew the successor’s scores before the deprecation email arrived.

items.q: Imagine rereading your operational notes two years and one full tool change from now. How much would still be true?
items.layman: Notes can be written at the level of clicks — “press Export, choose CSV” — or at the level of design: “the ledger is the source of truth; everything else can be regenerated.” Click-level notes die with the tool; design-level notes outlive it.

opts.t: There are no notes to reread.
Little. The notes are click-by-click paths through tools I would no longer be using.
Most. The notes separate design from operation — the what-must-hold-and-why outlives any tool; only the thin “click here” layer needs rewriting.
This has already happened once: the design layer survived the last migration untouched, and the port only rewrote the tool appendix.

items.q: A client loves your internal system and asks you to build them the same thing — inside their environment, on their tools, none of which you use. Can you take the job?
items.layman: A “stack” is the set of tools a system runs on. Rebuilding your own capability on someone else’s stack is the hardest test of understanding: nothing transfers except the design — what flows where, what rules must hold, what failures need detecting. If your knowledge lives in your tools, it cannot make the trip.

opts.t: No. Without my tools I don’t actually know how to build what I run.
Reluctantly — I would be reverse-engineering my own system from the outside, rediscovering decisions I never wrote down.
Yes. The design is documented tool-independently — data flow, rules, failure modes — so their stack is an implementation detail I can price.
Yes, and I have done it before. Ported once already — and each port fed its corrections back into the design docs.

items.q: Your main vendor ships a glossy new feature that could replace a piece of your system. Six such features have shipped over two years. What shape is your system now?
items.layman: Vendors pull systems toward their own idioms, one convenient feature at a time. The question is whether your documented design remains the reference — features adopted only where they serve it — or whether the system has slowly become a portrait of the vendor’s roadmap.

opts.t: The vendor’s shape. I adopt what they ship; my system is a portrait of their roadmap.
Mixed. Some adoptions were choices, many were drift — I could no longer draw the line between my design and their defaults.
My shape. A documented design is the reference; each feature is judged as an implementation detail and adopted only where it serves the design.
My shape, enforced at the boundary: vendor specifics stay quarantined behind interfaces I defined, so any adopted feature can be swapped back out — and at least one has been.

items.q: Someone asks you: in what ways can your system silently lie to you? Where does your answer come from?
items.layman: “Silently lie” means fail without an error — stale data presented as fresh, a partial sync that looks complete. Deep understanding includes a catalog of failure modes: what can go wrong and how each would be detected. A “stack” is the set of tools a system runs on; the catalog can be portable knowledge, or vendor-specific scar tissue.

opts.t: From scars, incompletely. I know the lies that have already burned me, and only those.
From a trawl through one vendor’s support threads and my old tickets — knowledge filed in a dialect only that tool understands.
From a written catalog in tool-independent terms: each failure mode, what causes it, how it would be detected — true of the design, whatever implements it.
From the catalog and its probes: each entry is paired with a live check, and the checks have run on more than one stack — the catalog is proven, not just written.

items.q: An engineer takes over daily operation of your system while you step back. She has never seen your tools, and the nightly jobs will not pause for her learning curve. What keeps the system alive through her first month?
items.layman: Running a system is its own knowledge: the rules that must never be violated (“invariants”), the written procedures for routine jobs (“runbooks”), what to watch to catch trouble early, and the ways it can fail without an error. Does that knowledge exist as a document that stands on its own, or as your reflexes inside particular tools?

opts.t: Me, on call. How to operate it lives in my reflexes for these particular tools — she runs it by asking me.
A pile of vendor-flavored notes — which buttons in which dashboards — that will expire with the tools and still assume my memory for the whys.
An operations document that stands alone: the invariants she must not violate, the runbook for each routine job, what to monitor, and the ways it can fail silently — written in terms no vendor owns.
That document, proven: someone has already run a real stretch from it without me, and every question she had to ask became a new line in it.

items.q: You need a capability no vendor sells — a strange join between your billing history and your writing archive. What do you build it from?
items.layman: A system understood at the design level has documented interfaces — defined points where its parts exchange data — so its owner can extend it personally. A system understood as a set of subscriptions can only grow by waiting for vendors.

opts.t: Nothing. If no vendor sells it, my system doesn’t do it.
A contortion — I bend an existing tool sideways until something approximately similar happens.
The system itself. Its interfaces are documented well enough that I can write the new piece against them and know it belongs.
The same materials as always: the system has grown by my hand repeatedly, each extension documented to the same standard as the core — vendors fill slots in my design, not the reverse.

items.q: Your marketplace dashboard shows a number called “conversion” that has been falling for a month. You have never been quite sure what it counts. What do you do with it?
items.layman: “Conversion” here is the share of people who view your listing and then buy. When a dashboard shows a number you cannot define, do you find out exactly what it counts before reacting to it, or act on the vibe of the graph?

opts.t: Nothing. It is one of several numbers I scroll past on the way to my sales total.
I assume it means fewer people are buying and try things at random until the line turns.
I look up what the number actually counts — views, clicks, purchases — so I know what a falling line can and cannot mean.
I did that when I first opened the dashboard; every number I glance at weekly is one I could define, and the rest I ignore on purpose.

items.q: The shared family calendar has double-booked the same weekend twice this term — an invitation someone accepted never showed up for you. What do you make of it?
items.layman: Shared calendars follow rules — who owns an event, which calendar an invitation lands on, what accepting actually does. When yours misfires, do you learn those rules, or add workarounds like texting everyone to confirm?

opts.t: The calendar is unreliable, so we confirm the important things by message instead.
I am more careful now — I open the app and check the weekend by eye before agreeing to anything.
I sat down and worked out how invitations actually land — whose calendar owns what — and found the setting that was eating them.
That, and I sent a test invitation between our accounts afterward to confirm the fix — the calendar earned its trust back on evidence.

items.q: The label printer for your small product line starts printing every third label askew. The manual has a troubleshooting section you have never opened. What happens?
items.layman: When a physical device misbehaves, do you consult what its maker wrote about it — the manual, the settings — or jiggle parts until it cooperates?

opts.t: I jiggle the roll, reprint the bad ones, and accept askew labels as a cost of doing business.
I search a forum for someone with the same printer and try whatever they tried.
I open the troubleshooting section — misfeeds are usually in there, and the fix teaches me what the feed mechanism needs.
I read it, fix it, and keep the symptom and cure written inside the supply box — the next misfeed will be a lookup, not an afternoon.

items.q: Your course platform announces that its lesson editor will be replaced next month. Your whole course lives in the old one. What do you do before the switch?
items.layman: When a tool you rely on schedules a change, do you meet the change early — read what differs, try the new version on something unimportant — or wait to be surprised on the day it lands?

opts.t: Nothing. I will find out what changed when my lessons open in it.
I skim the announcement and trust that platforms rarely break things badly.
I read what is changing and rebuild one throwaway lesson in the new editor now, so switch day holds no surprises.
I do that early and keep a short list of what behaves differently — the differences I find on a throwaway lesson are ones my real course will not have to teach me.

items.q: A subcontractor delivers their work as a file type you have never seen — the icon is blank and double-clicking gets you nowhere. What is your move?
items.layman: A file type (its “format”) determines which programs can open it. When you meet an unfamiliar one, do you learn what it is and how to open it, or make it someone else’s problem?

opts.t: I reply asking them to resend it as something normal.
I upload it to the first “open any file” website a search turns up and hope for the best.
I look up what the format is and what opens it — two minutes that usually also teach me why they chose it.
I do that, and keep a running note of formats I have met and what opens them — by now most deliveries are a lookup away.

items.q: Your reference manager inserts citations in the wrong style for the journal you are writing for. You have been correcting each one by hand. Is there another way?
items.layman: A reference manager stores your sources and inserts citations in a chosen style — the punctuation-and-order rules a publication requires. When output is wrong, do you fix the setting that governs it, or fix each symptom by hand?

opts.t: Hand-correcting works. The settings screen is where I would break something worse.
I asked a colleague once for the fix and will ask again when it recurs.
I find the style setting and learn how the tool decides formatting — one change upstream beats fifty corrections downstream.
I learned the setting, tested it on a scratch document, and noted where it lives — wrong-style output is now a thirty-second fix.

items.q: Your community platform’s spam filter keeps holding back a longtime member’s perfectly ordinary posts. You keep approving them one by one. Do you know why it flags them?
items.layman: A spam filter holds posts that match certain rules — links, certain words, posting speed. When it misfires, do you learn which rule is tripping, or just clear the queue each time?

opts.t: No. Approving takes one click; understanding sounds like a hobby.
I assume it dislikes links and told the member to post fewer of them.
I read how the filter decides and find the tripping rule — then adjust it, knowing what I am trading away.
I did, fixed it, and now skim the filter’s stated reasons whenever I clear the queue — each misfire teaches me one more of its rules.

items.q: Mid-sale, your shop’s card reader stops and shows only “ERROR 05.” The customer is waiting. What does that code mean to you?
items.layman: Payment terminals report problems as numbered codes — some mean try again, some mean the card is declined, some mean the machine needs attention. Do you know, or can you quickly find, what yours are telling you?

opts.t: Nothing. I turn the machine off and on and ask the customer for another card.
Trouble — I half-remember which codes pass and which don’t, and I gamble on the memory.
I keep the code list from the manual by the till — five seconds tells me whether to retry, re-dip, or switch to cash.
The list is by the till because past codes put it there — every new code gets looked up once and written down with what actually resolved it.

items.q: A new client requires you to work inside their project tool — one you have never used, with their whole team watching the board. What do your first thirty minutes in it look like?
items.layman: When you are dropped into someone else’s tool, do you learn how it behaves — what is visible to whom, what notifies everyone, where drafts can live — before acting, or find out by accident in public?

opts.t: I start working. Tools are tools; I will learn it by using it.
I copy what I see others doing on the board and stay within those moves.
I spend the first half hour learning what is public, what notifies people, and where I can work rough — before I touch anything that matters.
That, plus a private test item to see for myself what each action broadcasts — learned in private, so I never learn it in public.

items.q: On a screen-share, a fellow maintainer of your open-source project does in two keystrokes what takes you a dozen clicks in the same editor. The call moves on. Does anything else happen?
items.layman: When you see proof that your daily tool has a faster way, do you go and learn it, or file it under other people’s magic?

opts.t: No. They are a shortcuts person; I am not.
I ask what it was, nod, and forget it by the following week.
I ask, then practice it the same day on my own work — witnessed proof that my tool has depths is worth ten minutes.
I learn it and then skim the shortcut list it came from — one visible trick usually means a family of invisible ones.

items.q: You are away for a week, and a friend agrees to keep your market-stall business ticking over — orders, restocks, the usual questions. What do you hand them?
items.layman: For the routine running of your operation, does a written procedure exist — the steps, the order, what to check, what can wait — complete enough that a competent outsider could follow it? A “runbook” is exactly that: your written operating procedure.

opts.t: My phone number. The business runs out of my head, so I will be running it from the beach.
A hurried page of notes written the night before, covering what I could remember to mention.
The runbook I already keep: each routine task, its steps in order, what done looks like, and what genuinely can wait a week.
The runbook, which stays honest because I use it myself — and their week becomes its next revision, since every question they ask is a line it was missing.

items.q: The settings that make your product labels print correctly — the margins, the density, the one box that must stay unticked — came from a forum post years ago. Do you know what they do?
items.layman: Settings copied from someone else can work without being understood. “Configuration” is just the collection of settings a tool runs with. For configuration your product depends on, can you say what each setting governs — or only that changing anything invites disaster?

opts.t: No, and I never will. The settings are load-bearing and sacred; I photograph the screen before any update.
I know which two matter most, by reputation rather than understanding.
I looked up each one — I know what it governs and why the forum’s values suit my printer, so I could adapt them to a different one.
That, and my label notes record each setting with its reason — when a value must change, the note tells me which one and how far.

items.q: Your community’s member list exists in three places — the forum, the mailing list, and a spreadsheet — and this morning they disagree about forty people. Which one is right?
items.layman: When the same information lives in several tools, a “source of truth” is the copy you have decided is authoritative — the one the others get corrected against. Do you have one, or three rival versions?

opts.t: Unknowable. Whichever I opened most recently feels the most true.
I reconcile the forty by hand, case by case, without settling anything for next time.
The spreadsheet — I decided long ago which copy is authoritative and in what order the others get corrected from it, so disagreement is tedium, not mystery.
The same, and it is written at the top of the spreadsheet itself: which copy rules, how the others follow, and the monthly once-over that keeps the three from drifting far.

items.q: Setting up your workshop room follows the same order every time — projector before laptop, screen check before doors open. A helper asks which parts of the order actually matter. Can you tell them?
items.layman: Routines contain real constraints and mere habits. For your own procedure, can you say which steps must precede which — and what goes wrong if they don’t — or is the whole sequence one undifferentiated superstition?

opts.t: It all matters, probably. I do it in this order because this order has never failed me.
I can defend two or three of the orderings with stories of the mornings that created them.
Yes — I know which orderings are load-bearing and why, and which are just comfortable, so I can hand them the flexible parts safely.
The setup sheet already says so: each constrained step carries its reason, so a helper can improvise everywhere the sheet doesn’t forbid.

items.q: You need a source you half-remember reading last spring — something about attention spans, maybe a footnote. How does the search go?
items.layman: A note system has a scheme — rules for where things go and what they are called — or it has a pile with a search box. Can you state your scheme’s rules, and do they reliably lead you back to what you kept?

opts.t: Badly. I keep things in downloads, tabs, and hope; last spring is another country.
I search words I might have used and usually surface it eventually, along with doubt about what else is lost in there.
By the scheme: sources get filed under stated rules — topic, project, date — so I can reason about where spring-me put it and walk straight there.
The scheme is written inside the system itself, and when a search fails the rules get amended — every miss makes the next one rarer.

items.q: The marketplace deposits $412.87 for last week. Your own records say you sold $520 worth. Could you account for the difference to the penny?
items.layman: Between your sales total before deductions (the “gross”) and the payout sit fees — commission, payment processing, promotions, refunds. Do you know the fee model well enough to recompute the deposit yourself, or is the number simply what arrives?

opts.t: No. The deposit is what the platform says it is; mine is not to reason why.
Roughly — I know the headline commission and shrug at the remainder.
Yes. I know each fee, what it applies to, and in what order, so I can rebuild the $412.87 from my own sales list — and notice when I can’t.
My fee model is written next to my sales records, and when the platform changes a rate the note changes the same week — reconciling stays a five-minute habit.

items.q: A medical bill arrives for a visit you thought insurance had settled months ago. Is the paper in your hand explicable?
items.layman: A claim moves through stages — the provider bills the insurer, the insurer decides and issues a statement of what it paid and why (an “explanation of benefits”), and the remainder becomes your bill. Do you know the stages well enough to locate a surprise inside them?

opts.t: No. Medical paperwork arrives from a fog and gets paid to make it go away.
Partly — I call the number on the bill and let whoever answers explain my own situation to me.
Yes. I know the stages a claim passes through and which document each produces, so I can name where this bill diverged from what I expected — and query exactly that.
The family’s claims crib sheet — stages, documents, who to call for which discrepancy — has handled enough of these that the fog rarely survives a first read.

items.q: Two years ago you published a free budgeting template that people still download. A user asks why one formula treats the final month differently. Do you know?
items.layman: Work you made and shipped keeps needing its own explanation. Are the design decisions inside your published things written down — what each odd-looking part is for — or must you reverse-engineer your own reasoning like a stranger?

opts.t: No idea. Two-years-ago me had reasons and took them along.
I open the formula and puzzle it out from scratch, hoping the oddity was intentional.
The template’s companion notes say — each deliberate oddity is recorded with its reason, so the answer is a lookup, not an excavation.
The notes say, and they travel with each revision — every version states what changed and why, so any question about any version has a written answer.

items.q: A client disputes your invoice: their door-badge records say you were on site six hours; your time tracker billed seven and a half. Can you explain your own number?
items.layman: Time trackers make choices — how they round, what counts as idle, how overlapping timers resolve, whether preparation is included. Do you know the rules behind the number you bill, or does the tool tell you a number and you pass it on?

opts.t: Not really. The tracker says seven and a half, so seven and a half is what happened.
I would knock off the difference to keep the peace, none the wiser about whose number was right.
Yes — I know how my tracker rounds, what it counts that a door badge cannot see, and can walk the client through the reconciliation line by line.
That, and the counting rules are stated on the invoice template itself — written before any dispute, and reread whenever I change trackers, because the rules are mine, not the tool’s.

items.q: You send a subcontractor the same design file you use daily; on their machine the fonts are wrong and half the layers misbehave. Mystery or diagnosis?
items.layman: The same file behaves differently on different machines because of what surrounds it — installed fonts, program versions, linked assets that didn’t travel with the file. Do you have a picture of what your files depend on, or is “works for me” the end of your knowledge?

opts.t: Mystery. I export a flattened copy and we both agree not to ask questions.
Familiar annoyance — sending it zipped fixed it once, so I zip harder.
Diagnosis. I know what the file assumes from its surroundings — fonts, versions, linked assets — so I can ask two questions and name the missing piece.
Diagnosed once, written down: my sending checklist packages the dependencies and lists the known mismatches, so the next machine is boring.

items.q: A stranger submits a sizeable improvement to your open-source project — touching the corner of the codebase you understand least. Merging is one click. What earns it?
items.layman: Accepting outside work into your project means judging it. Can you build enough understanding of your own weakest corner to evaluate a stranger’s change — or do you rely on politeness, confidence, and hope? A “test” here is a small program that fails if the code’s claim is false.

opts.t: Enthusiasm. Someone cared enough to contribute; merging is the polite response.
A skim for anything alarming, plus the contributor’s evident confidence.
Study. I read the change until I understand that corner properly — tracing what it does and checking its claims against the documentation — and only then judge it.
Study, then proof: I write a test that would fail if the change is wrong about what it claims, and let the test — not my reading — cast the deciding vote.

items.q: Your community digest is landing in spam. Two knowledgeable members offer confident, incompatible explanations — one blames your sending domain’s records, the other your subject lines. Whose advice do you take?
items.layman: Email delivery is governed by real mechanisms — sender-authentication records a domain publishes, content filters, sender reputation. A “sending domain” is the address your email claims to come from; “headers” are the hidden routing information attached to every message. When experts disagree, can you go beneath both opinions to the mechanism, or only choose the more confident voice?

opts.t: Neither, or both — I try fixes in whatever order the suggestions arrived.
The one who sounds more certain, or whoever helped me last time.
I go under the opinions: I read how the mechanisms actually work, check my own records and headers against the documentation, and see which story the evidence supports.

I make the mail system itself testify: a bounced message’s headers name which authentication checks failed, I fix the named record, and a follow-up send confirms the verdict flips — evidence closes the argument, not the louder member.

items.q: A student emails: lesson four’s exercise fails on their machine, a setup you have never touched. You cannot see their screen. How do you debug what you cannot reach?
items.layman: Fixing a problem remotely means working from a model rather than a screen: knowing the exercise’s “dependencies” — the programs and versions it needs — what varies between setups, and which questions narrow the possibilities fastest. A “disposable environment” is a scratch computer setup you can create, break, and delete without consequence.

opts.t: I refund or apologize — outside my own setup, I have nothing.
I send generic advice — restart, reinstall, update — and hope one lands.
I reason from the exercise’s dependencies to what could differ on their machine, then ask two or three targeted questions that split the possibilities.
I recreate their setup in a disposable environment and make the failure happen in front of me — the fix, and the lesson’s new troubleshooting note, rest on a reproduction rather than a guess.

items.q: Three percent of your hardware product’s units come back dead. The fault could live in your design, a component batch, or the assembly house. Where do you even start?
items.layman: A failure with several possible parents is localized by decomposition: name the candidate causes, work out what evidence would distinguish them, and gather it. A “controlled comparison” changes one factor at a time so the results can only be read one way.

opts.t: With the assembler, loudly — someone downstream must have botched something.
With replacements and monitoring — ship spares, watch whether three percent becomes five.
With the returned units: I decompose the possible causes, work out what each would look like on a dead unit, and examine the bodies for which story they tell.
Then a controlled comparison — the same design across two component batches, or two assemblers — so the cause is isolated by evidence rather than argued from suspicion.

items.q: The utility bill for your house arrives at triple the usual amount. The phone agent says the reading is correct and the amount stands. Is that the end of it?
items.layman: Behind a bill sit primary documents — the “tariff” (the price plan your supply contract puts you on), the meter readings, the supplier’s own billing rules. Disputing well means reading them, not repeating the phone call louder. Do you know how to take a bureaucratic no back to its sources?

opts.t: Yes. The company computer says triple, and fighting computers is not a hobby I can afford.
I call twice more, hoping for an agent who sees it my way.
No — I pull the primary documents: my tariff’s actual rates, the reading history, the billing rules — and rebuild what the bill should say before I dispute it with citations.
And I collect the evidence that grades the dispute — dated photos of the meter, my own usage log — so the case rests on records the supplier cannot talk past.

items.q: You propose a small integration for a client; their in-house IT rejects it — “our security policy makes that impossible.” The project stalls on that sentence. What do you do with it?
items.layman: “Integration” means making two systems exchange data. A gatekeeper’s “impossible” usually compresses a real constraint into a refusal. Can you understand the constraint itself well enough to design within it — or does the happy path end where their sentence begins? A “proof of concept” is a minimal working demonstration.

opts.t: I take it at face value and quote the client for the manual alternative.
I push back rhetorically — surely other companies manage — and lose gracefully.
I ask what the policy actually requires, and read it where I can — then design a variant that satisfies the stated constraint, which is usually narrower than the refusal.
And I build a small proof of concept against their constraint and demonstrate it — a working thing that satisfies the policy argues better than I do.

items.q: Your marketplace sales dip for three straight weeks. The seller forums have a unanimous diagnosis: “the algorithm changed.” Do you accept the explanation everyone is repeating?
items.layman: “The algorithm” is the marketplace’s ranking system — folk explanations blame it for everything. Testing a theory means checking it against what the platform actually documents and what your own numbers say, then changing one thing at a time to see what responds. A “control” is the unchanged half you compare against.

opts.t: Yes. When the algorithm turns against you, you wait for it to turn back.
I adopt the forum’s counter-rituals — retitle everything, relist daily — and watch hopefully.
I check the theory first: the platform’s published ranking guidance, my own traffic and purchase numbers, seasonal history — and see whether the dip even lives where the folk theory says it does.
Then I run the discriminating test — one variable changed on half my listings, the rest left as a control — so the next three weeks produce an answer instead of a mood.

items.q: Drafting a long piece, you find the perfect statistic — striking, widely quoted, and load-bearing for your argument. It traces back to a single decades-old study. Does it go in?
items.layman: Judging a claim means reading the primary source — the original study — rather than its echoes: what was measured, on whom, how many, and whether the method could support the number. A “sanity check” is redoing a simplified version of the calculation yourself to see if the size is even plausible.

opts.t: It goes in with a link to the article where I found it. Widely quoted is its own peer review.
I confirm several reputable outlets cite it and consider that triangulation.
I read the original study — sample, method, what was actually measured — and only then decide whether the number can carry the weight my argument puts on it.
And I run the sanity check myself — re-deriving the figure’s rough size from data I can access — so the statistic survives arithmetic, not just attribution.

items.q: You split one project between two subcontractors — one designs the parts, another builds them — and you will never touch the middle yourself. What decides whether their halves meet?
items.layman: Splitting work requires understanding both halves well enough to define the boundary: exactly what one side hands the other, in what form, under what rules. An “interface” is that defined meeting point; an “integration test” is a small trial that passes only if the halves genuinely fit.

opts.t: Their professionalism. Both are good; good people’s work fits together.
A kickoff call where everyone agrees to stay in touch and flag surprises.
The interface I wrote: what crosses the boundary, in which format, under which rules — specified from my understanding of both halves, so each side builds against the same page.
The interface, plus an integration test defined on day one — a small trial both halves must pass together, so the fit is demonstrated midway, not discovered at the end.

items.q: Twenty minutes into your paid workshop, the live demonstration fails — an error where output should be, thirty people watching. The script cannot help you now. What happens?
items.layman: Live failure tests whether you understand the material or merely the rehearsed path. Can you diagnose in front of an audience by reasoning from how the thing works — and had you rehearsed failure itself? “Failure modes” are the specific, known ways a thing tends to break.

opts.t: I end the demonstration and promise a recording that works.
I switch to screenshots of it working and narrate what everyone would have seen.
I debug it aloud — the error, the mechanism, the likely causes in order — because reasoning through a failure is the material, whether or not it was on the slides.
It rarely gets that far: before every workshop I break the demonstration on purpose down its known failure modes, so most live errors greet a fix I have already rehearsed.

items.q: Packing orders, you notice — by pure chance — that the parcel in your hands holds the wrong variant. You swap it, seal it, ship it. Is that the end of the incident?
items.layman: A near-miss is a failure that luck intercepted. Systems improve when near-misses get the full treatment — cause found, lesson recorded, a check added — rather than a relieved shrug. A “check” is a small fixed step that would catch the same slip without luck.

opts.t: Yes. Nothing bad shipped; there is nothing to fix.
I resolve to pack more carefully, which holds until the next busy week.
No — luck is not a process. I work out how the wrong variant reached the parcel, record the cause, and add the check that would have caught it without the glance.
The check no longer depends on my attention at all — a barcode scan against the order at sealing refuses the mismatch, which is how the last two were caught.

items.q: Perhaps one customer in thirty reports that your shop’s online ordering page fails at payment. You have never once seen it fail yourself. What do you do with a fault you cannot summon?
items.layman: An intermittent fault resists debugging because the evidence evaporates. The competent response is to set traps: recording (“logging”) around the suspect steps so the next occurrence documents itself. “Instrumentation” means building that recording into the system so it runs by itself.

opts.t: Nothing — for the affected customers, apologies and a phone order. Ghosts win.
I try the page myself after each report, find it working, and file the mystery under gremlins.
I stop waiting to witness it: I list the plausible causes, add logging around each suspect step, and keep a written case file — so the next failure arrives carrying evidence.
The traps were already set — ordering has always logged its steps — so the report came in alongside its own diagnosis, and the fix shipped with a check for that cause.

items.q: The platform your open-source plugin extends ships an update, and your plugin breaks for thousands of users overnight. You patch it within the day. What does the episode leave behind?
items.layman: A “dependency” is software yours relies on; when it changes, yours can break. The lesson can be spent (one patch) or invested: the breaking mechanism understood and a test added. A “pre-release” is the version a platform publishes for testing before launch; a “compatibility test” is a small automatic check that fails when the platform changes something your code relies on.

opts.t: A patch and a bad day. The next platform update and I will meet the same way.
A habit of skimming the platform’s release notes, when I remember to.
An understanding of which platform surface actually broke me, recorded in my notes and written into the code as a compatibility test — this class of break now fails my tests before it fails users.
The tests now run automatically against the platform’s pre-release versions — breakage surfaces on their announcement schedule, not on my users’ screens.

items.q: A client project comes in at half your usual effort — cleanly, no corners cut. Pleasant surprise. Do you know why it went well?
items.layman: Understanding compounds only if causes are found — and success has causes as surely as failure does. Can you name what made the fast project fast, record it, and make it repeatable — or do good weeks remain weather?

opts.t: No, and I don’t look gift horses in the mouth. Some projects are just easy.
I have a feeling it was the unusually decisive client, but it is only a feeling.
I compare it against a normal project — what differed in the brief, the sequence, the reuse — name the cause, and record it so the next project inherits it deliberately.
My per-project notes track where the hours actually go, so the comparison was already made — the cause surfaced from the numbers, and it is now a standard part of how projects start.

items.q: For the third school term running, a permission-slip deadline is missed and a child of yours is the one without a signed form. Same failure, third occurrence. What changes?
items.layman: A recurring miss is a process fault, not a character fault. The competent response finds the cause — where the information enters the household and where it dies — and changes the process, ideally so the deadline announces itself. Vigilance is the plan that has already failed three times.

opts.t: Nothing structural. We apologize to the school and resolve to be more on top of things.
More vigilance — I now try to check the school app most evenings, when I remember.
I trace the route the information travels — where slips arrive, where they stall — find the actual break, fix that step, and write the new routine where the family will follow it.
The fix removed vigilance from the design: everything arriving from the school lands in one reviewed place, and deadlines surface themselves days ahead — the third miss stayed the last.

items.q: You keep a research journal — every dead end, every source that lied to you, every method that finally worked. Five years of it. When did you last actually reread any of it?
items.layman: Recorded lessons only compound if they are re-encountered at the moment of need. A journal can be a diary (write-only) or an instrument: organized so past-you reliably interrupts present-you before a known mistake repeats.

opts.t: There is no journal — five years of lessons live in whatever I happen to remember.
I write faithfully and reread never. It is a diary with delusions of usefulness.
Rereading is structural: entries are filed by method and by symptom, and consulting them is the first step of any new investigation — the journal gets a vote before I start.
Its hardest-won lessons no longer wait to be reread — they are distilled into the checklists inside my research procedure itself, so past-me interrupts present-me automatically.

items.q: Every cohort of your course, a familiar cluster of confused questions arrives at module three — the same misunderstanding in new handwriting. Three cohorts now. What has happened to module three?
items.layman: Recurring confusion is data about the material, not the students. A compounding response diagnoses the cause — where the explanation loses people — revises it, and adds a way to detect whether the revision worked, such as a short comprehension check inside the module.

opts.t: Nothing. Some concepts are hard; I answer the questions again each cohort.
I wrote a standard reply I paste when the questions arrive — the confusion stays, but answering is cheaper.

I diagnosed it: found the exact step where the explanation loses people, rewrote that passage, recorded the cause in my course log — and the module now carries a comprehension check at the danger point.
The check runs every cohort and I read its numbers — weak spots surface from the data before the questions arrive, and module three was rebuilt because the graph said so.

items.q: A defect reaches your client inside work a subcontractor did for you. The subcontractor is apologetic; the client is yours, not theirs. Beyond the apology, what does your operation learn?
items.layman: When delegated work fails, the compounding question is mechanical, not moral: what class of defect was it, why did your own receiving step (“intake”) let it pass, and what added check would catch its siblings? “Instrumented” means the checking is built in and runs without you. Blame changes suppliers; understanding changes systems.

opts.t: That this subcontractor was a mistake. I find another and expect better.
That I should look harder at deliveries — an intention with no particular shape.
The defect’s class and the gap it walked through: I work out why my intake missed it, record the cause, and my delivery checklist gains the check that catches its siblings.
Intake is instrumented now — the accumulated checks run on every delivery by themselves, before I even look, so each old defect class is a door that stays closed.

items.q: Your community digest goes out to ninety people who unsubscribed months ago — the complaint arrives within the hour. The unsubscribes happened in one tool; the sending happened from another. Where does your investigation end?
items.layman: Failures at the seam between two tools have causes like any other — one side’s list went stale. Closing well means finding which side, why, and adding something that notices the divergence before the next send. “Drift” is two copies of the same data quietly diverging.

opts.t: With apologies and hand-deleting the ninety from the sending tool. Investigation implies time I don’t have.
With a resolution to re-export the list before each send, most of the time.
With the seam understood: I find where and why the copies diverged, fix the actual break, and record the cause — and sends now start with a check that the two lists agree.
The seam now watches itself — the two tools are compared on a schedule and I am alerted on drift, which is why the next stale-list incident was caught with no complaint attached.

items.q: Lowering one temperature setting cured the warping that ruined a week of your product’s printed parts. You do not know why it worked. The parts look perfect. Case closed?
items.layman: A fix that works for unknown reasons is a loan against the future. Closing well means the mechanism is understood — why that setting produced that defect — confirmed by deliberately bringing the problem back once, and recorded in the “material profile,” your saved settings-and-reasons sheet for that material.

opts.t: Closed. Perfect parts ask no questions.
Closed with a sticky note — “don’t raise this back up” — reason unknown.

Not until I understand it: I learn the mechanism linking that temperature to warping, confirm it by reproducing the defect once on purpose, and the material profile records both the setting and its why.
That, and each material’s profile now includes a small test print whose dimensions I measure and log — drift back toward warping shows in the numbers before it shows in the products.

items.q: Strip away your community platform for a moment: what, in your own terms, is a “member”? If the answer only exists as the platform’s profile fields and status badges, what do you know?
items.layman: A “data model” is your own definition of the things your system tracks — what a member is, what states they pass through (joined, active, lapsed), what must always be true of the records. It can exist as your written concept — or only as whichever fields one platform happens to offer. “Invariants” are the rules that must always hold.

opts.t: A member is what the platform says: these fields, those badges. My community’s categories are the vendor’s categories, learned from their interface.
I have my own notions — who counts as active, what lapsing means — but they exist as habits of reading the platform’s screens, not as anything stated.
A written model of my own: what a member is, the states and transitions, the invariants — the platform merely implements it, imperfectly, and I know exactly where.
The model is the master: the community has already changed platforms once, and the records mapped across cleanly because their meaning was never the vendor’s to define.

items.q: You are invited to teach “build what you run” as a paid course — except every participant arrives with a different toolbox, none matching yours. What would your curriculum actually teach?
items.layman: Teaching a system to people on other tools is a hard test of understanding: only the design travels — what data flows where, what rules must always hold (“invariants”), how things fail and how failure is detected. Tool walkthroughs, by contrast, only teach your subscriptions.

opts.t: In honesty, my tools — the course would be a guided tour of my own setup, useless one toolbox to the left.
Principles with my tools load-bearing underneath: rename the products and my lesson notes stop making sense.
The design itself: data flow, invariants, failure modes and their detection — with my stack appearing only as one worked example among possible others.
That course has run: participants built the system on toolboxes I had never touched, and where their builds struggled, the design chapters — not the tool notes — got the revisions.

items.q: Your hardware side product has one manufacturer: the small shop that has made every unit so far. If you posted them nothing tomorrow — could a second shop produce a correct unit from your documentation alone?
items.layman: A “manufacturing package” is the documentation that fully specifies a physical product: drawings with tolerances (how much variation is acceptable), materials, assembly steps, and the checks that define a good unit. Product knowledge can live there — or in one shop’s accumulated habits and your phone calls.

opts.t: No. Half the product lives in that shop’s memory of what I meant — our history together is the real specification.
They would get files and a long email of caveats; the tolerances and the tricks live in practice, not on paper.
Yes. The package stands alone — drawings, tolerances, materials, assembly order, and the acceptance checks that define a good unit — the current shop follows it rather than remembers it.
Proven: a second shop has already produced passing units from the package unaided, and their questions were folded back into it — the product exists on paper first.

items.q: Your open-source plugin is, in the end, a clever idea expressed through one host application’s extension points. Where does the idea itself live?
items.layman: A plugin has two layers: the concept — what it computes, the rules it enforces, the model underneath — and the binding, the code that speaks one host’s “extension points” (the hooks an application offers to outside code). If the concept is only ever written in the binding’s vocabulary, the host owns your idea. “Invariants” are the rules that must always hold.

opts.t: In the binding. The plugin is its host-specific code; separated from those extension points, there is no articulable remainder.
In my head, approximately — the code is the only written form, and it speaks the host’s dialect throughout.

In a design document the code merely implements: the concept, its data model, its invariants, stated without the host’s vocabulary — and the boundary between idea and host is drawn in the code itself.
The separation is demonstrated: the same design document has driven a build for a second host, and both bindings stay thin because the idea refuses to live anywhere but the document.

items.q: Every subcontractor you hire must first be walked through your particular tools before they can produce anything. A colleague hires against written interfaces and cares little what tools her people use. What separates you?
items.layman: An “interface,” here, is a written meeting point for delegated work: what goes in, what must come out, in what form, under what rules — stated so the work can be done on any tools. “Invariants” are the rules the output must always satisfy. Delegation can run through such documents, or through apprenticeship in your vendor accounts.

opts.t: My system is its tools — there is nothing to hand a subcontractor except logins and a tour, so every hire begins with immersion in my stack.
I have briefs, but they are written in my tools’ vocabulary — screens, buttons, my accounts — so they only function as guided tours in document form.
Little, now: my interfaces state inputs, outputs, formats, and invariants in tool-neutral terms — subcontractors implement however they like, and the documents, not my logins, define done.
The interfaces are proven portable: different subcontractors have delivered against the same document on entirely different stacks, and their questions have only sharpened it.

items.q: Your partner offers to co-run the household’s administration — bills, renewals, the school calendar — but wants to use their own tools, not your carefully arranged app. Can the household’s system meet them halfway?
items.layman: A household’s operations can exist as a model — what obligations exist, how often each recurs (its “cadence”), what must never lapse (“invariants”), which accounts the money flows from — or only as one app’s screens and categories. Only the model can be shared across tools; screens can merely be shown.

opts.t: No. The household runs as my app’s structure — its categories are the only map, so co-running means adopting my app.
Partly — I could export lists, but the reasoning lives tangled in the app’s folders and my arrangement of them; outside that arrangement it is data without a story.
Yes. The model is written plainly — the obligations, their cadences, the invariants, the accounts they draw on — and my app is just my chosen way of running a design either of us could hold.
Demonstrated: we already run it across two toolsets against the same written model, and reconciling monthly against the model — not against either app — is what keeps both honest.

items.q: Your research notes owe their power to years of practice inside one note-taking app — its links, its queries, its daily views. A doctoral student asks you to describe your method. Can you, without describing the app?
items.layman: A note-taking method is a set of ideas — what a note contains, how notes connect, when they are revisited — that an app merely hosts. If the method can only be stated as one app’s features, the method is the app’s, on loan. “Queries” are saved searches — the app’s machinery for finding notes.

opts.t: Not really. My method is that app configured just so — asked for principles, I demonstrate features.
I can gesture at principles, but each one resolves into a feature when pressed — the method and the app have grown inseparable in my own telling.
Yes. The method is written as method — the unit of a note, the linking rules, the revisit cadence — with the app acknowledged as one hospitable implementation among possible ones.
The written method has already survived the trip: the student runs it in a different app entirely, from the document — and their questions improved the method, not my configuration.

items.q: You decide to sell your small marketplace business. The buyer’s adviser asks the uncomfortable question: once you and your subscriptions walk away, what exactly is being purchased?
items.layman: A sellable system is one whose substance is transferable: documented designs, procedures, an owned data history with its meaning intact, defined quality checks. The alternative — accounts configured by feel — transfers as anecdotes. “Due diligence” is the buyer’s inspection of what they are really getting.

opts.t: Logins. The business exists as years of accreted configuration inside its platforms, readable nowhere else — due diligence would find accounts, not a system.
Logins plus a sale-week summary written from the accounts, in the platforms’ own vocabulary — a description of settings, not of a design.

An operating design on paper that happens to run on those accounts: the procedures, the data history with its meaning documented, the quality checks — the accounts are furniture; the documents are the asset.
That, with the transfer already rehearsed: a manager ran the operation for a quarter from the documents alone, so the buyer purchases evidence rather than assurances.

items.q: Ten years of your shop’s sales history live in the till system, filed under codes like “MISC-2” and “OLD-PROMO” that only you and the till half-remember. What is that history worth outside the till?
items.layman: Data stays meaningful only with its “data dictionary” — a written key stating what each code, category, and field actually means, kept independent of the system that stores the records. Without one, exported records become numbers attached to forgotten decisions.

opts.t: Little. The categories mean what the till and I jointly remember they mean — exported, the history would be arithmetic without a story.
Some. I could reconstruct most codes from memory and context, slowly and with errors I would never detect.
Its full worth. A data dictionary I keep outside the till defines every code and category — the meaning of the history is mine on paper, whatever machine holds the records.
Proven worth: the history has already been pulled out and analyzed in other tools against the dictionary — ten years of decisions legible anywhere, because their meaning never lived in the till.

items.q: Each new agency client brings a different environment your system must exchange data with. Your platform’s menu of ready-made connectors covers some. When a client’s systems are not on the menu — what happens?
items.layman: A “connector” is a vendor’s pre-built link between two specific products. Beneath connectors sit open formats and protocols — publicly specified ways of structuring and exchanging data that anyone can implement. Fluency at that level makes any boundary negotiable; fluency in menus makes the menu your limit.

opts.t: I decline the client, or bolt on whatever third-party product claims to bridge the gap. The menu is the boundary of what I can promise.
I improvise — exports massaged by hand, half-understood glue found in forums — and each bridge is a fragile one-off I could not confidently rebuild.

Nothing dramatic: I understand the open formats and protocols underneath, so I can specify a clean exchange with the client’s systems whether or not a connector exists — connectors are conveniences, not capabilities.
Proven, repeatedly: integrations have shipped over plain open formats with no shared vendor at all, from a pattern I keep documented — new environments change the details, never the design.

items.q: An agent hands you work. You judge it. Then what happens to that judgment?
items.layman: When you correct AI output, does the correction get remembered anywhere so the same mistake stops recurring? “Write-back” = saving your feedback into the system’s long-term memory. “Verdict” = your ruling on a piece of output, plus the reason.

opts.t: I fix the output and move on.
I keep loose notes on recurring fixes.
Corrections get folded into prompts and instructions, manually.
Every verdict is captured in a grammar — accept / reject / rewrite, with a reason — and written back to durable memory.

items.q: Your automation reports “done.” How do you know that is true?
items.layman: If a system claims it finished, is there an automatic check that the result really exists and is correct — or do you just take its word for it? “Durable state” = the permanent record (files, database) where results must actually land.

opts.t: I trust it.
I spot-check when I remember to.
Logs exist; I read them when something breaks.
Writes are verified against durable state; silent failures are structurally impossible, or they alert me.

items.q: Do you know your error rate?
items.layman: Can you put a number on how often your AI and automated systems get things wrong — or is it just a feeling?

opts.t: No idea.
An anecdotal feel — “usually fine.”
I track failures when they are reported to me.
Measured: verdict logs give acceptance rates per agent, per task, trended over time.

items.q: A client receives something your system produced. Who checked it?
items.layman: Before AI-made work reaches another person, is there a check — by you, or an automatic one you designed — or does it ship straight out?

opts.t: Nobody. It ships straight through.
I skim it when I have time.
Everything external passes my review before it ships.
Tiered: high-confidence work auto-ships with verification; low-confidence queues for me. I set the thresholds.

items.q: A proposal you spent the morning on is finished. Your cursor is on the send button. What happens in the next sixty seconds?
items.layman: Before something leaves your hands, is there any deliberate check — a reread, a comparison against what the client asked for — or does finishing and sending happen in the same motion?

opts.t: I send it. Finishing is the check.
