I glance at it if something feels off.
I reread the whole thing once, slowly, before it goes.
I reread it against the client’s original request — the ask and the answer, side by side, every time.

items.q: A client replies-all to point out that yesterday’s deliverable spelled their company name wrong. After the apology, what happens to the mistake?
items.layman: When an error is caught by someone else, does it leave any trace with you — a note, a list of things to watch for — or does it evaporate once the embarrassment fades?

opts.t: Nothing. The embarrassment fades and so does the lesson.
I resolve to be more careful, which lasts about a week.
It goes on my list of known trouble spots — the things I now check for by name.
It joins a running list I consult before anything ships — every past catch, checked against, every time.

items.q: You are typing the amount into this month’s invoice. Where does the number come from, and what checks it?
items.layman: When money figures leave your hands, do you verify them against the record they came from — a time log, a contract, last month’s invoice — or trust the number you typed?

opts.t: From memory. If it’s wrong, the client will say so.
From memory, then a squint — does it look about right?
I check it against the source — the contract, the hours log — before I send.
Every invoice is compared against its source and against last month’s, a habit that has already caught real errors.

items.q: You finish writing a post and the publish button is right there. What stands between the draft and the public?
items.layman: For anything published where strangers can see it, is there a deliberate look before it goes live — links clicked, names spelled, the image actually attached — or is writing it the last step?

opts.t: Nothing. Writing it was the last step.
A quick skim, when I’m not in a hurry.
A deliberate pass: I click the links, check the names, look at it as a reader would.
The same short list of checks, every post, kept where I draft — it has caught a wrong link more than once.

items.q: You have just admitted to yourself the mistake you keep making — a transposed name, a forgotten field. Three pieces of work are drafted and waiting to go out. What happens to them?
items.layman: Naming a recurring mistake is one thing; going back to look for it is another. When you identify an error you tend to make, do you deliberately hunt for it in the work you haven’t shipped yet — or hope this batch was spared?

opts.t: Nothing. If it’s in there, a complaint will find it.
A worried glance at whichever draft is open, when the thought nags.
I sweep everything still unshipped for exactly that mistake before it goes out.
The sweep is a habit backed by a saved reference — naming a new mistake triggers a pass over everything still live.

items.q: The monthly numbers for your client are assembled, and one figure is triple what it was in the last report. Does anything catch that before they do?
items.layman: When a number in your reporting looks unusual, is there a habit that notices — putting this period next to the previous one — or does the anomaly ride out the door unexamined?

opts.t: No. If it’s wrong, their reply will tell me.
Maybe — if I happen to remember what the previous figure looked like.
Yes — this period sits next to the previous one, and anything that jumps gets explained or fixed first.
Yes — every report is checked against the prior one and its raw source, and I keep a note of what was checked.

items.q: You send a file to a client and realize an hour later it was the old version. What was the check that failed — and did it exist?
items.layman: Attachments are where errors hide in plain sight: the wrong file, the draft instead of the final. Do you open what you attach before sending, or trust the filename?

opts.t: There was no check. I attach and send in one motion.
I check the filename, which is exactly how the old version got through.
I open the attachment itself and look at it before sending — the file, not the name.
I open it and check it against what was promised — right file, right version, right contents — as a fixed habit.

items.q: You are about to publish a quote from a customer conversation as a testimonial. What happens before their words appear under their name?
items.layman: Using someone’s words publicly is a small act with a long memory. Do you verify the quote against the original conversation — exact words, right person, permission — or publish what you remember?

opts.t: I publish what I remember them saying.
I paraphrase from memory and soften it, so it’s probably safe.
I go back to the original message and copy their exact words — right person, right context — before it goes up.
Exact words checked against the source, permission confirmed, and the source saved next to the published quote.

items.q: A week after you delivered a research summary, you suddenly doubt one statistic in it. What do you do with the doubt?
items.layman: When you suspect something you already shipped is wrong, is there a move — going back to the source, correcting the record — or does the doubt get filed under too-late?

opts.t: File it under too late. It’s shipped.
Lose some sleep, and quietly hope nobody quotes that line.
Go back to the source, check the figure, and send a correction if it’s wrong.
Check it, correct it if needed, and add that class of figure to what I verify before shipping next time.

items.q: Honestly: the last few times something you shipped turned out to be wrong, how did you find out?
items.layman: The channel through which your errors reach you says everything about your checking. Is it complaints — or your own eyes, before anyone else’s?

opts.t: A complaint. That is the only channel there is.
Sometimes a complaint, sometimes stumbling over it later by accident.
Usually my own reread before sending — complaints are the exception, not the system.
Almost always my own checks against a saved reference — and the rare miss that reaches a client updates the checks.

items.q: It is newsletter morning. Between the finished draft and the send, what exists?
items.layman: A “quality gate” = a fixed set of checks a deliverable must pass before it ships. “Versioned” = every change to it kept, with dates. For your recurring sends, is the gate a written checklist you follow every time, or whatever occurs to you that morning?

opts.t: Coffee and the send button.
Whatever checks occur to me that morning — some mornings more than others.
A written pre-send checklist — links, names, subject line, the offer — followed every issue.
That checklist, versioned — dated, with the reason each line exists — and it is the only path to the send button.

items.q: A mistake gets past your checklist and a reader catches it. What happens to the checklist?
items.layman: A checklist that never changes is a snapshot of the mistakes you had already made when you wrote it. A “changelog” = a dated list of every change and why. When a new failure slips through, does the written check absorb it — or does the list stay frozen?

opts.t: What checklist?
Nothing — the list stays as it was; I just resolve to be sharper.
The failure becomes a new line on the checklist, worded so it would have caught this one.
A new line, dated, with a note of the incident that earned it — the checklist is a changelog of everything that ever got past me.

items.q: You are about to ship your first-ever episode of something new — a format you have never delivered before. How does “good enough to ship” get decided?
items.layman: For a brand-new type of deliverable there is no habit to lean on. Do you write down what good looks like before shipping — criteria you could check against — or ship when it feels done?

opts.t: It ships when I’m tired of working on it.
It ships when it feels done — the bar exists, but I couldn’t state it.
I write the bar down first — what this must contain and do to count as good — and check the episode against it.
The written bar becomes the standing checklist for the format, refined against each of the first few episodes.

items.q: Pull up the checks you ran on last month’s client report, then the month before. Are they the same checks?
items.layman: Repeatability is the difference between a procedure and a mood. For a recurring deliverable, do the same written checks run every time — or does each month get whatever version of you shows up?

opts.t: There were no checks to compare.
Roughly similar, probably — they live in my head, so who knows.
The same, because they are written down — the report doesn’t ship until the list is walked.
The identical list, walked and ticked each month — the walk itself leaves a record I could show you.

items.q: It is 11 p.m., the deadline is midnight, and you are too tired to trust your own eyes. What protects the deliverable?
items.layman: Judgment degrades with fatigue; a written procedure doesn’t. When you are at your worst, is there a checklist that doesn’t care how you feel — or does quality drop with your blood sugar?

opts.t: Nothing. Tired me ships tired work.
I try to remember my usual checks, which is exactly what fatigue is bad at.
The written checklist — I walk it line by line precisely because I can’t trust feel tonight.
The checklist, plus a rule it enforces: anything failing two lines at this hour waits for morning.

items.q: Invoicing day. Before the batch of invoices goes out, what procedure runs?
items.layman: A “procedure” = written steps followed the same way each time. For invoices — amounts, rates, client details — is there a documented check you walk through, or a confident scan?

opts.t: No procedure. I write them and send them.
A scan for anything obviously wrong, done with confidence and no list.
A written procedure: each amount against the contract or hours log, each client’s details, checked off per invoice.
That procedure, with a worked example attached — and a monthly record that it was walked, so a skipped step is visible.

items.q: A client sends you a messy spreadsheet to clean and return. Before the cleaned file goes back, how do you know nothing went missing?
items.layman: Reformatting other people’s data is where silent loss happens — dropped rows, broken totals. Is there a written completeness check — counts and totals compared before and after — or does the file just look fine?

opts.t: It looks fine. I scroll it and send it.
I eyeball the obvious columns and hope the middle held.
A written completeness check: row counts and key totals compared before and after, every time.
That check, plus a saved comparison sheet returned with the file — the client sees the proof, not just the product.

items.q: A colleague asks, over coffee, exactly what checks yesterday’s deliverable passed before it reached the client. Can you list them?
items.layman: If the checks are real, they are enumerable: you can say what was checked, in what order, against what. Can you name your gate — or only insist that you are careful?

opts.t: I can say I was careful. That is the whole list.
I could reconstruct roughly what I probably looked at.
I can list them, because they are written — the deliverable’s checklist says exactly what passed.
I can hand over the checklist with yesterday’s ticks on it — what was checked, when, and against what.

items.q: You are updating your website — new case study, new pricing. What happens between “saved” and “live”?
items.layman: Public pages fail in predictable ways: dead links, broken layout on phones, an old price surviving in a corner. Is there a documented pre-publish walk — or does saving equal shipping?

opts.t: Saving is shipping. I find breakage when a visitor does.
I click around the new page for a minute, if I think of it.
A written pre-publish list: links, phone layout, prices consistent everywhere they appear — walked before it goes live.
That list, one version per page type — and any price change triggers the every-place-it-appears check by name.

items.q: You take two weeks off and a trusted freelancer covers your deliverables. Could they run your quality checks from what is written down?
items.layman: This is not about the freelancer’s skill — it is about where your standards live. If the checks exist only in your head, nobody covering for you can run them. Is the gate on paper?

opts.t: No. The checks are me; while I’m away, there are none.
Partly — I’d record a rushed voice note and they’d improvise the rest.
Yes — each deliverable type has a written checklist with what good looks like; they run what I run.
Yes, and it’s proven — someone already has, and their questions during that week made the checklists sharper.

items.q: Overnight, an agent updated two hundred records in your CRM. It is 9 a.m. What do you actually do about that?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. A “CRM” = the database of your customer relationships. When a machine changes two hundred things while you sleep, is there a sampling discipline — a deliberate subset checked against the source — or do problems surface when a customer call goes strangely?

opts.t: Nothing. Problems surface when a call goes strangely.
I scroll the list and stop if something catches my eye.
I check a fixed sample of records against their source before I rely on any of them.
A sample sized by risk — big accounts always, the rest at random — and the defects found get counted, not just fixed.

items.q: Your nightly data pipeline has shown green for thirty-one consecutive days. When did you last look at what it actually produced?
items.layman: A “pipeline” = an automated process that moves and transforms data on a schedule. “Green” = its own report that it ran without crashing — which says nothing about whether the output is right. Is there a scheduled human look at the product, or only faith in the status light?

opts.t: The green light is the look.
I look when something downstream breaks — which is how I learn it had been wrong for weeks.
On a schedule: a recurring review where I open the actual output and check it against expectations.
Scheduled reviews with a written scope — and every discrepancy found gets logged and counted across months.

items.q: A client emails: a figure in the report your system generated last week was wrong. You fix it and apologize. Then what happens to the incident?
items.layman: Errors that others report are free data about your system’s failure modes — but only if they land somewhere. Is there a failures log — what went wrong, where, when — or does each incident vanish into the apology?

opts.t: Nothing. The apology was the whole afterlife of that error.
A mental note that this report type is dicey.
It goes into a failures log — what failed, where it came from, the date — that I actually reread.
Logged and counted: incidents per source per month, and the counts decide where my review attention goes next.

items.q: An AI wrote you a research summary, dense with statistics and citations, due to a client under your name. What happens to the citations?
items.layman: AI-written research fails plausibly — real-sounding numbers, confident citations to sources that say something else or don’t exist. Before it ships under your name, do the claims get checked against the actual sources?

opts.t: Nothing. If it reads well, it ships.
I spot-check the one or two numbers that look surprising.
Every citation gets opened; every load-bearing number gets traced to its source before delivery.
Traced and marked — the delivered version distinguishes verified claims from unconfirmed ones, and the unverifiable don’t ship.

items.q: You hand your agent a type of task it has never done before. How much review does its first month get — and how did you decide?
items.layman: An “agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. Trust in a delegate should be earned per task type, not granted globally. Is there a deliberate ramp — full review at first, loosened against evidence — or does new work inherit whatever trust the old work earned?

opts.t: The same trust as everything else — which is to say, no review.
Gut feel: I watch it closely until watching gets boring.
A deliberate ramp: first outputs get full review, and the review loosens only as the record justifies it.
A ramp with numbers — review depth per task type is set by its tracked failure record, not by how boring vigilance became.

items.q: Five pieces of agent output wait for your review; the client deadline is tonight; reviewing all five takes longer than you have. What ships?
items.layman: Review discipline is only real if it survives pressure. “Risk-tiered” = ranked in advance by how much damage an error would do. When the review queue collides with a deadline, does unreviewed work quietly go out — or does something else give instead?

opts.t: All five ship. The deadline reviewed them.
I skim the two that feel important and wave the rest through.
Nothing external ships unreviewed — I cut scope or renegotiate the deadline instead.
A rule made in advance decides: outputs are risk-tiered, and each tier has a stated fate when time runs short — pressure executes the rule, not the exception.

items.q: An agent drafted a personalized email to three hundred prospects, and the send is one click. What happens before the click?
items.layman: A mass send is irreversible — three hundred small errors delivered simultaneously. “Merge fields” = the placeholders that pull each recipient’s name and details into their copy. Is there a pre-flight check on the list, the fields, and a sample of the drafts?

opts.t: The click. I read the first draft and trusted the other 299.
I skim a handful of drafts and send.
A pre-flight: the recipient list verified, merge fields checked against the data, a structured sample of drafts read end to end.
All of that, plus a staged send — a test batch to my own inbox first, and the full send only after the test survives inspection.

items.q: Your agent translated your onboarding guide into a language you cannot read, and the client is waiting. How do you review what you cannot read?
items.layman: “Back-translation” = translating the translation back into your language to compare it with the original. When output exceeds your own ability to judge it, do you construct a check anyway — or does “I can’t evaluate this” quietly become “ship it”?

opts.t: I can’t read it, so it ships. Confidence by necessity.
I run it through a second AI and eyeball whether the result feels right.
A defined check: back-translation compared against the original for the load-bearing sections, and a native reader for anything client-facing.
That, plus a running record of reported translation errors per language — the languages that fail more get the deeper check.

items.q: You catch yourself typing the same correction to agent output for the third time this month. What breaks the loop?
items.layman: “Write-back” = saving a correction into the instructions or memory the system actually rereads, so it binds every future run. A correction repeated by hand is judgment being spent; the question is what turns it into judgment kept.

opts.t: Nothing. I am the loop — I’ll type it a fourth time.
I scold the agent in chat, which lasts exactly one conversation.
The third repeat is the trigger: the correction gets written into the instructions the agent loads every run.
The loop can’t reach three — each rejection is logged with its reason, and recurrence automatically promotes the correction to a standing rule.

items.q: Last month you reviewed thirty pieces of agent work and rejected six. A collaborator asks: why those six? What can you answer from?
items.layman: A “verdict” = your ruling on a piece of output — accepted, rejected, rewritten — plus the reason. A “fixed grammar” = the same small set of ruling types used every time. Judgments made and forgotten cost the same effort as judgments recorded. Can the six rejections be answered from records, or only from whatever your memory kept?

opts.t: From memory, which by now has kept maybe one of the six.
From scattered chat threads, if I can find which conversations they were.
From the verdict record: each rejection logged at the time, with what failed and why.
From a verdict log in a fixed grammar — accept, reject, rewrite, each with its reason — queryable by month, agent, or failure type.

items.q: An agent-run process quietly stopped writing to your CRM ten days ago — no error, no claim, just absence. How does that reach you?
items.layman: The dangerous failure is the silent one: nothing reports “done” falsely, because nothing reports at all. “Durable state” = the permanent record — files, database — where results must land. “CRM” = your customer database. Does anything notice what is missing from the record?

opts.t: Through a confused customer, in about a month.
When I next happen to look at that corner of the system.
Through routine reconciliation — on a schedule, I compare what should have landed in the records against what did.
Through the system itself: expected writes are checked against durable state, and absence raises an alert within a day, not a month.

items.q: Two agents can do the same job, and you are deciding which keeps it. What does the decision stand on?
items.layman: “Verdict” = your recorded ruling on one output, with a reason. “Acceptance rate” = the fraction of an agent’s outputs you accepted rather than rejected or rewrote, computed from those verdicts. Is the keep-or-cut decision standing on measured rates — or on which agent most recently impressed or burned you?

opts.t: On vibes — whichever one feels smarter this week.
On memory of recent wins and disasters, which mostly means the disasters.
On the count: accepted versus rejected for each, over the same period, from my review records.
On acceptance rates per task type, trended over time from the verdict log — including where each agent’s failures cluster.

items.q: You swap the model behind your drafting agent for a newer one. Monday morning, does it repeat every mistake the old one spent a year being corrected out of?
items.layman: An “eval” = a saved test set that grades an AI against known examples before it gets real work. A year of corrections is an asset only if it survives the swap. Does accumulated judgment live inside the replaceable component — or outside it, where the successor inherits it?

opts.t: Yes — the corrections lived in old chats, and the new model starts from zero.
Mostly — I re-teach the big lessons by hand as they resurface.
No — it loads the same memory and instruction files where every correction was captured, and inherits them on day one.
No, and it proved that first: the newcomer passed an eval built from the old one’s logged failures before touching real work.

items.q: Agent-written code took your booking system down for an afternoon. You fix it. Where does the lesson land?
items.layman: A “regression” = an old, already-fixed failure that returns. A “verdict” = your ruling on the incident, with its reason. Post-incident lessons either become part of the system — instructions it rereads, a check that would catch the recurrence — or become a story you tell. Which is it?

opts.t: In the story. I’ll tell it well, and re-live it eventually.
In a note to myself to review that kind of change harder.
In the system: the standing instructions the agent loads gain the rule, and my review checklist gains the failure.
In an executable guard: a test that fails if the mistake ever returns, plus the logged verdict with its reason — regression made structurally loud.

items.q: You approve fifty pieces of agent output a week, and lately your thumb approves faster than your eyes read. What keeps “approved” meaning something?
items.layman: Approval at volume decays into a rubber stamp — a click that records attention that didn’t happen. Is there structure that keeps the ruling honest: explicit criteria, recorded reasons, deliberate deep looks at work already waved through?

opts.t: Nothing. Approved means the button worked.
Recent burns — I slow down for a week after each incident, then speed back up.
Each approval records what I actually checked, against explicit criteria — an approval with no named check can’t be entered.
That, plus scheduled random deep-audits of already-approved work — and my own approval accuracy is a number I track like any agent’s.

items.q: In March you told your support agent: never promise a delivery date. It is July. Does the rule still bind — and how do you know?
items.layman: Instructions given in chat die with the chat. A rule survives only in memory the system rereads every run — and “still written down” is not the same as “still obeyed.” Do you know the rule holds, or assume it?

opts.t: The rule died in March, with that conversation.
It’s in a document I paste in when I remember to.
It lives in the instruction file the agent loads every run — captured once, binding since.
It lives there with its date and reason — and a periodic check replays date-bait scenarios to verify the rule holds in behavior, not just in text.

items.q: An auditor asks you to prove that your system's “lessons learned” actually change its behavior. What can you show them?
items.layman: “Provenance” = a record of where each stored lesson came from. Could you demonstrate — with records, not anecdotes — that corrections you made months ago still shape what your system does today?

opts.t: Nothing. Lessons live in my head.
Chat histories where I corrected things, scattered across tools.
A memory file of verdicts the system reads, with dates and reasons.
Verdict logs with provenance, linked to acceptance-rate changes measured over time — reproducible on any stack.

items.q: The platform that hosts your agents announces it is shutting down in ninety days. What happens to two years of your recorded corrections?
items.layman: A “verdict log” = the record of your rulings on system output, with reasons. If that history exists only as chat scrollback inside one vendor’s product, the discipline dies with the product. Does your judgment history survive the company that hosted it?

opts.t: It dies. The corrections only ever existed as scrollback in their interface.
I could pull their proprietary export — a format nothing else reads, so a graveyard with a download link.
Nothing happens to it. The verdicts already live in open files outside the platform; the platform only ever read them.
Nothing — demonstrably: the log has already survived one such move intact, and the new stack’s agents query it daily.

items.q: A new agent joins your stack tomorrow and needs to know your quality standards. Do you retell them, or can it read them?
items.layman: “Machine-queryable” = structured so software can search and use it without a human translating. “Provenance” = the record of where each rule came from. Standards taught tool by tool are locked inside those tools; standards written once, in open formats, get inherited instead.

opts.t: Neither, really — the standards exist only as old chats and settings inside the tools that were taught them.
I point it at scattered notes across three tools, each in that tool’s own format.
It reads the standards and verdict files directly — open format, structured, machine-queryable, no retelling required.
It already did — its first outputs showed it had absorbed the rules, with their provenance, before I said a word.

items.q: A client’s auditor picks one deliverable from last year and asks: what checked this, what was found, and what changed as a result? What exists to show them?
items.layman: “Provenance” = the record of where something came from and what happened to it along the way. A “verdict” = the recorded ruling on a check’s result, with its reason. Per-deliverable accountability means each artifact carries its verification history — not a general assurance that you are careful.

opts.t: My word, delivered confidently.
Screenshots excavated from a vendor dashboard that doesn’t export — and might not still have them.
The deliverable’s own verification record — which checks ran, what was found, the verdicts and dates — in files I hold.
A chain an outsider can walk without me: from the deliverable to its checks to the verdicts to the rules those verdicts later changed.

items.q: Your automation platform’s dashboard says your workflows succeed 98% of the time. Could you recompute that number without the vendor?
items.layman: A quality metric you cannot recompute is a claim, not a measurement. Do the raw run records land somewhere you own, in a format you can query — or is the 98% the vendor’s number about the vendor’s product?

opts.t: No. I don’t even know what the 98% counts as success.
Partly — the raw logs exist, but in their format, in their system, on their retention schedule.
Yes. Run records land in storage I own as they happen, and my own query produces my own rate.
I already do — my number comes from my records, and the vendor’s dashboard gets reconciled against mine, not the other way around.

items.q: Suppose you rebuilt your operation on entirely different tools next quarter. Which parts of your quality discipline arrive on the other side?
items.layman: The discipline is the checklists, the gates, the thresholds for what auto-ships, the verdict history — “verdict history” = the record of your rulings on past output, with reasons. If those were features of the old tools, the move resets you to zero judgment. If they are artifacts you own, the new tools inherit them.

opts.t: Little of it. The gates were settings inside the old tools; I’d be rebuilding the discipline from memory.
The ideas arrive in my head; the records and thresholds stay behind.
Substantially all of it — gates, thresholds, and history are stack-neutral files the new tools get pointed at.
All of it, as measured history rather than hope: the apparatus has moved before, and error rates held flat through the move.

items.q: Your platform stamps each agent output with an “AI quality score” before it ships. What is inside that number?
items.layman: “Black box” = a check whose criteria you cannot read or change. “Versioned” = every change kept with its history. A gate you cannot inspect is a gate you do not own — you know the score, not the standard. Are the checks that guard your work readable, editable, portable?

opts.t: No idea. A number appears; above the threshold, it ships.
The vendor documents the criteria in prose, but the check itself can’t be read, edited, or taken elsewhere.
Rules and code I own: I can read exactly what each check tests, change it, and run it anywhere.
That, versioned — each rule carries the incident that earned it, and the same checks have run identically on two different stacks.

items.q: Your rule is: contract summaries never ship without review; routine social posts ship automatically. Where is that policy written — and could it move?
items.layman: A review policy — what auto-ships, what queues for a human, at what confidence threshold — is judgment made durable. Encoded as one vendor’s settings toggles, it is unexportable judgment. Encoded as an artifact you own, tools come and go beneath it.

opts.t: It isn’t written. It’s toggles I once set across one platform’s settings pages.
The toggles, plus a memo describing them — and the memo and the toggles drift apart quietly.
A policy file I own, readable by human and machine — the tools obey it, and moving tools means pointing new ones at it.
That file, with history and a reason per rule — and a second stack has already enforced it unchanged.

items.q: Your vendor’s dashboard says Tuesday’s job passed your quality gate. Your own notes say it never ran. Which record wins — and why?
items.layman: “Source of truth” = the one record that is authoritative when records disagree. “Provenance” = the trail showing where each entry came from. If the vendor’s log is the only real record of what passed your gates, your accountability is a tenant in their building. Whose log settles a dispute?

opts.t: Theirs, by default — there is no record of mine to disagree with.
Mine exists, as a copy-paste trail I keep by hand and couldn’t really defend.
Mine. Tools report into a log I own, in a format I control — their dashboards are views, not verdicts.
Mine, and that has been tested: a real dispute was settled from my log, and its provenance forced the vendor’s record to be corrected.

items.q: Over three years, your failures became an eval — the test set every model must pass before touching your work. Who actually owns it?
items.layman: An “eval” = a saved set of test cases — built here from your past failures — that grades a model’s outputs before it earns real work. If those cases live inside one vendor’s evaluation feature, your hardest-won asset is theirs. Can the eval leave?

opts.t: There is no eval. I trust each new model’s reputation and start the corrections from scratch.
The vendor does, in effect — my failure examples were uploaded into their evaluation feature and exist only there.
I do: the cases are files in an open format, and any candidate model, on any platform, can be graded against them.
I do, provenly — a candidate on a different stack ran the eval before earning the job, and every case still traces to the incident that created it.

items.q: You are about to post the announcement for your community’s monthly call — date, time, timezone, joining link. What happens between typing it and posting it?
items.layman: Announcements carry small facts that are easy to get wrong — the date, the timezone, the link. Before members see it, do you check those against where they actually live — the calendar, the meeting tool — or post what you typed?

opts.t: I post it. If the date is wrong, the comments will say so.
I read it over once — which checks the spelling, not the facts.
I check each fact against its source — the calendar entry, the actual link opened fresh — before posting.
The same source-check every announcement, plus a look at the posted version itself — a habit that has already caught a wrong year.

items.q: You have just finished recording a lesson for your paid course and the upload screen is open. Does anyone watch the recording before your students do?
items.layman: A recording can fail in ways the recording session hides — dead microphone minutes, the wrong window shared, an abandoned take left in. Before paying students see it, does the file itself get watched?

opts.t: No. I recorded it, so I know what’s in it.
I scrub the timeline for anything visually odd, at speed.
I watch it back before it goes up — the file that will play, not my memory of the session.
I watch it against a short list of past recording failures — audio, screen, endings — and the list grows when a new one slips through.

items.q: A customer’s order for your small hardware product is boxed and the courier arrives in an hour. What happened between shelf and sealed box?
items.layman: Physical fulfilment errors are cheap to make and expensive to unwind — the wrong variant, a missing cable, someone else’s address label. Before the box seals, is there a deliberate look at what is actually inside it and on it?

opts.t: I packed it, which is the same thing as checking it.
A glance in the box before the lid goes on, if the morning is calm.
Contents against the order line by line, and the label against the buyer’s address, before it seals.
That check on every parcel, in the same order every time — it has caught a wrong variant twice, which is why it exists.

items.q: Someone using your open-source project reports a problem, and you type out the command that should fix it. Do you press reply — or something first?
items.layman: “Open-source” = software you publish for anyone to use. Advice in a public thread is a deliverable too: a command posted from memory may not run, or may not do what you remember. Do you try it before a stranger does?

opts.t: Reply. It’s from memory, but my memory wrote the project.
I reread the command for typos and send it.
I run it first, in a clean setup that resembles theirs, and post what actually worked.
I run it and paste the real output under the command — the habit exists because an untested one-liner once cost a stranger their evening.

items.q: A subcontractor’s invoice lands in your inbox. It looks about right. What happens before you pay it?
items.layman: “Subcontractor” = someone you hire to do part of the work you sell on. Paying is shipping money. Do you check the amount against what was agreed and what was delivered — or pay against the feeling of “about right”?

opts.t: I pay it. They’re trustworthy, and checking feels rude.
I squint at the total and pay unless something jars.
I check it against the agreement and the delivered work — rate, days, what was actually handed over — before paying.
Every invoice against the agreement and the delivery, as a fixed habit — it once caught a double-billed week, politely.

items.q: You are copying figures from an insurance letter into an online claim form — policy number, dates, amounts. What checks the copy?
items.layman: Forms that move money or coverage punish small transcription slips — a swapped digit, last year’s date. Once the numbers are typed, do you verify them against the letter before submitting, or trust your typing?

opts.t: Nothing. Typed is submitted.
A quick read-over of the form on its own, without the letter.
The letter beside the screen, each field checked against its line, before I submit.
Field against source, then a saved copy of exactly what was submitted — kept with the letter, so any dispute starts from evidence.

items.q: You are booking flights for the whole family, and the confirmation screen wants payment. What happens to the names and dates before you pay?
items.layman: Bookings are unforgiving about small errors — a name that doesn’t match the passport, a date shifted by one. Before the charge lands, do the details get checked against the documents, or does the confirmation screen get trusted?

opts.t: I pay. The form remembered our details, so it’s handled.
I glance at the summary line — airport codes and a date.
Names against the passports, dates against the plan, each passenger, before paying.
That check every booking, against the documents themselves — it caught a middle-name mismatch once, which paid for the habit forever.

items.q: The print shop sends a proof of your new flyers — five hundred copies once you approve. How does the proof get read?
items.layman: A “proof” = the printer’s preview of exactly what will be printed. Print is unforgiving: an error approved is an error five hundred times. Is the proof checked against the source details, or approved from a thumbnail?

opts.t: Approved from the thumbnail in the email. It looked like my flyer.
I read the proof through once on screen, quickly.
Slowly, against the sources — the phone number dialled, the address checked, prices against the current list — before approving.
Printed at home and read on paper against the sources, every print job — paper has caught what the screen smoothed over.

items.q: Your paid workshop starts tomorrow morning. Tonight, do the slides, links, and demo get touched — or trusted?
items.layman: A live session multiplies small failures in front of everyone — a demo that no longer runs, a link that moved, fonts that broke on export. Before people who paid show up, does the material get a deliberate run-through?

opts.t: Trusted. They worked when I made them.
I flick through the slides in bed, reading titles.
A run-through tonight: every link clicked, the demo executed end to end, slides advanced on the machine I’ll present from.
The same run-through before every session, from a short standing list — it exists because a dead demo once ate ten minutes of forty.

items.q: You are writing the marketplace listing for something you make — dimensions, weight, what it fits. Where do those numbers come from?
items.layman: Listing specifications from memory is how returns are born: the item that doesn’t fit, the weight that changes the postage. Do the numbers get measured against the physical object, or recalled?

opts.t: From memory. I made the thing; I know it.
From an old listing of something similar, adjusted by eye.
From the object itself — measured and weighed while the listing is open — before it goes live.
Measured, and the measurements kept in a note beside the listing — so the next variant gets checked against the record, not the recall.

items.q: Enrollment for the next run of your course opens at nine tomorrow. What decides that the doors are actually ready to open?
items.layman: A launch has many small levers — the payment link, the dates on the page, the welcome email, the capacity cap. A “quality gate” = a fixed written set of checks that must pass first. Is opening governed by a written list, or by how ready you feel?

opts.t: Feeling ready. I open the doors and watch for smoke.
A mental lap of the obvious things, different each launch.
A written launch list — payment link tested, dates consistent everywhere, welcome email sent to myself first — walked before the doors open.
That list, versioned — each line dated with the launch mishap that put it there — and no cohort opens without the walk.

items.q: You run the same paid workshop every few weeks. Twenty minutes before people arrive, what is happening?
items.layman: Recurring sessions invite drift: the link that changed, the file share that expired, the recording never switched on. Is the final twenty minutes governed by a written pre-session routine, or by whatever you remember to poke?

opts.t: Arriving myself. The session starts when they do.
Poking at whatever I remember failing last time.
A written pre-session routine — room link, materials access, recording on — the same list every session.
That routine, and each walk leaves a ticked copy with the date — so the session where a step got skipped is findable, not deniable.

items.q: A unit of your hardware product is assembled and ready to ship. What must be true before it goes in the box?
items.layman: For a physical product, “works when I finished it” and “works” are different claims. Is there a written per-unit check — functions tried, contents complete, label right — or does assembly count as inspection?

opts.t: Assembly counts as inspection. If I built it, it ships.
I switch it on and trust the rest.
A written unit checklist — each function tried, contents complete, label against the order — every unit, no exceptions.
That checklist plus a reference unit — a known-good example each new unit is compared against — so “pass” means matches the standard, not looks fine.

items.q: Your open-source library is due a release tonight. What stands between the code and the publish command?
items.layman: “Open-source library” = code you publish for others to build on. A “release” = the packaged version users install. Releases fail in repeatable ways — missed version numbers, absent notes, untried packaging. Is there a written release procedure, or a remembered one?

opts.t: Nothing written. I publish and see who shouts.
A remembered sequence, performed slightly differently each time.
A written release list — tests passing, version bumped, notes written, the package installed once myself — walked in order.
That list is the only road to publishing — steps in a fixed order, and the botched release of last spring is a named line on it now.

items.q: A subcontractor is about to start a piece of work you will sell on to a client. When the work comes back, what will it be judged against?
items.layman: “Subcontractor” = someone you hire for part of the job. “Acceptance criteria” = the written definition of what the returned work must contain and pass. Is that definition on paper before the work starts — or invented at the moment of judging?

opts.t: Nothing stated. I’ll know bad work when I see it.
The brief implies it; the judging is improvised on return.
Written acceptance criteria per type of work — what it must contain, what I will check — set down before they start.
The criteria travel with the brief, so the sub checks before returning — the gate runs twice, and their copy has caught things before mine could.

items.q: It is the first weekend of the month — bills, renewals, the household’s small paperwork. How does that session run?
items.layman: Household admin fails quietly: the missed renewal, the payment that changed, the bill paid twice. Is there a written monthly routine — the same items walked each time — or a shuffle through whatever surfaced?

opts.t: There is no session. Things get handled when they growl.
A pile and a memory — I handle what surfaced and hope that was all of it.
A written monthly list — each bill against the bank statement, renewals by date — the same walk every month.
Each line names its source to check against, and the dated sheet from last month sits beside this one — a skipped item is visible as a gap.

items.q: An article of yours is finished and the publication’s deadline is today. What happens to the facts in it before it goes?
items.layman: Prose hides factual load: names, dates, figures, links, quotes. A “fact-check pass” = a separate walk through the piece verifying each of those against its source, distinct from reading for style. Does one exist in writing — or is rereading the whole check?

opts.t: Rereading is the check. If it flows, it goes.
I double-check whichever fact worried me while writing.
A written fact-check pass — every name, number, quote, and link verified against its source, ticked per item, every piece.
The ticked copy is kept with the draft — which claims were checked against what — so a challenge later starts from the record, not from panic.

items.q: A paid ad campaign you built for a client goes live at noon — budget, audience, copy, landing link. What runs before noon?
items.layman: Live spend converts errors into money at a steady rate — an extra zero in the budget, the wrong audience, a landing link that goes nowhere. Is there a written go-live check for campaigns, or a confident final glance?

opts.t: The glance. Noon arrives and so does the spend.
I check the part that burned me last time and call it diligence.
A written go-live list — budget figure against the approval, audience against the plan, the link followed to its page — walked before launch.
That list, plus its standing rule: any line touching money is checked twice, once cold — and a launch that fails a line waits, whatever the clock says.

items.q: You are putting a new product live on a marketplace — photos, price, shipping weight, returns text. What must be true before you press publish?
items.layman: A listing is a small contract: the price against your costs, the weight that sets the postage, the promises in the returns text. Is publishing governed by a written listing checklist, or by whether the page looks finished?

opts.t: Looking finished is the bar. Publish.
I compare it by eye to an older listing and adjust.
A written listing checklist — price against the cost sheet, weight from the scale, photos against the actual variant — walked before publish.
The checklist with a filled example beside it — a model listing done right — so every future listing is checked against a worked standard, not a memory of one.

items.q: It is closing time at your shop. Between the last customer and the lights going off, what has to happen?
items.layman: Close-of-day is where small losses hide — the card machine total that doesn’t match the till, the day’s online orders never marked collected, the back door that didn’t lock. Is closing a written procedure, or a remembered ritual?

opts.t: Lights off. Whatever didn’t happen tonight surfaces eventually.
The ritual I mostly remember, thinner on late nights.
A written closing sheet — card totals against the till, the day’s orders reconciled, the doors — the same walk nightly.
The sheet is signed and kept, and any mismatch is written down with its amount that night — so a slow leak shows up as a pattern, not a surprise.

items.q: An AI moderator tends your community overnight — removing posts, warning members, approving newcomers. Its decisions are live before you wake. What do you do with them?
items.layman: “AI moderator” = software that enforces your community rules for you. “Error rate” = how often its decisions are wrong, as a number. Its rulings on people are output too. Is there a review discipline — decisions checked, mistakes counted — or does silence from members count as accuracy?

opts.t: Nothing. Silence from the community means it’s working.
I skim its log when a member complains loudly enough.
A daily pass over its decisions — every removal and warning reviewed, wrongful ones reversed.
Removals reviewed always, lesser actions sampled — and every overturned call is counted, so its error rate on people is a number I know, per month.

items.q: An AI assistant marks your students’ assignments and writes their feedback. The feedback goes out under your course’s name. Who reads it besides the students?
items.layman: “AI assistant” = software doing multi-step work for you — here, grading. “Rubric” = the written standard the grading should follow. Feedback that is wrong teaches the wrong lesson twice. Is its marking reviewed against your standard, and are its misses tracked?

opts.t: Nobody. The students read it; that’s what it’s for.
I read a few when a student pushes back on a grade.
A regular audit: a sample of marked work re-graded by me against the rubric before I trust the batch.
A scheduled audit with counts — misses tallied per module, and the modules where it misgrades most get the deepest sampling.

items.q: Fifty units of your product arrive from the small workshop that assembles them for you. The boxes look fine. What happens before any of them reach customers?
items.layman: Work you contracted out is still work you ship. “Incoming inspection” = checking a delivered batch against your standard before it enters your stock. “Spec” = the written description of a correct unit. Is there an inspection — sampled, recorded — or do sealed boxes go straight to shelves?

opts.t: To the shelves. The workshop is good; that’s why I use them.
I open one box from the top, look, and generalize.
A fixed sample from every batch, tested against the spec, before the batch is accepted.
Sample size set by the workshop’s track record — and every defect found is recorded per batch, so the record decides the checking, not my mood.

items.q: An agent tidies your open-source project’s issue tracker — labelling reports, closing the ones it judges stale or duplicate. Closed issues are people told “no.” Does anyone check its judgment?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI that performs multi-step work for you. “Issue tracker” = the public list where users report problems. A wrongly closed report is a real bug dismissed and a contributor snubbed. Is its triage reviewed, and are its wrong calls counted?

opts.t: No. Closed is closed; the tracker looks tidy.
I rely on users to reopen anything that mattered to them.
A weekly pass over everything it closed — wrong closes reopened before the reporter has to ask.
The weekly pass, plus a count — wrong closes per hundred, trended — and the month that number rose, its closing rights narrowed.

items.q: Three subcontractors produce client work that goes out under your studio’s name. A busy month, work flowing through. What stands between their “finished” and your “sent”?
items.layman: “Subcontractor” = someone you hire for part of the work you sell on. Their output carries your name the moment you forward it. Does all of it pass your review first — and does each person’s miss record exist anywhere besides your impressions?

opts.t: Forwarding. Their finished is my sent.
I open the work of whoever burned me most recently.
Everything passes my review before the client sees it — no exceptions for busy months.
Everything reviewed, and each catch logged per person — review depth per sub follows their record, and “I trust them” has a number in it.

items.q: An agent reads the school’s emails and keeps your family calendar — term dates, matches, the dentist. You plan life against that calendar. When do you check its entries?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you — here, turning emails into calendar entries. “Reconciliation” = a full compare of the calendar against every source email. A wrong entry surfaces as a missed appointment weeks later. Is there a routine check of entries against sources, or is the calendar trusted because it is tidy?

opts.t: Never. Tidy is trusted; wrong surfaces at the school gate.
I check an entry when something about the week feels off.
A weekly look: new entries checked against the emails they came from, before the week is planned around them.
The weekly check plus a term-start reconciliation — and each miss found goes in a tally, so I know how often the calendar lies.

items.q: An agent read twenty customer interviews and handed you five tidy themes. The themes will steer what you build next. What happens between the tidy and the trusted?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI doing multi-step work for you — here, summarizing interviews. Summaries fail invisibly: a theme nobody quite said, a strong quote built from a mild remark. Do you test the themes against the raw transcripts before they carry weight?

opts.t: Nothing. Tidy is convincing, and convincing is enough.
I read the quotes it chose and nod along.
I pull a few full transcripts and check each theme against what those people actually said, before the themes steer anything.
A fixed rule: every theme must survive contact with named transcripts, and the ones that don’t are counted — the miss rate follows the agent, not my impressions.

items.q: An agent drafts your replies to client emails, in your voice, ready to send. By Friday, forty have gone out. How many did you read first?
items.layman: “Agent” = an AI doing multi-step work — here, writing email as you. A sent reply is a commitment made in your name. Do drafts pass your eyes before sending — all of them — and do you know how often you had to step in?

opts.t: Few. The voice is convincing, so the sending became automatic.
The ones to clients I’m nervous about, when I have a minute.
All forty. Nothing sends in my name unread — the reading is the job now.
All read, and every intervention noted — a weekly count of what I had to fix, per client and per kind of ask, so I know where it can’t be trusted yet.

items.q: Overnight, a pricing agent nudged the prices on forty of your marketplace listings. Margins live and die in those nudges. What does your morning look like?
items.layman: “Pricing agent” = software that adjusts your prices to compete. “Cost floor” = the lowest price that still covers your costs. A price below the floor sells fast and loses money quietly. Is there a morning review of what changed, and a record of how often it goes wrong?

opts.t: Like any morning. The prices are whatever they are now.
I look at my bestseller’s price and infer the rest survived.
A morning pass over every change — each new price against its cost floor before the day’s sales run on it.
The pass, plus a running count of its violations — how often it priced below floor, per month — and that count sets how tightly I watch it.

items.q: Your bookkeeper — or the software that plays one — has categorized the quarter’s transactions, and the accounts look pleasingly complete. What happens before you file on top of them?
items.layman: Categorized accounts are someone else’s judgment about your money, rendered tidy. Miscategorized expenses surface as wrong tax later. Do the categories get reviewed — sampled against receipts — before anything official stands on them?

opts.t: Nothing. Complete-looking is filed.
I scan the totals and query anything that offends me.
A deliberate sample checked back to receipts and statements before the quarter is filed.
The sample, and every miscategorization logged with who or what made it — a quarterly error count that decides how much checking next quarter gets.

items.q: Each week you overturn a few of your AI moderator’s calls — the sarcasm it read as abuse, the spam it waved through. Where do those overturns go?
items.layman: “AI moderator” = software enforcing your community rules. An “overturn” = your ruling that its decision was wrong. If overturns only fix the single case, the same misreading returns weekly. Do your rulings get written into the policy the moderator actually loads?

opts.t: Into the case. I fix the post, and the ruling dies there.
Into my sense of its weaknesses, which I re-explain in passing.
Into the written policy it loads — each overturn becomes a line or an example the next shift runs on.
Into the policy with the reason attached — and overturns are tallied per rule, so I can see which rules are actually learning and which just churn.

items.q: Your course’s AI assistant answers student questions around the clock. Some answers you’d have signed; a few you’d have burned. How does it come to answer less badly next cohort?
items.layman: “AI assistant” = software answering in your course’s name. “Threshold” = the recorded level of trust at which it may answer without you. If your corrections live only in the moment, each cohort meets the same wrong answers. Are verdicts on its answers captured into what it reads — and does its freedom depend on its record?

opts.t: It doesn’t. Each cohort meets the assistant fresh, mistakes included.
I correct the worst answers in the thread and move on.
Corrections go into the notes it loads — the wrong answer of one cohort becomes standing instruction for the next.
Verdicts logged per topic, and its freedom set by them — strong topics it answers alone, weak ones route to me, thresholds moved by the record, not by hope.

items.q: Unit forty-one fails your bench test — same fault as unit twelve, you think, though you couldn’t say for sure. What does your production record know that you don’t?
items.layman: A “bench test” = the check each unit passes before shipping. “Failure codes” = a fixed short list of categories every fault is filed under. A fault fixed per-unit and forgotten will be rebuilt into future units. Are failures recorded by category, with fixes written into the build instructions the next batch follows?

opts.t: Nothing. Failures are fixed at the bench and forgotten by dinner.
A drawer of sticky notes and a strong feeling about unit twelve.
Each failure logged by type with its fix — and the recurring ones amended into the build instructions the next batch is assembled from.
Failure codes counted per batch and trended — a code that spikes flags itself before I would have felt the pattern.

items.q: Your release agent reports the new version “published” — notes posted, package up. Somewhere a user is already typing the install command. On what grounds do you believe the agent?
items.layman: “Agent” = software doing multi-step work — here, publishing your library. “Registry” = the public index that serves your package to installers. “Smoke test” = a quick check that the basics work. “Published” is a claim about the world: the registry either serves the new version or it doesn’t. Is the claim verified, or accepted as reported?

opts.t: Its own report. “Published” printed in green is the evidence.
I glance at the registry page when I happen to think of it.
A post-release check I run: install the package fresh, confirm the version the world gets is the one that shipped.
The check runs itself after every release — fresh install, version compared, smoke test — and a mismatch alerts me before the first user finds it.

items.q: You have explained “no orphaned headings, captions under every figure” to three subcontractors this year, one at a time, from memory. What does the fourth one get?
items.layman: “Subcontractor” = someone you hire for part of client work. “Verdict” = your ruling on returned work, plus the reason. Feedback repeated verbally to each new person is judgment spent, not kept. Do your recurring corrections live in a standing brief each new sub receives — one that grows as verdicts accumulate?

opts.t: The same speech, fourth performance, whatever I remember of it.
A forwarded email thread from the last sub, as documentation.
The standing brief — every recurring correction written in, and each new verdict that repeats gets promoted into it.
The brief, where each rule carries its reason and returned work is logged against it — accept, revise, reject, with why — so the brief provably shrinks the revise pile.

items.q: You told your grocery agent “no more substitutions of the coffee” after the third disappointing pouch. Next order, the same brand of disappointment arrives. What failed — and would you have known without the pouch?
items.layman: “Agent” = software doing multi-step work — here, ordering groceries. Telling it something is not the same as the rule binding. Was the correction written where it reads before ordering — and does anything verify that a written rule actually held, short of bad coffee?

opts.t: I told it in chat; chat is where the rule died. The pouch is my alerting.
The rule is in a note I paste in when I remember to set up the order.
The rule lives in the preferences it loads each order — written once, read every run.
Written there, and checked there — each order is compared against the standing rules after it lands, and a rule that failed to bind gets flagged, before the kettle is involved.

items.q: Your drafting agent’s work comes back from clients with the same class of markup it earned in January — hedged openings, buried asks. It is October. Where did nine months of markups go?
items.layman: “Drafting agent” = software writing first drafts in your name. “Markup” = the corrections readers make on a draft. Corrections that never land in the style rules the agent loads are judgment evaporating monthly. And a rule written is not a rule proven — does anything test that old failures stay fixed?

opts.t: Into the drafts, one at a time. The agent writes like January forever.
Into my growing irritation and an occasional stern instruction in chat.
Into the style rules it loads — each recurring markup captured as a rule with its reason, retired from my workload.
Captured, and re-proven — drafts that once failed are re-run against the current rules on a schedule, so a rule that quietly stopped working shows up in the replay, not in a client’s margin.

items.q: One client has rejected first drafts four campaigns running — different work, same flavor of no. Your agency is small and the pattern is expensive. What exists between you and rejection number five?
items.layman: A “verdict” = a ruling on work, with its reason — here, the client’s. Rejections carry reusable information only if the reasons are captured somewhere your process rereads. Does the next deliverable get checked against the recorded history of this client’s no’s before they ever see it?

opts.t: Optimism. Draft five will be different because it must be.
My memory of their tastes, consulted while drafting, unevenly.
Their rejections are logged with reasons in the client’s file — and drafting starts from those rules, not from scratch.
Logged in a fixed form — what was rejected, why, dated — and nothing goes to this client without first passing their own recorded history; the file is the gate.

items.q: Your marketplace agent drafts replies to buyer questions, and you keep striking the same sentence — the one promising delivery “in two or three days” to places it takes six. What happens after the strike?
items.layman: “Agent” = software doing multi-step work — here, answering buyers. Striking a bad sentence fixes one reply; the machine that wrote it is untouched. Do rejections get recorded with their reason, and do repeat reasons become standing rules the agent loads?

opts.t: Nothing. I strike it again tomorrow, a little faster each time.
An exasperated instruction in that day’s chat, gone by the next session.
The correction is written into the instructions it loads — the delivery-promise rule now binds every reply.
That, and every outgoing draft is checked against the record of struck phrases before it sends — a reply repeating a rejected promise never reaches the buyer, and the block is logged.

items.q: A customer arrives for a four o’clock appointment your phone agent swears it booked. The diary shows nothing. Somebody is wrong in front of everybody. What would have caught this on Tuesday?
items.layman: “Phone agent” = software answering your calls and taking bookings. “Reconciliation” = comparing its claims against the diary’s actual entries. Its “booked” is a claim; the diary — the record your day runs on — is the truth. Is every claimed booking verified against the diary, or discovered against a customer’s face?

opts.t: Nothing. The face is the reconciliation.
I skim the diary when the week looks suspiciously quiet.
A routine reconciliation — the agent’s claimed bookings checked against the diary’s entries before each day begins.
Verified at the moment of writing — booking claimed, diary checked, mismatch flagged the same hour — and the daily discrepancy count stays at zero, or I hear about it.

items.q: Your community lives on one platform today, and a second space is opening — same people, different software. Your moderation standards and years of precedent rulings: what actually transfers?
items.layman: “Precedent rulings” = past decisions about what your rules mean in hard cases. “Portable” = usable outside the tool it was made in. If the standards exist only as one platform’s moderation settings and log scrollback, the second space starts lawless. Do the standards live somewhere both spaces can enforce?

opts.t: Little. The rules are that platform’s settings; the precedents are its log scrollback.
The rules are pinned as posts I could copy; the reasoning behind them is nowhere.
A policy file I own — rules, precedents, reasons, in plain readable files — and each space’s tools are configured from it.
Both spaces already enforce the same file, and every precedent traces to the incident that set it — a new moderator, human or software, inherits the law, not the folklore.

items.q: You are asked to run your course inside a corporate client’s own system — second platform, same course. Your rubric, your bank of known misconceptions, your feedback rules: can they make the trip?
items.layman: A “rubric” = the written standard work is graded against. The teaching quality of a course lives in this apparatus, accumulated over cohorts. If it exists as one platform’s grading settings and comment history, it is that platform’s asset. Is it yours to move?

opts.t: No. The rubric is the platform’s grading form; the history is its comment threads. The trip is a rebuild.
I could screenshot the settings and reconstruct something like it, from memory and exports nothing else reads.
Yes — rubric, misconception bank, and feedback rules are files I own, in open formats; the client’s platform gets pointed at them.
They already have — the course runs in two places off the same files, and each rubric line traces to the cohort incident that earned it.

items.q: A new assembly partner asks for your product’s test procedure and its defect history before they quote. Where does that answer come from?
items.layman: The test procedure and the record of past failures are the quality memory of a physical product. If they live inside a former partner’s systems — their forms, their portal — your product’s standards are hostage to a relationship. Can you hand over the apparatus in a form a stranger can run?

opts.t: From the old partner, if they’ll answer. The tests were their forms; the history is in their portal.
From a folder of PDFs they once sent me — readable, but nothing anyone could run or query.
From my own files — the procedure, the defect categories, the per-batch history, in open formats I hold and can hand over.
Handed over already, and proven — the new partner ran the same tests from my files alone, and their first batch’s results reconciled cleanly against the old history.

items.q: A contributor to your open-source project asks to run “the quality checks” on their own laptop before submitting. Is that a request you can grant?
items.layman: “Open-source” = code you publish for others to build on. “Repository” = the project’s own folder of files that everyone downloads. If the checks that guard your project exist only as one hosted service’s configuration — runnable there, inspectable nowhere — your quality gate is a rented room. Can the checks themselves travel?

opts.t: No. The checks are whatever the hosted service does; I couldn’t list them myself.
Partly — the service’s settings are public, but half the checks are its built-in magic, reproducible only there.
Yes — the checks are scripts inside the repository; the service merely runs them, and so can any laptop.
Yes, and each check carries the incident that earned it — the same gate has run identically under a second runner, because the checks, not the service, are the gate.

items.q: A subcontractor you found through a freelance platform has become essential, and the work is moving off-platform. Their two-year quality record — and the standards you hold them to — are coming along. Are they?
items.layman: “Subcontractor” = someone you hire for part of the work you sell on. On a platform, the track record is often star ratings and chat scrollback — the platform’s data, in the platform’s shapes. The standards and the history either exist as files you own, or the move erases them.

opts.t: No. The record is their star rating and a thousand messages in the platform’s inbox.
I could export the chat — a transcript nothing can query, which is a record the way a haystack is a filing system.
Yes — my acceptance standards and the log of rulings on their work are open files I hold; the platform was just where we talked.
Yes, provenly — the off-platform brief was generated from those files, and the sub confirmed it matched two years of actual rulings, no chat archaeology required.

items.q: A new specialist asks for your child’s history — medications tried, reactions, what was ruled out and why. Six patient portals hold six fragments. What do you actually hand over?
items.layman: “Patient portal” = a clinic’s own website for its slice of the records. The verified history — what was tried, what happened, what was ruled out — either exists as a record you keep, each entry traceable to its source letter or result, or it exists as an evening of logins and guesswork. Which is it?

opts.t: The guesswork. Six logins, my memory as the index, and hope nothing lived in a seventh.
A shoebox of printouts and screenshots — everything, in no order, provable in no direction.
The family health file I keep — conditions, medications, reactions, decisions — each entry noting which clinic’s letter or result it came from.
That file, with its trail intact — when two portals disagreed about a dosage, my record settled it, because every entry traces to a source document.

items.q: An editor challenges a statistic in a piece you published fourteen months ago. Your defense lives — where, exactly?
items.layman: For a writing practice, the verification apparatus is the trail from each published claim back to its source. If that trail lives inside one reference tool’s cloud — searchable only there, exportable never — your credibility has a landlord. Can you walk claim to source without the tool?

opts.t: In the tool, if my subscription is current and its search is kind. Otherwise, in luck.
In a browser-history sense — I could probably re-find the source in an afternoon of searching.
In my own claims index — plain files linking each published claim to its source and the date I verified it, readable without anyone’s software.
The challenge is an hour’s work, and has been before — the editor got the source, the verification date, and the note of what exactly was checked, straight from the index.

items.q: A large client’s procurement team, before signing, asks you to document your quality controls — not describe them, document them. What lands on their desk?
items.layman: “Procurement” = the department that vets suppliers. “Quality controls” = the gates, checks, and records that govern what you ship. If yours are features of the tools you happen to rent, the honest documentation is a list of subscriptions. What exists in a form an outsider can inspect?

opts.t: A confident paragraph naming the tools I use, which is a list of other people’s products.
Screenshots of settings screens — evidence that gates exist, in a form no one can verify or reuse.
The apparatus itself: my policy file, gate definitions, and sample verdict logs — tool-independent documents they can read and question.
That, plus the audit already passed — their reviewer reproduced a month of my quality figures from my logs alone, without access to any of my vendors.

items.q: The marketplace’s seller dashboard says your defect rate is 0.4%, and your reputation there hangs on it. You are opening a second sales channel next month. What quality record arrives with you?
items.layman: “Defect rate” = the share of orders that went wrong. A number computed by one marketplace, from data held by that marketplace, is their opinion of you — persuasive, unportable, unauditable. Do you keep your own record of orders, failures, and rulings that any channel could be measured against?

opts.t: None. My quality record is their dashboard, and it stays behind like furniture.
Spreadsheets I occasionally paste dashboard numbers into — a copy of their opinion, none of the underlying facts.
My own order-and-defect log, in open files — every order, every failure, every ruling — from which I can compute my rate for anyone who asks.
That log, already doing the work — the second channel’s quality process was stood up from it directly, and where the marketplace’s number disagrees with mine, I can show the arithmetic.

items.q: You are selling your shop, and the buyer’s accountant asks a blunt question: prove the quality claims — the low refund rate, the complaint handling, the redo rate. Prove them how?
items.layman: “Due diligence” = the buyer’s inspection of your claims before money moves. “Redo rate” = how often work had to be done again. Quality claims are worth what the records behind them are worth — and records locked in a till system’s subscription, in its formats, may not even outlive the sale. What can an outsider actually verify?

opts.t: My word and my reviews page. The till system has reports, but I’ve never got anything out of it.
Whatever the till vendor’s export produces — files in their shapes, meaningful mainly to them.
My own records — refunds, complaints, redos, each logged with date and resolution, in open files an accountant can query without my systems.
Those records have already outlived one till system — migrated intact when I switched — and three years of them can be queried and cross-checked against the bank without me in the room.

items.q: Your primary AI provider triples prices or shuts down. What breaks?
items.layman: How dependent are you on one company? Could you switch providers without losing your data, your system’s memory, and your workflows?

opts.t: Essentially everything.
I would lose history but could restart.
Core data is exported regularly; switching is painful but survivable.
Memory lives in a portable open format; providers are swappable parts.

items.q: Where does your accumulated judgment — decisions, taste, lessons — actually live?
items.layman: If someone audited your “learned wisdom,” where would they find it? Scattered chat histories? One app’s cloud? Or organized files you own, in an open format any tool can read?

opts.t: In my head and scattered chat histories.
Inside one vendor’s cloud.
In my own notes or vault, exported and organized.
In an open, portable substrate with verified writes — queryable by any agent I run.

items.q: What can an agent in your stack do without asking you?
items.layman: Could one of your AI tools delete files, send emails, or spend money without your approval? Do you actually know the answer?

opts.t: I have not thought about it.
Whatever the tool’s defaults allow.
Scoped permissions per agent, set deliberately.
Least-privilege by design: sensitive actions are gated, logged, and reviewable.

items.q: How would you know if your system’s memory had been quietly corrupted or poisoned?
items.layman: If bad or false information slipped into your system’s long-term memory, would anything catch it — or would the system just start acting on it? “Provenance” = a record of where each memory came from.

opts.t: I would not know.
I would notice odd outputs, eventually.
I audit memory contents manually, on occasion.
Write-integrity checks and provenance on every entry; tampering is detectable by design.

items.q: Your laptop dies on a Tuesday morning — not sleeping, dead. What did it take with it?
items.layman: If the machine you work on stopped forever today, would your important files exist anywhere else — a copy on an external drive or in a cloud folder — or was the laptop the only place they lived?

opts.t: Everything current. The laptop was the only place most of it lived.
Some things survive by accident — email attachments, files I happened to share.
Little of consequence — my important files also live in a cloud folder or on a drive I copy to now and then.
A morning’s work at most. Copies are a standing habit, and I could tell you exactly what exists where.

items.q: A service you barely remember signing up for announces a breach: passwords leaked. What else does that password open?
items.layman: A “breach” means attackers copied a site’s user data, passwords included. If you reuse one password across accounts, a leak at one obscure site can unlock your email or your bank. A “password manager” is an app that invents and remembers a different password for every account; a “second proof of identity” (two-factor) is a code from your phone required along with the password.

opts.t: Honestly — most of my accounts. It is more or less the same password everywhere.
A handful of accounts share it; I would have to guess which.
Just that one site. A password manager gives every account its own password.
Nothing — every account has its own generated password, and the important ones ask for a second proof of identity besides.

items.q: A client asks for the contract you both signed two years ago. How long does it take you to produce it?
items.layman: For your handful of genuinely important documents — contracts, tax records, credentials — do you know where each one lives, or would you be searching email, downloads, and old folders hoping it surfaces?

opts.t: Unclear it still exists. I would be excavating old email and hoping.
Ten or twenty minutes of digging — it is somewhere in the pile.
A minute. Important documents live in one known place, sorted.
A minute, for any client and any year — one place, one naming scheme, no exceptions.

items.q: You leave your phone in a taxi. What does the person who finds it get?
items.layman: A phone is a key ring: email, messages, saved logins, payment apps. If a stranger picked yours up, does a lock screen stop them — and could you locate or erase the phone remotely, from another device?

opts.t: Everything — there is no lock, or a code anyone could guess.
A locked screen, and that is the whole plan. What happens next is out of my hands.
A locked phone I can locate and erase from my laptop.
A locked phone I can erase remotely — and I confirmed the locate-and-erase feature works before I ever needed it.
