items.q: A new tool needs your API key, and the setup guide says “just paste it here.” Where does that key spend the rest of its life?
items.layman: An “API key” is a password-like string that lets software act on your account — often with broad power and no second check. A “password manager” is an app that stores such secrets encrypted. Once pasted into a chat, a note, or a shared doc, a key sits there readable to whoever finds it.

opts.t: Wherever pasting put it — chat logs, note apps, maybe a doc I once shared.
In a private note I would rather you not see, but at least I know which note.
In the tool that needs it and in my password manager — nowhere else.
Nowhere readable — keys live in the manager, get pasted only into the tool, and are deleted when the tool goes.

items.q: Your email provider locks your account this morning — suspicious activity, no timeline. What stops working?
items.layman: Email is the master key of a digital life: password resets, client contact, receipts, and sign-ins for other services all route through it. If it froze, do you know what depends on it — and is any of it copied elsewhere?

opts.t: Nearly everything, and I would be discovering what as it failed.
A lot — I know email is the hub, but I have never looked at what hangs off it.
It would sting, but I know what depends on that account, and the important attachments and contacts are saved outside it.
Little — key contacts and documents are copied out as a regular habit, and a second address exists purely for recovery.

items.q: You once shared a budget spreadsheet with “anyone with the link.” Who can read it today?
items.layman: Link-sharing settings outlive the moment: a document shared broadly stays readable to whoever holds the web address — forwarded, leaked, or guessed — until someone changes the setting. Do you know what you have left open?

opts.t: No idea. Whatever I have shared over the years is still set however I left it.
Probably a few open links out there; I would have to hunt through each app to know.
That one is closed — I share to named people, and I turn links off when the moment passes.
Named people only, always — and I skim my shared-files list now and then to catch anything left open.

items.q: Somewhere out there, an app you abandoned last year still holds your data. Which app, and what data?
items.layman: Tools you stop using do not stop holding what you gave them — files, contacts, payment details keep sitting in the dormant account. Can you name your abandoned accounts, and say what each one still knows about you?

opts.t: Could not begin to list them. Sign up, drift away, forget — that is the lifecycle.
I could name a few after some thought, but not what each still holds.
I can name them — and when I leave a tool, I make a point of taking my data out and closing the account.
The list is short and shrinking: leaving a tool means export, delete, close — the same three moves every time.

items.q: Months of thinking — plans, drafts, decisions — live in your chat history with an AI assistant. If that history vanished tonight, what would remain?
items.layman: Chat logs feel permanent but sit inside one company’s account: a deleted conversation, a closed account, or a policy change can erase them. Anything valuable that exists only inside the chat exists at that company’s pleasure.

opts.t: Nothing. The chats are the only copy of all of it.
Whatever I happened to paste elsewhere — I have felt the risk without acting on it.
The valuable parts — decisions and drafts worth keeping get copied out into my own files.
Essentially everything — copying keepers out of chat is a reflex, so the history is a convenience, not a vault.

items.q: An email arrives: “New sign-in to your account from a device you don’t recognize.” What do you actually do?
items.layman: Alerts like this are either real warnings or “phishing” — a fake email imitating a service to trick you into typing your password into a lookalike site. Either way the response matters: check through the real site, never through the email’s own links. A “second factor” is a code from your phone required alongside the password.

opts.t: Nothing — those emails all look the same, and I have learned to ignore them.
Click the button in the email and see where it leads.
Go to the service directly — not through the email — check the sign-in history, and change the password if anything looks off.
The direct check, plus: sessions signed out, password rotated, and a second factor added if the account somehow lacked one.

items.q: Your replacement laptop arrives in the mail. What guides the rebuild — the dead machine’s ghost, or a page you wrote?
items.layman: Rebuilding a working machine means reinstalling tools, signing into accounts, restoring files, reconnecting services. Is there a written list of what your setup consists of — or must memory, and the old machine’s, supply it?

opts.t: Neither — I would install things as I noticed them missing, for weeks.
Memory, mostly. I would reconstruct the setup by trial and error over a few days.
A written setup list: the accounts, the tools, where the files come from, in order.
A list I have actually rebuilt from once, corrected where reality disagreed, and kept current since.

items.q: Describe your backup in one breath: what gets copied, where it goes, and on what day?
items.layman: A backup that exists as a vague intention — “my stuff is mostly in the cloud, I think” — is different from a written routine: named folders, a named destination, a named day. Can you state yours without checking?

opts.t: I cannot — there is no backup to describe.
Roughly: things end up in a cloud folder, when I remember to put them there.
Exactly: these folders, to that drive and that cloud, on this day of the week — it is written as steps, and I follow them.
Exactly — and the written routine keeps a history of its own changes, with a dated note from each time it ran.

items.q: The AI workspace holding your project conversations offers a download-your-data button. When did you last actually press it?
items.layman: Most tools offer an “export” — a downloadable copy of what they hold about you. An export routine means downloading on a stated schedule and putting the file somewhere known, so the copy outside the tool stays reasonably current.

opts.t: Never. I did not know, or did not care, that the button existed.
Once, ages ago, to see what came out. The file is somewhere.
Last month — exporting is a written monthly step, and the files land in one dated folder.
Last month, per the routine — and I have opened a past export to confirm the contents are really in there, readable.

items.q: A client asks, mid-call: “Where exactly do you keep our files, and who else can get to them?” Can you answer before the call ends?
items.layman: Answering needs an inventory: a written record of which tools and places hold client material, and who — people or connected services — can reach each one. Without it, the honest answer is a guess.

opts.t: No — I would stall, then reconstruct an answer over the next few days.
Half an answer from memory, delivered with more confidence than it deserves.
Yes — a written record lists where client material lives and who can reach it, and I would read from it.
Yes, and I could send it: the record is current, dated, and written to be shown, not just kept.

items.q: Quick audit: how many API keys have you issued, and to which tools? Could you produce the list in five minutes?
items.layman: An “API key” is a password-like string that lets one piece of software act on your accounts. Keys accumulate quietly. An inventory means a written list: which key, for which tool, with what powers, created when.

opts.t: No. I do not know how many exist, let alone where they are used.
I could name a few from memory and would miss the rest.
Yes — a written list covers every key: what it is for, where it lives.
Yes, with dates — the list records when each key was made, and stale ones get deleted whenever I walk it.

items.q: You need last quarter’s version of a file you have since ruined. Do you know the exact steps to pull it from your backup?
items.layman: Having backups and knowing how to get things out of them are different skills. Written restore steps — open this, find that, copy it here — make recovery a procedure instead of an adventure.

opts.t: There is no backup to pull from.
The copy probably exists, but getting it out would be an evening of fumbling.
Yes — the steps for finding and pulling an old version are written down, right next to the backup routine itself.
Yes, and I have walked them once for real — the written steps have survived contact with an actual recovery.

items.q: Name every person and every connected service that can currently open your client-projects folder. Is your list complete?
items.layman: Access accumulates: collaborators added for one task, tools connected for one experiment. A written access list — who and what can reach which folder or account — is the difference between knowing and assuming.

opts.t: No idea — whoever I have ever added, plus whatever apps asked.
I could guess the people; the connected services would be a surprise.
Yes — a written list says who and what can reach it, updated whenever access changes.
Yes — and each grant carries a note of why and until when, so reading the list also shows what is overdue for removal.

items.q: You have decided to stop using a tool that has held your work for two years. What does leaving actually involve?
items.layman: Leaving a tool cleanly has steps: download your data, disconnect anything linked to it, cancel payment, close the account. Done ad hoc, steps get skipped and data gets stranded. Is your leaving-a-tool process written down?

opts.t: I stop logging in. The account and the data just sit there.
I cancel the payment and mean to export things — and usually do not.
A written checklist: export the data, disconnect what is linked, cancel, close — walked in order.
The checklist, plus proof: the export gets opened and checked before the account closes, and the file lands in my dated exports folder.

items.q: Your phone — the one that generates your login codes — is destroyed. Where are the recovery codes that get you back in?
items.layman: “Two-factor” logins require a code from your phone in addition to your password. Services issue one-time “recovery codes” for exactly this disaster — but they only help if you stored them somewhere deliberate, findable when the phone is gone.

opts.t: What recovery codes? I clicked past that screen.
Saved somewhere at the time — a screenshot, a download — I would have to hope.
In one deliberate place I can reach without the phone, stored when each account was set up.
In that one place, listed per account — and the place itself is named in my setup document, so future-me cannot lose it.

items.q: One of your tools emails: “We’re updating how we store customer data.” Without opening the app, can you say what of yours it actually holds?
items.layman: Every connected tool holds some slice of your working life — files, contacts, messages, payment details. A data inventory is a written note per tool: what I have put in, what it can see. Without one, policy-change emails are unanswerable.

opts.t: No — I skim the email, feel vaguely uneasy, and archive it.
Broad strokes only: “files, probably, and my email address at least.”
Yes — my tool inventory lists what each service holds of mine, so I can judge the change from my desk.
Yes — and that entry was already reviewed this year, because the inventory gets walked on a stated rhythm, not just written once.

items.q: A scheduling tool asks to connect to your email, and the consent screen lists what it will be able to do. What happens in the ten seconds before you click?
items.layman: Connected apps request “OAuth scopes” — a menu of powers you grant, from “see your calendar” to “read, send, and delete all your email.” The consent screen is the one moment those powers are stated plainly. Do you read it as a contract, or dismiss it as a formality?

opts.t: Click. The screen is a formality standing between me and the feature.
A skim and a wince — I notice it wants a lot, and grant it anyway.
I read the scopes, and if it demands more than the job needs, I look for a narrower option or a different tool.
Read, narrowed where the tool allows — and recorded, because every grant goes into my written map of what can reach what.

items.q: Mid-task, an agent stops: it needs access to a second folder to continue. Granting is one click; the task is stalled. What do you do?
items.layman: An “agent” is an AI tool doing multi-step work with real access to your files or accounts. Mid-task permission requests trade scrutiny against momentum — the pressure is to click yes and keep moving. What is your actual behavior in that moment?

opts.t: Yes, obviously — and while I am in there, I widen its access so it stops asking.
Yes, with a flicker of doubt that dissolves the moment the task resumes.
I look at what is in that folder first, grant the narrowest access that unblocks the task, and prefer temporary over permanent.
The same — and the grant is written into my permission map with a reason, because access granted under deadline pressure is exactly the kind worth rereading later.

items.q: The project tool that holds your working history is a running record of everything you have built. How old is your copy of it — the one outside the tool?
items.layman: Data inside a service is theirs to show you; a copy outside it is yours unconditionally. An “export” is a download of your data in a usable form. The question is not whether you could export — it is how stale the last one is.

opts.t: There is no outside copy. The tool is the record.
There is an export from some previous year, made during some previous scare.
Weeks old at most — critical tools get exported on a regular rhythm, to storage I control.
Days old — exports run on a schedule written down per tool, and each arrival is noted, so a missing one is visible.

items.q: You are wiring an agent into your file storage so it can manage project documents. What slice of the drive does it get?
items.layman: File-storage connections can be scoped: the whole drive, or one folder and nothing above it. An agent granted the whole drive can read tax records and old contracts it never needed. “Least privilege” means granting the smallest access that does the job.

opts.t: The whole drive — that is what the connector defaulted to, and it works.
The whole drive, uneasily — scoping it felt like friction I would get to later.
One dedicated folder. The agent operates inside it; the rest of the drive does not exist as far as it is concerned.
One folder — and the grant sits on my written map beside every other connection, which is the page I check before adding anything new.

items.q: Four different tools act on your main account through keys you have issued. When you retire one of the tools, what do you revoke?
items.layman: An “API key” is a password-like credential that lets software act on your account. One key shared across tools means cutting any of them off breaks all of them; a separate key per tool means each can be severed alone. “Revoke” means permanently invalidate a credential.

opts.t: Nothing — everything shares one key, and revoking it would break the other three.
Nothing yet — the keys are separate, I think, but I would have to spelunk to say which is whose.
That tool’s own key — each tool got its own, so retiring one is a single clean cut.
Its key, the same day, and the record updates — my key list says what each credential is for, and per-tool keys are simply how connections get made here.

items.q: There is a tool you have not opened since winter. Its connection to your email is still live. When does it get severed?
items.layman: Connections outlive usage: a tool you have abandoned can keep the access you granted in its honeymoon week — silently, indefinitely. Disconnecting means going into your account’s security settings and revoking the grant yourself; the tool will not do it for you.

opts.t: Never, in practice — I have never once looked at what is still connected.
Whenever something reminds me — a news story, a strange email — and then only that one tool.
When I stop using a tool, revoking its access is part of stopping — abandoned tools do not keep live connections here.
It is already severed — and a periodic walk through each account’s connected-apps list would have caught it regardless.

items.q: A collaborator asks for a copy of the workflow you built. Your API keys are embedded in it. What do you hand over?
items.layman: Shared automations and configuration files often carry live credentials — “API keys,” password-like strings granting your access — inside them. Sharing safely means stripping the secrets so the recipient supplies their own, or issuing them a separate credential you can later cancel without touching yours.

opts.t: The file as-is. If my key is in there — well, we are collaborators.
The file, plus a request to “keep it private.” The key ships inside.
A stripped copy — my keys come out, placeholders go in, and they connect their own accounts.
A stripped copy — and if they truly need my system, they get their own credential, scoped to the task and revocable without touching mine.

items.q: You are about to paste a client’s financials into an AI chat to speed up the analysis. What happens between copy and paste?
items.layman: What you paste into an AI tool leaves your custody and lands under that tool’s terms — possibly retained, possibly reviewed by humans, possibly used for training. Data minimization means sharing only what the task needs: names stripped, identifiers redacted, confidential material reserved for tools whose terms permit it.

opts.t: Paste. It is a chat box, not a filing cabinet — it never occurred to me the data goes anywhere.
A pause, a shrug, paste — I know it is someone else’s data on someone else’s server, and the deadline wins.
The numbers get stripped of names and identifiers first, and confidential material only enters tools whose terms I have actually read.
The same — and the rule predates the deadline: my written tool notes say which services may see client material at all, so the decision was made on a calm day.

items.q: Everyone says they have backups. When did you last restore from yours — not check that files exist, but actually rebuild something and work from the result?
items.layman: A backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a system. A “restore drill” means deliberately recovering files — or a whole machine — from backup on a calm day, to prove the copy is complete and the steps work before a disaster grades them.

opts.t: Never — and I am quietly unsure the backups are even running.
Never restored. The backups run; I have watched the progress bar and called it confidence.
Recently — I have done a real restore and worked from the result, so I know the copy is whole and the steps are true.
On a schedule — restore drills are calendared and logged, and the last one caught a folder that had silently dropped out of the routine.

items.q: Your agent worked unattended overnight — files touched, messages sent, records changed. This morning, how do you know what it actually did?
items.layman: An “agent” is an AI doing multi-step work with real access. An “audit trail” is a log the agent cannot avoid writing: every file opened, message sent, record changed — timestamped, kept outside the agent’s reach, reviewable. Without one, your knowledge of the night is whatever the agent chooses to report.

opts.t: I do not, beyond what looks different. The night is a black box.
It writes me a summary of what it did — which I trust, because there is nothing to check it against.
The trail — every action lands in a log the agent does not control, and I review the log, not the summary.
The trail, triaged — sensitive actions surface to me automatically, the rest gets sampled on a schedule, and the log has already contradicted a summary once.

items.q: Those exports you faithfully download each month — have you ever opened one in a different tool and confirmed your working life is actually in there?
items.layman: An “export” — the downloadable copy of your data — can be hollow: truncated history, dead links to attachments that never came along, structures only the original tool can parse. Testing an export means loading it somewhere else and checking the substance arrived. Until then, exit is a theory.

opts.t: There are no exports to open.
Never opened one. The download completing is the whole verification.
Yes — I have loaded a sample into another tool and checked that the substance made the trip: history, attachments, structure.
Yes, on a rhythm — a trial load into a second tool is part of the routine, and it once exposed an export that had been silently dropping attachments for months.

items.q: One of your agents tries to open a folder outside its granted scope. The attempt fails — nothing sensitive was reached. Do you ever hear about it?
items.layman: “Scope” means the boundaries you set on what a tool or agent can reach. Failed attempts at the boundary are the early signal — a bug, a hijacked instruction, a misconfiguration — visible before any damage. A boundary that blocks silently protects you; one that blocks and reports teaches you.

opts.t: There are no scopes for it to bump against — the attempt would not have been denied in the first place.
No. The boundary held, presumably, and that is where the story ends.
Yes — denials are logged and I read them, because an agent probing its boundary is news whether or not it got through.
Yes, promptly — boundary violations raise an alert the day they happen, and one such alert has already exposed a misbehaving workflow before it cost anything.

items.q: You realize an API key has been sitting in a file you shared publicly three weeks ago. What happens in the next hour?
items.layman: An “API key” is a password-like credential; leaked, it means someone may have been acting as you. The response has two halves: revoke the credential and issue a fresh one (“rotation”), and establish the blast radius — what the key could reach, and whether the access logs show it was actually used.

opts.t: Panic, mostly — I am not sure how to revoke it, and there is no way to know if anyone used it.
Revoke it, eventually, after working out what breaks — and then live with never knowing whether it was used.
Revoke and reissue within the hour; the key was scoped, so I can state the worst case, and the access logs tell me whether it was exercised.
Minutes — rotation is a practiced procedure, the logs are already watched for unfamiliar use, and scoped keys meant the worst case was bounded before the leak ever happened.

items.q: A document your agent is summarizing contains hidden text: instructions telling it to forward your files to an outside address. What stands between that sentence and your data?
items.layman: “Prompt injection” means malicious instructions planted inside content an AI reads, hoping the AI obeys the document instead of you. The defense is structural, not hopeful: the agent should not hold the power to send data out in the first place, and sensitive actions should require a human yes — and leave a log either way.

opts.t: Whatever the model happens to do. The agent could send files if asked — I had just never pictured the asking coming from a document.
The model’s own judgment — I am relying on it noticing the trick, because nothing structural stops the send.
Structure — the agent cannot reach outside addresses, anything resembling send-data-elsewhere is gated behind my explicit approval, and the attempt itself would land in the log.
Structure, plus evidence — outbound actions are gated and logged, and I have fed my own setup a poisoned document on purpose, to watch the gate hold.

items.q: It is the first Monday of the quarter. Does anything in your calendar force the question: who and what can still reach my systems, and should they?
items.layman: Access rots upward: grants outlive the tasks, tools, and collaborators that justified them. A scheduled access review is a recurring, calendared walk through every live permission — human and software — revoking whatever no longer earns its place. Unscheduled means unmanaged.

opts.t: No. Access is granted at need and reviewed never.
No calendar entry — reviews happen when something spooks me, which averages about once a year.
Yes — a recurring review, walked against my written map of grants, and every walk ends with the stale ones revoked.
Yes, and it leaves a record — what was checked, what was cut — and the interval itself is tuned by how much the last few reviews found.

items.q: A subcontractor’s engagement ended Friday. It is Monday. What can they still open?
items.layman: Offboarding a person means finding every grant they accumulated — folders, tools, shared credentials — revoking each one, and verifying against a record rather than against memory. Whatever you miss, they keep: silently, indefinitely.

opts.t: Honestly? Probably everything they could open on Thursday.
The big things are cut — the folder, the main tool — and memory assures me there was nothing else.
Nothing — every grant was listed when it was made, so revocation was a checklist walked against a record, not a memory exercise.
Nothing, verifiably — the revocations are logged, and a sweep of account activity afterward confirmed no lingering grant survived the walk.

items.q: Your backups stopped working two months ago — the copies are stale, the failure was silent. What tells you, and when?
items.layman: Backup routines fail quietly: a full disk, an expired credential, a renamed folder. The dangerous state is not “no backups” — it is “believed backups.” Detection means something checks that fresh, complete copies actually landed, and complains when they do not.

opts.t: The disaster tells me — I would discover the stale copies at the exact moment I needed them.
Chance tells me — I would notice eventually, poking around for some unrelated reason.
A check tells me — on a schedule, I verify that recent copies actually landed and look complete, so a silent failure has a short lifespan.
The failure announces itself — a missing or undersized backup raises an alert within a day, and that alert has already caught a real failure once.

items.q: An agent confidently cites a “fact” about your best client — one you have no memory of recording. Can you trace where that entry came from?
items.layman: “Provenance” means a record attached to each memory entry stating its origin: which conversation, which document, which agent wrote it, and when. “Quarantined” means set aside and not acted on until verified. Without provenance you cannot distinguish an entry you would endorse from one that drifted in — you can only believe the memory, or not.

opts.t: No — the memory lives inside a vendor’s product, and it does not say where entries come from. I would be asking the black box about itself.
Sort of — I could search old chats hoping to find the moment, but nothing links the entry to its source.
Yes — every entry carries its origin: source, author, timestamp. I would read the record and know within a minute whether to keep or cut it.
Yes, and the trace has been exercised — suspect entries have been run to ground before, and anything lacking a valid origin is quarantined by rule, not by my noticing.

items.q: Every cloud account you have is frozen for seventy-two hours — a false fraud flag, nobody to call. What still runs, and from what?
items.layman: This probes custody: whether your system’s essential substance — memory, data, configurations, keys — exists under your direct control, or only as a reflection inside accounts someone else can freeze. Sovereignty is measured in what survives the lockout.

opts.t: Nothing runs. Everything essential is a login I no longer have.
Fragments — scattered local copies of uncertain age. I would limp, not run.
The core holds — memory, data, and configuration live in open files under my custody; the clouds are conveniences wrapped around a substrate I hold.
It has been proven — I have run the essential system from local custody deliberately, so the seventy-two hours would be an inconvenience with a known shape.

items.q: Open your system’s long-term memory right now — no tools, no vendor, just you and the raw store. What do you see?
items.layman: A system’s memory can be a readable artifact — plain files in open formats a human can inspect — or an opaque blob only one vendor’s software can render. The difference decides whether the memory is truly yours: you can only audit, correct, and carry what you can read.

opts.t: Nothing to open. The memory exists behind a login, in whatever form the vendor keeps it.
A database dump I once pulled — technically mine, practically unreadable without the product wrapped around it.
Readable files: entries in an open format, organized, plain enough to audit with my own eyes and any text tool.
Readable files that others have read — a second tool and a second person have each navigated the store without me, which is what convinced me it is genuinely open.

items.q: A buggy agent spends an hour writing garbage into your system’s shared memory. What limits the damage, and what undoes it?
items.layman: When many processes write to one memory, a single defect can silently overwrite years of accumulated knowledge. Write governance means writes are constrained — agents may add but not destroy — recorded, so every change has an author, and reversible, because the store keeps its own history and can be rolled back to any earlier state.

opts.t: Nothing and nothing — writes land destructively in a store I cannot inspect, so the garbage simply becomes the memory.
Luck limits it; undoing it means manually hunting for what changed, with no record of what did.
Writes cannot destroy — the store keeps full history, every change has an author, and rolling back that hour is an operation, not an archaeology.
That hour has effectively happened before — a bad write was caught by the checks, traced to its author, and rolled back cleanly. The design has been paid for and proven.

items.q: Count the places your secrets live — every key, token, and credential your system runs on. Is the answer “one vault” or “I’d have to look”?
items.layman: “Secrets” are the credentials that grant your system its powers: API keys, tokens, passwords. To “rotate” one is to replace it so the old stops working. Sovereign custody means one encrypted vault under your control that issues secrets to each consumer (each tool or agent that needs one) and records who holds what — versus secrets scattered across vendor dashboards and config files, unrotatable because unlocatable.

opts.t: I would have to look, and the looking would not finish — secrets are pasted wherever they were needed, some in places I have forgotten.
Two or three places, plus stragglers — a manager holds many, vendor dashboards hold the rest, and no record says which.
One vault — every credential is issued from it, the record shows which consumer holds what, and rotating any single one is routine.
One vault, exercised — a full rotation has actually been performed with everything kept running, and the vault’s record matched reality when audited.

items.q: Your provider’s trust page says: “Your data is encrypted, isolated, and never used for training.” Which of those claims can you verify without taking their word?
items.layman: Vendor assurances are promises, not proofs. Independent verifiability means the architecture lets you check: you hold the encryption keys yourself, you keep your own copies or “hashes” — short fingerprints of data that change if the data changes — or what they hold is worthless without what stays with you. Whatever cannot be verified must be trusted, and trust is not custody.

opts.t: None — and worse, I could not leave if the claims proved false. The data has no existence outside their systems.
None — I have read the terms carefully, which is diligence, but everything past the login screen is faith.
The ones that matter — encryption under keys I hold, plus my own authoritative copies, mean their honesty is nice but not load-bearing.
Tested — the design assumed the vendor could lie, my copies and keys have been checked against theirs, and the claims I cannot verify cover data I never gave them.

items.q: A vendor in your stack quietly amends its terms: customer content may now feed model training. How much does your exposure change?
items.layman: Policy changes reprice whatever a vendor holds. If your substrate — memory, documents, accumulated knowledge — sits in their systems in readable form, your exposure moves whenever their lawyers do. Architecture can make the answer “almost nothing”: they only ever held encrypted or “ephemeral” slices — data passing through for a moment, never stored.

opts.t: Completely — they hold years of my working substance in the clear, and my options are consent or loss.
Substantially — I would begin an exodus I should have begun years ago, under deadline, on their schedule.
Barely — by design they hold ephemeral or encrypted slices; the substance lives with me, so their policy reprices almost nothing.
It has been rehearsed — a previous policy change was absorbed by cutting one integration in an afternoon, because every vendor’s blast radius was engineered small before it was needed.

items.q: Ten years from now, you need to open this year’s decision log. Every tool you currently use is dead. What are the odds it opens?
items.layman: Formats decide how long knowledge survives. Open, plain formats — text, standard structures — outlive companies; proprietary formats live exactly as long as the software that reads them. Longevity is a design choice made at write time, not at rescue time.

opts.t: Near zero — this year’s decisions live inside products, and dead products do not open.
A coin flip — some of it is in files, but in formats whose future depends on someone maintaining a converter.
Near certain — the log is plain text in open structures, chosen precisely so that nothing but a text reader ever needs to exist.
As certain as these things get — the archive has already outlived two generations of tools unconverted, which is the only durability test that counts.

items.q: Your access logs — the record of who touched what — live inside the same platform they monitor. If an intruder owned that platform for a day, what would the logs say?
items.layman: A record its own subject can edit is testimony, not evidence. Tamper-evident logging means the trail is written outward — copied as it happens to storage the monitored system cannot alter — or sealed with integrity checks so any edit is detectable. Who guards the guards is an architecture question.

opts.t: Whatever the intruder wanted them to say — the logs are just rows in the system they would own.
Probably the truth, resting on “probably” — nothing separates the record from the recorded.
The truth — logs stream outward as they are written, into custody the platform cannot reach, so erasing tracks there does not erase them everywhere.
The truth, provably — the outward trail is integrity-sealed, and I have compared it against the platform’s own account to confirm the two cannot quietly diverge.

items.q: Your newsletter has grown to four hundred subscribers, every address held inside the sending platform. Does that list exist anywhere else?
items.layman: The people who follow your work are data too — a list of addresses that lives, by default, only inside the tool that sends the emails. Keeping your own copy means downloading the list to your own files now and then, so the audience is yours and not merely the platform’s.

opts.t: No. The platform is the list — the thought had not occurred.
There is an old copy from some earlier moment — a year stale, maybe more.
Yes — I download the list to my own files every so often, deliberately.
Yes — downloading it is a standing habit, and I could tell you without looking how fresh my copy is.

items.q: You spent a season recording your course — hours of video, now uploaded and live. Where are the original files this morning?
items.layman: When you upload a video, the platform keeps a copy for streaming — often compressed, sometimes hard to get back out. The originals are the master files — the full-quality recordings — on your own machine or drive. Do they still exist under your control, or did the upload become the only copy?

opts.t: Wherever uploading left them — deleted for space, probably. The platform has the course now.
Scattered — some originals survive in a downloads folder, some went wherever old files go.
On my own drive, one folder per lesson — the platform streams copies; I keep the masters.
On my drive and on a second copy besides — keeping masters of anything I publish is simply how publishing works here.

items.q: The calendar that runs your family’s logistics — school runs, appointments, trips — lives in your personal account. What happens when your partner needs to change something?
items.layman: Shared lives often run on data owned by one person: a calendar, a contact list, an address book sitting inside a single personal account. The basic move is shared custody — a calendar both adults can open and edit from their own accounts, rather than one person relaying changes through the other.

opts.t: They ask me, and I make the change — the calendar is mine, viewed over my shoulder.
They can see it, mostly — I shared a view once, though editing still routes through me.
They open it and change it — the family calendar is shared property, editable from both accounts.
Shared and editable both ways, and that is the pattern — whatever the household runs on, each adult can reach from their own account.

items.q: A subcontractor starts Monday and needs to get into your project tool. What do you actually hand them?
items.layman: The quick move is to share your own username and password so a helper can work as you. The deliberate move is separate access — their own login, added to just what they need — so what they do is done as them, and parting ways later never means changing your own passwords.

opts.t: My username and password, pasted into the chat — it is the fastest way in.
My login, but spoken aloud rather than written down, which feels slightly better.
Their own login — I add them as a separate user with access to the project.
Their own login, always — nobody works as me, and removing someone never touches my own credentials.

items.q: A source you rely on — a long article you have cited twice — has vanished from the web. What remains of it on your side?
items.layman: Web pages disappear: sites die, links break, pieces get taken down. Research kept as a list of links thins every year. Keeping copies means saving the page itself — a file in your own storage — at the moment you decide a source matters, so its survival stops depending on someone else’s website.

opts.t: A dead link in my notes. The source is gone, along with whatever I did not quote.
The quotes I happened to pull out at the time — the rest of the argument is lost.
The whole piece — sources that matter get saved into my own files when I first use them.
The whole piece, like every source I lean on — saving a copy is part of citing, not a separate chore.

items.q: The design files for the small hardware product you sell — the models, the cut layouts — live on the memory card in the workshop machine. Is that the only place?
items.layman: A physical product often depends on a handful of digital files: the design, the settings, the layout the machine reads. A memory card in a machine is one small, losable object. The basic question is whether those files also live somewhere deliberate — a folder on your computer, with a further copy elsewhere.

opts.t: That card is the product. If it corrupts or walks off, I redraw everything from memory.
Versions of the files exist on my laptop somewhere — older than what the card holds, I suspect.
The card carries copies — the real files live in a folder on my machine, and the card gets refreshed from it.
The folder is the source, and it is copied onward too — a dead card costs me ten minutes and a re-copy.

items.q: The tablet that takes payments at your stall has been suggesting a software update since spring. It is now autumn. What is your relationship with that notification?
items.layman: Updates are unglamorous security: many exist to close holes that let strangers into a device. A machine that handles money and customer cards, left without updates for seasons, is a door ajar. The basic habit is applying updates within days, on a quiet evening — not never.

opts.t: We have an understanding — it suggests, I dismiss. It has been months, maybe longer.
I update when something breaks or nags hard enough — so, a few times a year, under protest.
Updates get applied within a week or so, deliberately, on a quiet evening — this one included.
Already applied — anything that touches money or customers gets updated promptly as a rule, and I could tell you each device’s state.

items.q: After your workshop, an attendee hands you a USB stick — “my notes for you, have a look tonight.” What happens to that stick?
items.layman: A gifted or found USB stick is a classic way for hostile software to reach a machine: plugging it in can be enough. The careful basics: unknown media never goes into the computer that holds your working life — ask for the files through a channel that scans them, or open the stick only on a device that holds nothing important.

opts.t: Into the laptop it goes that evening — it would be rude not to look.
Into the laptop eventually, with a vague unease I do not act on.
Not into my main machine — I ask them to email the files instead, or open the stick on a machine that holds nothing.
The same, as a settled rule — unknown media never touches the computer my work lives on, however friendly the source.

items.q: Every supplier invoice and signed form your little business generates ends its life in a box under the counter. What is your plan for the box?
items.layman: Paper is a storage format with no copies: one flood, one fire, one move, and the records are gone. The basic countermeasure is duplication — photographing or scanning what matters into your own files as it arrives, so the box becomes a convenience rather than the only copy.

opts.t: The box is the plan. If something happened to it, the records would simply be gone.
The critical few get photographed when I think of it — the rest live and die as paper.
Paper that matters gets scanned to a folder as it comes in — the box holds duplicates, effectively.
Everything is scanned on arrival, named so I can find it, and the habit has held for years — the box could burn.

items.q: You are selling your old laptop this weekend. Between now and the handover, what happens to what is on it?
items.layman: A sold or donated machine carries your files, saved logins, and signed-in sessions unless they are deliberately removed. “Wiping” means erasing the machine back to its factory state, so the next owner starts blank. Dragging files to the trash is not wiping — much of that can be recovered.

opts.t: I drag my stuff to the trash, empty it, and hand the machine over.
I sign out of what I remember and delete the obvious folders — the rest I assume is fine.
A proper wipe — the machine is erased to factory state before it leaves the house.
Wipe, after confirming the few things only it held are safely copied — the same routine every device gets on its way out.

items.q: Three volunteers help run your community space. A member complains that “an admin” removed their post. Can you say, from a written record, what each volunteer’s account can actually do?
items.layman: Community platforms hand out powers by role: removing posts, banning members, changing settings, seeing email addresses. A roster is a written record — which person, which role, which powers, granted when — so the question is answered from a page rather than from a feeling.

opts.t: No — I set the roles up long ago and could not say now who can do what.
Roughly, from memory — I would have to open the settings and reverse-engineer the rest.
Yes — a written roster lists each volunteer, their role, and what that role permits.
Yes — and the roster carries dates and reasons, and gets corrected whenever a role changes, so it has stayed true to reality.

items.q: Your paid course is forty videos, a workbook, three spreadsheets, and a quiz. If you had to gather the master files for all of it, is there a page that says where each piece lives?
items.layman: A digital product is really a set of files scattered across folders, drives, and tools. A manifest is a written list of every piece — each video, document, and asset — with where its master copy (the original file) lives. Without one, the product exists only as the assembled surface students see.

opts.t: No page. Gathering the masters would be a week of searching and some quiet losses.
A partial list from launch week, never touched since — it names most of the videos, at least.
Yes — a manifest lists every asset and where its master lives, kept alongside the course itself.
Yes — the manifest is versioned, each course revision notes what changed, and I once regathered everything from it as a test.

items.q: Your hardware side product ships in small batches. Somewhere between your head, your machine, and your suppliers lives the knowledge of how to make one. How much of it is written down?
items.layman: A physical product rests on records: design files, machine settings, the parts list, which supplier sells the odd component. A build record gathers these into one written document — versions included — so the next batch starts from a page, not from recollection.

opts.t: Almost none — the product is a performance I give from memory each batch.
Fragments — a parts list in one note, some settings in another, the rest in my hands.
A build record: design files named and versioned, settings, parts, suppliers — one document, followed each batch.
That record, plus its history — each batch’s deviations get written back in, and the last batch was run from the document alone, deliberately, to prove it complete.

items.q: While you are unreachable for a week, your partner has to file the insurance claim for the leaking roof. What do they work from?
items.layman: Households run on scattered records: policy numbers, account logins, the broker’s name, the folder with the photos of the roof. A written household record — one findable page saying where these things live — lets another adult act without you narrating from a distance.

opts.t: From whatever they can find — realistically, the claim waits for my return.
From memory of things I have mentioned, plus some hunting through my email.
From a written page we both know the location of — policies, accounts, key contacts, where documents live.
From that page — which each of us has used in earnest at least once, and which gets corrected whenever it sends either of us somewhere stale.

items.q: Your open-source project is more than its code — a website, a package listing, a build service, a handful of accounts. Could you produce the full list of what the project depends on?
items.layman: Projects accumulate infrastructure: the site host, the name registration, the service that runs the tests, the registry that distributes releases. An inventory is a written list of every such account — what it is, what it does, how it is reached. Without one, parts of the project exist only as forgotten logins.

opts.t: No — I would rediscover the accounts as things broke, one outage at a time.
Most of it from memory, with a nagging sense of a service or two I would miss.
Yes — a written inventory names each account, what it does for the project, and where access lives.
Yes — dated and kept current, and the last time I walked it, it disagreed with reality in one place, which is exactly what walking it is for.

items.q: A promising paper crosses your desk on a busy morning. Where does it go — and is “where it goes” a rule you could recite, or a fresh decision every time?
items.layman: A research practice generates a stream of incoming material: papers, clippings, links, scans. A written intake routine says what happens to each — where it is filed, how it is named, what note gets made — so the archive builds itself the same way every time instead of by mood.

opts.t: Wherever it lands — downloads, open tabs, a pile. Future-me is the filing system.
One of a few usual places, chosen by feel — findable later, with effort and luck.
A recited rule: saved to the archive, named by the convention, source noted — the same written steps each time.
That rule, versioned — it has been revised twice as the archive taught me what future-me actually needs, and the revisions are dated.

items.q: Just before midnight, a subcontractor delivers the finished work — half attached to an email, half in a chat thread. Where is all of it by Friday, and what says so?
items.layman: Incoming work product arrives through whatever channel is nearest — email, chat, shared links. Without a written rule for where deliverables land, finished work stays scattered across inboxes indefinitely. An intake rule names the destination and the steps: collect from channels, file, confirm receipt.

opts.t: Still in the email and the chat thread — that is where it lives now, indefinitely.
Moved somewhere sensible if I get to it — each delivery improvises its own filing.
In the project’s folder under my control — the written intake rule says collect, file, confirm, and it was followed.
Filed per the rule — and the rule itself carries a date and a history, having been tightened after a deliverable once went missing in a thread.

items.q: Friday afternoon at your shop: a week of paper — receipts, signed forms, a supplier note — sits by the register. Describe, step by step, what happens to that pile?
items.layman: Businesses that live partly on paper need a bridge into their records: a routine that says when the paper gets scanned or photographed, where the images land, and how they are named. Stated steps on a stated day — or a pile that simply grows.

opts.t: It grows. There is no step two.
Some Fridays I photograph the important-looking ones into my phone, which becomes its own kind of pile.
Scan the pile, file by month and type, mark the paper as done — written steps, walked every Friday.
Those steps — and the routine sheet records its own amendments, like the day refunds earned a folder of their own after a scramble.

items.q: The client asks which of the five files named some variant of “final” is the one they actually approved. How do you answer?
items.layman: Files multiply: final, final-2, final-CLEAN. A versioning convention is a written rule that makes one copy authoritative — how files are named, where the approved version lives, what marks it as approved — so “which is the real one?” has an answer that is not archaeology.

opts.t: By opening all five and reconstructing history from their differences.
By date-modified and gut feel, delivered with cautious confidence.
By rule: the approved copy lives in one place, named by the written convention, and nothing else claims that name.
By rule — and the rule carries a dated history of its own amendments, since it was tightened the last time an ambiguity slipped through.

items.q: A renewal notice arrives for a web address you only half-remember buying. How many do you own, held where, expiring when?
items.layman: Web addresses (domains) are rented, not owned outright: miss a renewal and the name can be taken by someone else — along with any email or website that hangs off it. An inventory is a written list of every domain, which company holds it, and its renewal date.

opts.t: Unknown, unknown, and unknown — this notice is how I find out about them.
I could name most of them; the where and the when would take an afternoon of logins.
It is written down: every domain, its registrar — the company holding it — and its renewal date, in one list.
Written and walked — the list gets reviewed yearly, and one walk caught an address quietly set to renew against a card that no longer existed.

items.q: You are adding a helper bot to your community server — it will post a weekly digest. The invite screen offers it the administrator role. What role does it end up with?
items.layman: A “bot” is a software helper added to a community platform. Invites grant it a role, and roles carry powers: posting is one thing; banning members, deleting channels, and reading private messages are others. “Administrator” means all of them at once. The deliberate move is a role holding only what the job needs.

opts.t: Administrator — that is what the invite suggested, and the digest does get posted.
Administrator, with a mental note that it is too much, filed under later.
A role that can post in one channel — the digest needs nothing else, so nothing else was granted.
The posting role — and the grant sits on my written map of what can reach the community, which gets reread as bots come and go.

items.q: The answer-bot for your course promises better replies if you feed it everything — student emails, purchase records, progress data. What does it actually get?
items.layman: Tools that answer questions on your behalf often ask for a standing feed of data to draw on. Everything is the convenient option; the deliberate one is a curated slice — course content and past questions with names removed — because the job does not need students’ personal details, and that data is theirs, not yours.

opts.t: Everything — the connect-all button, because better replies are the point.
Everything, after a pause — the students’ data went in with the rest, and I try not to dwell on it.
Course content and past questions with names stripped — the slice the job needs, decided before connecting.
The curated slice — and a note records what was withheld and why, because feeds of other people’s data get re-decided on a schedule, not once.

items.q: A fulfillment service will pack and ship your orders once it connects to your store. The connection request lists what it wants to reach. What happens with that list?
items.layman: Store connections work through granted access, and the request states the reach: orders and shipping addresses, or also customer payment details, pricing, and the power to edit products. Fulfillment — packing and shipping — needs to read orders and write tracking numbers; anything beyond that deserves an argument for itself.

opts.t: Approved on sight — packing and shipping is the goal, and the list stood in the way.
Skimmed, winced at, approved — it reaches more than shipping needs, which I noticed and accepted.
Read against the job — it gets orders and tracking, and when it asked for more, I went looking for a narrower grant.
Read, narrowed, and dated — the grant carries a note of why it reads what it reads, and the store’s connections get rewalked whenever the setup changes.

items.q: In one enthusiastic evening last month, you gave an assistant app your whole mailbox and calendar so it could manage family logistics. It works well. What happens now?
items.layman: An “assistant app” here is an AI helper handling scheduling and reminders. Grants made in enthusiasm tend to be broad — a whole mailbox rather than the school-and-family slice the job needs. Working well is not the same as scoped well — “scoped” meaning limited to a deliberate slice — and the deliberate move is going back to narrow it.

opts.t: Nothing happens now — it works, the grant stands, the evening is forgotten.
A twinge when I think of it, which is rarely — the breadth stays, because narrowing is friction.
I went back — it now reads the family calendar and a school-mail folder, not the whole mailbox.
Narrowed — and the episode changed the pattern: new helpers start narrow here, and standing grants get reread on a rhythm so enthusiasm cannot compound.

items.q: A contributor has earned deeper involvement in your open-source project. The platform’s dropdown offers several levels of access. Which one do they get?
items.layman: Project platforms grade access into levels: some let a person merge code, higher ones change settings, delete the project, or publish releases in its name. Granting deliberately means matching the level to what the person actually does — not handing over the top level as a gesture of trust.

opts.t: The top level — they have earned it, and distinctions between levels feel bureaucratic.
Something high, chosen quickly from the dropdown without reading what it includes.
The level that lets them merge in their area — settings, releases, and deletion stay with me.
The matched level, recorded with a date — and the project’s access list gets rewalked when involvement changes, in either direction.

items.q: A read-later tool wants to save clippings straight into your notes vault — the same vault holding a decade of your thinking. Where exactly may it write?
items.layman: A “vault” is your collected notes — the files a decade of thinking lives in. Tools that write into your systems have a write scope: everywhere, or one designated inbox folder. A tool that can write anywhere can also overwrite; one confined to an inbox can only add, and its additions are easy to review.

opts.t: Anywhere — it asked for the vault, and the vault is what it got.
Anywhere, technically — I assume it behaves and only ever adds new notes.
One inbox folder — it adds clippings there, and nothing outside that folder is writable to it.
The inbox only, like every writing tool here — outside things add to a doorstep I review, and the vault’s interior stays mine alone to edit.

items.q: You run three clients’ accounts — their ads, their sites, their inboxes — from the same laptop where you run your life. How separated are those worlds?
items.layman: Holding clients’ access alongside your own invites mingling: a session left open, a file saved to the wrong drive, the wrong account one tab away. Compartmentalizing means each client’s access lives in its own walled space — a separate browser profile (a walled-off browser identity with its own logins) and separate storage — deliberately apart from your personal accounts and files.

opts.t: One browser, one desktop, everything signed in at once — separation is a matter of attention.
Loose folders and a habit of checking which account I am in before acting — usually.
Walled — each client gets its own browser profile and storage area, so a wrong-window mistake has nowhere to land.
Walled by default, and written — the separation scheme is documented per client, and taking on a client now begins with building their compartment.

items.q: A designer joins for exactly one week to refresh your brand assets. The folder access you grant on Monday — when does it end?
items.layman: Access granted for short engagements tends to outlive them: the week ends, the grant stays. Granting with an expiry — an end date set at the moment of granting, or a dated reminder that forces the question — means the access dies with the engagement instead of quietly surviving it.

opts.t: It does not — grants here end when something makes me think of them, which nothing does.
In principle when the week ends; in practice whenever I next stumble across it.
Friday — the grant got an end date when it was made, or failing that, a dated reminder to cut it.
Friday, by expiry set at grant time — short access here is born with an end date, and my list of grants shows none outliving its reason.

items.q: Your writing app announces a new assistant that “reads your whole library to personalize suggestions.” It is on by default. What is your move?
items.layman: Tools you already trust sometimes expand their own reach through feature updates — a new capability that reads more of your data than the tool previously touched, switched on without asking. The deliberate move is treating the update like a fresh access request: read what it now reaches, decide, and limit it or turn it off accordingly.

opts.t: None — I did not register the announcement, so the assistant reads what it reads.
A raised eyebrow and nothing else — it is on, it is convenient, the library is probably fine.
I treated it as a fresh access request — read what it touches, then limited it to one project folder or turned it off.
Limited on arrival — updates that widen a tool’s reach get the same review as new tools, which is why release notes are, for me, security reading.

items.q: The connector service that glues your tools together holds live links into your mail, storage, calendar, and store. Tallied together, do you know what that one service can reach?
items.layman: A connector service — a hub that passes data between your tools — accumulates access one convenient link at a time. Each link seemed small; the hub’s total reach is their sum: one account that, compromised or misbehaving, touches everything at once. Knowing the sum is the point.

opts.t: No — each link was added in a moment of need, and no moment ever asked for the total.
Approximately — mail and storage for sure, plus an uneasy et cetera.
Yes — the hub’s links are listed in one place and read as a whole, and links that no longer earn their reach get cut.
Yes — the tally lives on my written map with each link’s reason, and the hub draws the strictest scheduled review precisely because it is the sum of everything else.

items.q: A follower messages you: an hour ago, your account posted a link that looks nothing like you. How does the next hour go?
items.layman: A hijacked audience account spends your credibility until you take it back. What matters is machinery, not composure: sign-in alerts that would have told you before a follower did, and a practiced lockdown — end all active sessions (signed-in devices), change the password, revoke (disconnect) linked apps, post a notice — executed rather than improvised.

opts.t: Badly — I would be discovering the password-reset flow live, unsure what else the intruder reached.
Password change first, then improvisation — no alerts existed, so the follower was my detection system.
Contained — sign-in alerts had already fired before the message, and the lockdown steps are ones I know cold: sessions ended, password changed, linked apps revoked.
Contained fast — alerts fire on new sign-ins, the lockdown is a drilled sequence, and a past rehearsal caught a forgotten linked app that would have survived the real thing.

items.q: Your course platform swears each student sees only their own account. When did you last check that claim yourself — from the outside, as a student?
items.layman: Platforms enforce boundaries between customers — in theory. Verifying means testing from outside your admin view: a real test-student account, walked into the fences to see what a student can actually reach — other students’ details, unpublished lessons, your admin pages. Trust the claim, or hold the evidence.

opts.t: Never — the setting exists, so the boundary presumably does.
Once, at launch, by glancing at the student view through my admin preview — not quite the same thing.
Recently — I keep a real test-student login and have walked it into the fences: other students’ data, unpublished content, my admin pages. It sees only what it should.
On a schedule — the test-student walk is calendared and logged, and it once caught a settings change that had quietly exposed the full member list.

items.q: Your partner holds emergency access to your password vault — the break-glass arrangement for the day you cannot be asked. Has it ever been through a live test?
items.layman: A “vault” is the app holding your passwords; “break-glass” access is a pre-arranged way for a trusted person to get in during an emergency. Like backups, such arrangements fail quietly — expired invitations, forgotten master passwords, steps that only worked on the setup screen. A drill means the partner actually performs the access, calmly, before it is ever needed.

opts.t: There is no arrangement — the vault’s contents are reachable by me alone.
The arrangement exists on paper — set up once, never touched, hopefully still valid.
Yes — we ran the access once for real: they got in, found the critical entries, and we fixed what confused them.
Yes, on a rhythm — the drill recurs yearly and gets noted when done, and the last one surfaced an expired recovery email that would have sunk the real event.

items.q: Deep in your seller account, someone changes the bank details your marketplace pays out to. What happens in the minutes after that click?
items.layman: Payout details are where the money leaves the platform toward you — a favorite target of intruders. “Gated” means the change is blocked until a second confirmation (a code to your phone) is supplied; “loud” means it raises an immediate notification through a channel an intruder cannot silence. Gated and loud, the wrong change surfaces in minutes — not at month-end when a payout goes missing.

opts.t: Nothing — the change would sit until a payout failed to arrive and I went looking.
An email, probably, into the folder where marketplace mail goes to be skimmed on weekends.
A confirmation code the intruder does not have, and an alert to my phone — the change is gated and loud by design, and I have confirmed those settings are on.
Gated, loud, and rehearsed — I once made a test change to watch the alert land, and payout alerts route somewhere no mail filter can bury them.

items.q: Saturday morning, twenty minutes before the market opens — and the tablet running your till will not turn on. What kind of morning is it?
items.layman: Small businesses concentrate operations into one device: sales, prices, card payments. A tested fallback means the backup path — a spare device, a phone app, a paper routine with the price list — has actually been run for a real stretch of trading, so the primary dying is an inconvenience with a known shape rather than a closed stall.

opts.t: A closed stall, or cash-only guesswork — everything lived in that tablet.
A scramble around a theoretical backup — my phone has the app, though it has never taken a real payment.
A slower morning — the fallback exists and has carried real trading at least once, so I know it holds.
A rehearsed morning — one market day a season deliberately runs on the fallback, and the last such run exposed a stale price list before any real failure could.

items.q: Your notes vault syncs between three devices. If the sync quietly mangled files last Tuesday — duplicates, conflicts, a folder half-emptied — what would have told you by Friday?
items.layman: Sync is software, and it fails in soft ways: conflicted copies (the same note forked into two versions), silent overwrites, folders that stop syncing at all. Believed-in sync is like believed-in backups. Detection means something routinely checks the vault’s health — file counts, conflict markers, an integrity pass — and complains promptly when copies disagree.

opts.t: Nothing — I would find the damage weeks later, mid-search, and wonder how far it had spread.
Luck — I might notice a conflicted-copy filename during ordinary work, if one crossed my path.
A check — a periodic pass over the vault flags conflicts and odd file counts, so Tuesday’s damage surfaces within the week, bounded.
An alert — the integrity check runs on schedule and complains the same day, and it has already caught a conflicted copy that was quietly overwriting the canonical note behind my back.

items.q: An agency engagement ends amicably. Three weeks later, what of the client’s — files, credentials, connected access — still lives in your systems, and could you prove the answer?
items.layman: Exits have two sides: the access they revoke from you, and the copies you still hold of them. A verified wind-down works from the engagement’s access-and-data record: return or delete what was theirs, hand back credentials, disconnect what was linked — each step checked off and confirmable afterward, not assumed.

opts.t: Honestly, most of it — copies and logins linger wherever the work left them.
The obvious things are gone; the long tail of copies and grants is a matter of faith.
Nothing beyond what the contract says I keep — the wind-down ran from the engagement’s record, each return and deletion checked off.
Nothing, provably — the completed record went to the client, and a scheduled sweep of my own systems afterward confirmed no stray copy or live grant had escaped the walk.

items.q: The standing instructions your AI tools read — the files that steer their behavior — differ today from what you remember writing. What tells you what changed, and when, and by whom?
items.layman: Agents and assistants act on instruction files the way staff act on a handbook — which makes those files part of your substrate. Under change control, every edit is recorded: versions kept, differences viewable, author and date attached. Without it, the handbook can drift — or be tampered with — and your only record is memory.

opts.t: Nothing — the files are edited live, in place, and today’s version is the only version.
My memory of past edits, which is exactly the thing currently failing.
The history — instruction files are versioned like code here, so what changed, when, and from what is a lookup, not a reconstruction.
The history, watched — edits to steering files raise a notice for review, and one such notice has already flagged a change I did not recognize before it steered anything.

items.q: Pick the oldest credential in active service anywhere in your stack — every tool and service you run. When was it last replaced because a schedule said so, not because something went wrong?
items.layman: To “rotate” a credential — a password, key, or access token — is to replace it so the old one stops working. Rotation done only after incidents means every credential’s age equals your exposure window. Scheduled rotation replaces the important ones on a calendar — and proves in passing that you still know how.

opts.t: Never — credentials here are load-bearing antiques, replaced only by catastrophe.
Once or twice, after scares — the calendar has never demanded one.
Within the last cycle — credentials that matter carry rotation dates, and the calendar, not an incident, retires them.
On schedule, with a log of each rotation — and the drill pays twice: one rotation revealed a tool silently dependent on a key nobody had listed.

items.q: One of your agents can spend real money — ordering supplies, topping up ad budgets. What stands between it and an unusual thousand-dollar afternoon?
items.layman: An “agent” is an AI doing multi-step work with real access — here, to payment. Gating means hard limits set outside the agent’s reach: per-purchase caps, a monthly ceiling, human approval above a threshold. Verified means the spending lands in a log you actually read, and odd patterns raise an alert before the card statement would.

opts.t: Its own judgment — the payment method is connected, and the limits are whatever the model decides is sensible.
A cap written into the agent’s instructions — which is to say, a request, not a wall.
Walls it cannot move — caps live at the card and account level, purchases above a threshold wait for my yes, and every spend lands in a log I review.
Walls, plus tripwires — spending anomalies alert me the same day, the caps get tested deliberately now and then, and one alert has already caught a runaway retry before it compounded.

items.q: After a long vote, your community decides to move platforms. Its accumulated substance — years of guides, threads, member knowledge — is the reason people stay. How much of it makes the move?
items.layman: A community’s real asset is its accumulated knowledge, and platforms hold it by default in forms only they can render. Sovereign stewardship keeps the archive in open formats — readable by any software — under custody you or the community control, so the platform is a venue, and changing venues moves the memory too.

opts.t: Almost none — the archive is the platform’s shape, and leaving means starting over with a link to the old place.
Fragments — whatever a scraping weekend rescues, in whatever form it comes out.
Substantially all of it — the archive has always lived in open formats under our own custody, with the platform as a display.
All of it, provenly — a section was migrated onto the new platform as a rehearsal before the vote, which is partly why the vote passed.

items.q: Five years from now you want to reissue this year’s course — new platform, new format, maybe print. Does the course exist anywhere as itself, apart from the platform it currently wears?
items.layman: A course built inside a platform — lessons as pages, quizzes as widgets, sequence as settings — exists as that platform’s configuration. A canonical form is the course as portable files under your custody: text, media, and structure in open formats any tool can read, from which any platform edition can be rebuilt.

opts.t: No — the course is the platform configuration. Reissuing would mean rebuilding from the student-facing surface.
Partly — the videos exist as files; the structure, quizzes, and sequencing live only inside the platform.
Yes — the canonical course is a set of open-format files under my custody, and the platform edition is a rendering of it.
Yes, exercised — the same canonical files have already produced a second edition on a different medium, which is what convinced me the structure truly lives with me.

items.q: A unit from your third production batch comes back with a fault. Can you reconstruct, from your own records, exactly what that batch was — the design revision, the settings, the parts — as it stood then?
items.layman: A shipped product is a snapshot of your files at a moment. “Provenance” here means each batch’s record — which design revision, which settings, which parts — kept with full history, so any past state can be reconstructed. Without it, old batches exist only as the objects themselves, and faults can only be guessed at.

opts.t: No — the files have been overwritten by later revisions; batch three survives only as the units out in the world.
Roughly — current files plus memory of what changed since, which blurs by the batch.
Yes — every batch is a dated, labeled snapshot in my archive: design revision, settings, parts list, all held with history.
Yes, and it has been done — an earlier fault was traced by rebuilding that batch’s exact state from the archive, down to the supplier lot.

items.q: Thirty years of family photographs sit in your archive. Digital files decay silently — a flipped bit here, an unreadable file there. When one of them rots, what notices?
items.layman: “Bit rot” is the slow corruption of stored files — copies going subtly bad while nobody opens them. A “checksum” is a short fingerprint computed from a file; recompute it later and any change shows. Sovereign custody of an irreplaceable archive pairs open formats and multiple copies with scheduled fingerprint checks, so decay is detected and repaired from a good copy — not discovered decades late.

opts.t: Nothing — the archive lives inside one photo service, in its formats, and its health is that company’s business, not mine.
Nothing — copies exist on my own drives, but nothing ever verifies them; rot would surface at some future opening.
A verification pass — the archive carries checksums, and a periodic check compares the copies and flags any file that has drifted.
The pass, proven — a scheduled check once caught a corrupted decade on one drive, and that decade was restored from the copy that still matched.

items.q: Someone claims a build of your library circulating online contains code you never wrote. Can anyone — without asking you — establish what you actually released?
items.layman: “Signing” a release means sealing it with a cryptographic key only you hold, producing a proof anyone can check: this exact file came from this key. A “mirror” is an independent server redistributing copies. With signed releases and a published key, authenticity is independently verifiable — the platform’s word, and yours, become unnecessary. Without it, what-you-released is testimony.

opts.t: No — my releases exist wherever the registry put them, distinguished from tampered copies by nothing but the registry’s say-so.
They could compare the suspect file against the registry’s copy — which proves only that two copies match, not what I released.
Yes — releases are signed with my key and the check is documented, so any third party can verify authorship without me.
Yes, and third parties do — a packager downstream verifies signatures as routine, and their check once flagged a mirror serving an altered file.

items.q: Strip away everything derived — the summaries, the indexes, the embeddings your tools have built. From what remains in your custody, could the whole apparatus be rebuilt?
items.layman: Systems accrue derived data: search indexes, generated summaries, “embeddings” (numeric fingerprints AI tools use to find related material). Sovereign design keeps the sources — the documents and records everything derives from — as the canonical layer (the authoritative originals), held in open formats under your custody, so derived layers stay disposable and rebuildable. Entangled design lets a derived store quietly become the only copy.

opts.t: No — much of what my tools know exists only as their internal state, and the sources it came from are partly gone or scattered.
Unevenly — some sources are held, but a few derived stores have quietly become primary, with nothing behind them.
Yes — sources are the canonical layer, held in open formats under my custody; everything derived is declared disposable and points back to them.
Yes, provenly — I have deleted and regenerated the entire derived layer from sources as an exercise, and the rebuilt system matched the old one where it mattered.

items.q: For each client whose systems you build and run, ask one structural question: if your relationship dissolved tomorrow, whose accounts would their property be sitting in?
items.layman: An agency-of-record builds things that must outlive the engagement. “Substrate” here means the underlying accounts and data a system runs on. Sovereign design keeps ownership with the client — their accounts hold the site, the data, the history — while you hold delegated, removable access. Entangled design accumulates client property inside your accounts, making every ending a hostage negotiation conducted politely.

opts.t: Mine — their sites, data, and history live in my accounts, and dissolution would mean a long, delicate extraction.
Mixed — some clients own their substrate; for others, pieces settled into my accounts and never moved out.
Theirs — ownership sits in client accounts by design, and what I hold is delegated access that can be revoked in an afternoon.
Theirs, and it has been proven — an engagement ended, my access was removed, and everything kept running untouched, which is the whole design stated as an event.

items.q: Your marketplace dashboard knows your sales history, your customers, your margins. Close the dashboard: what do your own records know?
items.layman: Selling through a marketplace, the platform’s dashboard becomes the memory of the business by default — held in its formats, on its terms. Sovereign custody means your own books: sales, customers, and costs recorded under your control in open formats, with the dashboard as one view rather than the source of truth. A “second consumer” is anyone or anything other than you that reads your records directly.

opts.t: Little — the dashboard is the books. My records are whatever it shows me while I am signed in.
A trail of ad-hoc downloads, gappy and differently shaped — a shadow of the dashboard, not an account of the business.
Everything material — sales, customers, and costs flow into my own open-format records on a rhythm, and my books, not the dashboard, are the reference.
Everything — and a second consumer proves it: my accountant works entirely from my records without touching the platform, and the year’s accounts have closed from them alone.

items.q: Count the independent disasters it would take to erase your system’s memory entirely — how many distinct places, companies, and failure modes stand between your archive and zero?
items.layman: Copies only protect you if they fail separately: two copies in one house share a fire; two services on one account share a lockout; three copies synced instantly share every deletion. Failure independence means copies split across different places, custodians, and mechanisms — including one that does not update instantly, so even a bad change cannot reach every copy at once.

opts.t: One — everything ultimately lives with a single provider under a single login, however many icons it wears.
Two, arguably — a local copy and a cloud copy, though one house fire or one synced deletion blurs the arithmetic.
Three or more, by design — copies split across places and custodians, one of them delayed so that even my own worst command cannot reach them all at once.
Enough, and measured — recovery from each surviving copy has been rehearsed in turn, so every layer of the arithmetic has actually been exercised.

items.q: Your family’s medical history is spread across three patient portals, two clinics’ filing rooms, and an insurer’s archive. Whose record is it, in practice?
items.layman: Health records are substrate you may need decades from now, held by institutions with their own lifespans and formats. Practical custody means maintaining your own consolidated copy — visits, results, prescriptions, immunizations — in open formats under your control, updated as care happens, so any new clinician can be handed the history whole.

opts.t: Theirs — each institution holds its fragment, and assembling the whole would mean months of requests, if it worked at all.
Mostly theirs — I hold a folder of whatever discharge papers and results happened to be handed over.
Ours — a consolidated copy lives under my custody in open formats, and each appointment’s records are added as they arrive.
Ours, and it has moved — a change of clinic was handled by handing over the record complete, and the new practice worked from it on day one.
